stories.title: Felix Auger-Aliassime advances with opening-round win at U.S. Open
stories.summary: Auger-Aliassime, the third-ranked man at the U.S. Open, won his first-round singles match on Monday night by defeating Australia's Rinky Hijiata 7-5, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Felix Auger-Aliassime is well aware that New York claims to be the city that never sleeps.

After starting late and then playing for three hours and 19 minutes — and enduring a 55-minute rain delay between the second and third set — the Montreal tennis star can relate to the lack of rest in The Big Apple.

Auger-Aliassime, the third-ranked man at the U.S. Open, won his first-round singles match on Monday night by defeating Australia’s Rinky Hijiata 7-5, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5.

“We’ve known each other since we were like 10 years old, but this is the first time we’ve played one another. He caused me a lot of problems out there … but most importantly I’m through to the next round,” said Auger-Aliassime after the match.

The Canadian finished with 17 aces, 48 winners and 11 double faults. He had 50 unforced errors. Auger-Aliassime won 18 of 22 service games, and six of 21 return games. He advances to play Russian Karen Khachanov, who beat Roman Burruchaga of Argentina in three straight sets.

Meanwhile, Denis Shapovalov of Richmond Hill, Ont., will play his second-round men’s singles match Wednesday against Luca Van Assche of France. Shapovalov defeated Miomir Kecmanovic of Serbia in four sets on Sunday, while Van Assche beat Britain’s Cameron Norrie, also in four sets.

Leylah Fernandez of Laval, Que., is scheduled to play her second-round women’s singles match Wednesday against Mananchaya Sawangkaew of Thailand. Fernandez bounced Shuai Zhang of China in straight sets on Sunday, while Sawangkaew defeated Panna Udvardy of Hungary in straight sets.

stories.title: BC Conservatives lose another MLA, seventh to leave party caucus since mid-August
stories.summary: Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA Á’a:liya Warbus cited a ‘critical breakdown in communications’ in decision to leave party
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The BC Conservative caucus lost another MLA on Monday, the seventh to leave the ranks of the province’s Official Opposition party since mid-August.

The exodus presents a growing challenge to party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay as the former Conservative MP runs in a by-election to win a seat in the provincial legislature.

Monday’s departure of Á’a:liya Warbus, the only Indigenous MLA on the party benches, is the latest domino to fall for the BC Conservatives. A succession of defections, senior staff departures and internal controversies has rocked the party since Ms. Findlay was elected leader in late May, throwing both her leadership and the Conservatives’ future into question.

The upheaval is also a boon to Premier David Eby ’s NDP, which won 47 seats to the Conservatives’ 44 in the 2024 election and could now benefit from a fractured opposition and divided centre-right.

Ms. Warbus, who represented the Chilliwack-Cultus Lake riding and served as the party’s house leader, joins Peter Milobar, Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman. All have left the caucus since Aug. 14 and now sit as independent MLAs.

Mr. Milobar and Mr. Paton last week announced their intention to form a new political party with Mr. Milobar as interim leader. They will be up against former BC Liberal cabinet minister Mike Bernier, who was named leader of the CentreBC party in July, in vying for the votes of those seeking a more centrist political home than Ms. Findlay’s Conservative Party.

The BC Conservatives did not respond to an interview request on Monday.

In announcing her decision, Ms. Warbus cited the party’s departure from core issues and a “critical breakdown in communication” under Ms. Findlay’s leadership, both with the public and internally, across MLAs and staff.

“Caucus members have learned of hirings, firings, critic appointments and leadership positions through any and all channels including social media before being informed by leadership,” Ms. Warbus said in a statement.

She also highlighted the inability of the caucus to discuss serious allegations that surfaced last week, which prompted the firing of operations director Apollo Chung after audio recordings circulated purportedly capturing a staffer discussing a fundraiser “so we can steal everything.”

Another recording allegedly captured Ms. Findlay telling caucus members that if an MLA gave up their seat to trigger a by-election, she “could give them a role as a senior adviser in the same portfolio.” Reann Gasper resigned as Abbotsford-Mission MLA on Aug. 22, giving Ms. Findlay a chance to run; she has since become the leader’s deputy chief of staff. It is a violation of the Criminal Code to offer a legislator an inducement to resign from office.

Neither Ms. Findlay nor the party have confirmed the authenticity of the recordings. Ms. Findlay announced Mr. Chung’s firing on Aug. 26 in a one-sentence statement, with no reason given. In a post to social media the following day, she referenced a “surreptitious recording” and called allegations that comments about the party’s future plans May constitute a criminal offence “a political smear job and nothing more.”

A caucus meeting that was planned for Monday was cancelled without explanation on Sunday. Ms. Warbus said it reflected “the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions.”

In an interview, Ms. Warbus said “a number of staff hirings and firings” happened without so much as a courtesy e-mail to MLAs, causing confusion and leaving them not properly informed to speak on behalf of the party and do their jobs effectively. She also underscored the seriousness of the allegations raised by the leaked audio recordings.

“There were some very critical, pivotal points in the past two weeks that deserve time, answers, accountability and transparency,” she said.

Ms. Warbus said unity is needed among like-minded people, and that divisions, personal attacks and culture wars are unhelpful.

“I’m open, and my door’s open, my phone’s open, to anybody that wants to have those conversations,” she said. “I think we have to come together before we can ask British Columbians to govern at all.”

Ms. Warbus is not alone in citing a breakdown of communications as a factor in leaving the party. Randy Hawes resigned as the B.C. Conservatives’ riding association president for Abbotsford-Mission on Aug. 24 after learning through media reports that Ms. Gasper had stepped down.

In an interview, the former BC Liberal MLA and former mayor of Mission said he was shocked by the outcome of May’s leadership contest, when Ms. Findlay was elected on the fourth ballot with 51 per cent of the vote, to Caroline Elliott’s 49 per cent.

“She’s what I would call hardcore right-wing, and I don’t think that’s what the BC Conservative Party was supposed to be,” Mr. Hawes said.

He cited as examples Ms. Findlay’s attack on Mr. Milobar during the leadership contest, suggesting he is in a conflict of interest because his wife is Indigenous, and a July report that Ms. Findlay and her senior staff directed MLAs to no longer use the term “First Nations” in describing people but instead use terms such as “Indian.”

Mr. Hawes also said that Ms. Findlay did not repudiate comments made by her husband, Brent Chapman, the party’s South Surrey MLA, who in old social-media posts described Palestinian children as “inbred walking, talking, breathing time bombs” and suggested mass shootings such as Sandy Hook were fake.

“My conscience will not allow me to sit in a party that has that woman at the head,” Mr. Hawes said.

He, too, is hopeful that Mr. Milobar’s and Mr. Bernier’s groups will work together.

“What’s going on now is insane,” he said. “As far as people who are in the centre, you can’t split that vote. You need a uniting formula.”

stories.title: Polls close in federal by-elections in Ontario, Quebec and B.C.
stories.summary: The Liberals previously enjoyed comfortable victories in two of the ridings, but Quebec’s Chicoutimi-Le Fjord could be a tight three-way race
stories.author: Ian Bailey, Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
Polls have closed in three federal by-elections Monday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals expected to hold on to seats in British Columbia and Ontario and a tight three-way race anticipated in a riding in Quebec.

That result would bolster the government’s slim majority in the House of Commons, while additional by-elections loom given the recent departure of several MPs. Results in the by-elections were not immediately available after polls in Ontario and Quebec closed at 9:30 local time, and the B.C. riding closing a half hour later.

Monday’s votes were held amid a tense trade war with the United States, which recently intensified after Mr. Carney pulled out of negotiations with the U.S., saying American proposals were unacceptable.

The microbrewery in La Baie, Que. where the Liberals were holding their election night party was filling up with volunteers and members of the party’s Quebec caucus minutes before polls closed.

“The mood is optimistic,” said Joël Lightbound, a Liberal MP for Louis-Hébert in the Quebec City region, and the Prime Minister’s Quebec lieutenant. “A by-election is always its own beast, but we’re all reasonably optimistic.”

The Liberals previously enjoyed comfortable victories in two of the ridings up for grabs: North Vancouver-Capilano and the Toronto riding of Beaches-East York.

The third riding facing a by-election, Quebec’s Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, was most recently held by the Conservatives. The MP there, Richard Martel, first elected in 2018, departed in July for a seat in the Senate.

The former hockey coach was re-elected in the riding in 2025 with a lead of about 1,500 votes over the Liberal and Bloc Québécois candidates. Mr. Martel received 34 per cent of the vote compared with 31.19 per cent for the Bloc candidate and 31.12 per cent for the Liberals.

This time around, an intensely competitive three-way race was on in the rural riding, which includes part of the city of Saguenay.

The Conservatives were running Régis Gaudreault, a lawyer and teacher at the Cégep de Chicoutimi. The Bloc candidate was Caroline Dubé, a former director of the office of Bloc MP Mario Simard. The Liberal candidate was Daniel Gobeil, the former chair of the Quebec dairy producers association.

A Liberal defeat there could raise questions about support in Quebec for the federal government’s trade agenda, which is now playing a major role in the provincial election campaign that began last week. Quebeckers head to the polls on Oct. 5.

In North Vancouver-Capilano, Mr. Carney’s former deputy chief of staff, Braeden Caley, was running for the Liberals.

Jonathan Wilkinson had represented the area since 2015, initially as the MP for North Vancouver, and then for the current riding. The former federal cabinet minister was named Canadian ambassador to the European Union earlier this year.

Given Mr. Caley’s former role in the Carney government, if elected, he could potentially be considered as a future cabinet minister.

Other candidates in North Vancouver-Capilano included Conservative Stephen Curran, a lawyer who also contested the riding in 2025; Stephen Tweedale for the NDP; and the Green Party’s Shelley Luce, an environmental scientist.

Beaches-East York became vacant when Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith departed for an unsuccessful attempt to enter provincial politics; he is now running for a seat on Toronto city council.

Tanveer Shahnawaz, a onetime assistant to Mr. Erskine-Smith, ran to succeed his former boss as the Liberal candidate in Beaches-East York. Mr. Erskine-Smith won the riding with 67.75 per cent of the vote in 2025.

Other candidates in Beaches-East York included the Conservatives’ Jim Syrbos, the Ndp’s Shannon Devine and the Greens’ Bruce Livesey.

The three by-elections were held while the House of Commons is on a summer break. MPs return on Sept. 21.

Additional federal by-elections are expected in the coming months. Quebec Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault has resigned his Montreal seat of Laurier–Sainte-Marie, months after he left Mr. Carney’s cabinet over a difference of opinion over the government’s energy and environment policies. Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall is also expected to officially resign imminently.

stories.title: Former Calgary teacher and sexual abuse convict Fred Archer back in court
stories.summary: Eighty-two-year-old Fred Archer appeared in a Calgary courtroom Monday to face charges stemming from allegations of sexual incidents going back decades.
stories.author: Tyler Barrow
stories.content: Eighty-two-year-old Fred Archer appeared in a Calgary courtroom Monday to face charges stemming from allegations of sexual incidents going back decades. Archer faces charges of sexual assault, sexual interference and sexual exploitation in connection with alleged incidents between June 1994 and September 1995 involving a boy who was then aged 13. The boy, who cannot be identified due to a publication ban, is referred to as JR in court. During opening arguments, Crown Prosecutor Gianna Argento told Justice Brandy Shaw that Archer first befriended JR’s father and later developed a “very close relationship” where Archer ended up in a caretaker role over JR. She told court Archer would look after JR while his father worked out of town for weeks. Archer is accused of sexually abusing JR during a 15-month period. JR went to John Ware School, where Archer was a teacher. Archer’s lawyer, Tim Dunlap, rejected the allegations, telling the court JR’s allegations are “for profit.” Archer was convicted for abusing boys in the 1990s at Springbank Middle School. He was also named along with another former teacher in a massive class-action lawsuit against the Calgary Board of Education involving a $15.7-million payment to 55 former students of John Ware School. The trial is set to last five days.

stories.title: Woman randomly stabs 2 people in New York City’s Times Square, killing 1, then is killed by police
stories.summary: A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: NEW York — A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials. The shooting happened just before 4:30 p.m. next to a New York Police Department substation, just outside One Times Square, the building that hosts the city’s annual New Year’s Eve ball drop celebration. It is one of the most heavily touristed and policed spots in all of New York. The 49-year-old woman from Queens pulled out two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man who had just come out of the subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife, striking him in the abdomen, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference. Seconds later, the woman stabbed a 32-year-old woman also in the abdomen, Tisch said. Both victims were taken to the hospital. The woman died and the man is in stable condition, according to police. Police didn’t say if the victims were tourists visiting the city or residents. Videos posted on social media show a group of at least 10 officers gathered around the woman, who was holding two large kitchen knives. Officers tried to convince the woman to drop the knives for several minutes before using a Taser, Tisch said. The woman told them: “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” according to Tisch. The video shows the Taser not incapacitating her and the woman walking quickly toward the officers while waving the knives in front of her. Two officers then shot the woman, according to police. In the video posted by bystanders, the woman fell to the ground, where an officer handcuffed her. Officers rolled her onto her back and rendered first aid. “This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said. The woman has a “documented mental health history with the Nypd,” which include incidents in 2018 and 2019 but no arrest history with the department, Tisch said. She didn’t provide additional details. Police are investigating. Tisch said there was no evidence suggesting it was a terrorist attack. The names of the victims have not been released until next of kin are notified, according to police. “We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers, saying more people could have been hurt or killed if not for their actions. The Nypd temporarily closed part of 7th Avenue and warned the public to stay away from the area. Police tape cordoned off the area as a large group of law enforcement officers worked nearby. Violent crime has fallen sharply in New York City so far this year, with homicides down 24 per cent and on pace to potentially hit their lowest level in decades. But this is the second killing this year in Times Square. A man was fatally stabbed in the same area in May. Hallie Golden, The Associated Press

stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Family members of an Indigenous woman who died after a hate-fuelled attack say they want the Parole Board of Canada to explain why they weren’t told of a decision to give the man who killed their sister full parole earlier this month.

Indigenous leaders joined Connie and Melissa Kentner on Parliament Hill Monday morning for a news conference calling for a review of the parole board’s decision to release Brayden Bushby, who served five years of an eight-year sentence for manslaughter in the high-profile 2017 death of the two women’s sister, Barbara Kentner, in Thunder Bay.

“When the parole board makes a decision like this, they are not deciding in a vacuum. There is a family on the other side of that decision, which is us. There is a community on the other side of that decision, which is where we live. There are Indigenous women and girls watching. There are families who are asking themselves whether the justice system will protect them and whether their voices will matter if something happens to them,” Connie said.

Mr. Bushby was convicted of manslaughter in 2020 after he pleaded guilty to aggravated assault for throwing a trailer hitch at two of the Kentner sisters from a passing car, hitting Barbara in the stomach and rupturing her small intestine. He was sentenced to eight years in prison in 2021.

On Aug. 13, the parole board granted Mr. Bushby full parole with conditions and notified media of its 13-page decision on the case by e-mail on Aug. 18. At that time, The Globe and Mail contacted Melissa Kentner, who wasn’t aware Mr. Bushby had been released from prison.

She also said no one in her family was contacted by the parole board to inform them of its decision or told that Mr. Bushby was even being considered for full parole, even though family members had registered for such notification.

“They know our e-mails, for some of us, our cellphones haven’t changed since 2017 and still we were not invited to participate in the parole process as victims,” Melissa said in a statement.

The parole board did not respond to a request from The Globe Monday. In its decision, the board said it determined Mr. Bushby would not pose undue risk to the public.

Melissa said she no longer feels safe knowing Mr. Bushby is free, and neither do her children.

Six months after Barbara, a 34-year old Anishinaabe mother, was struck with the trailer hitch hurled at her and Melissa as they walked down a Thunder Bay street, she died from injuries to her abdomen.

Evidence from the preliminary hearing and trial heard that on the night of the assault, Mr. Bushby, a Thunder Bay resident, was intoxicated after a day of ice fishing and drinking. He and three friends went driving around the city, and Mr. Bushby told his friends he wanted to “yell at hookers.”

That night, Melissa said, she saw a vehicle approach them with someone hanging out the window. Then she heard someone yell, “I got one!” as it drove off. Barbara was behind her on the ground and had been hit in the stomach with a trailer hitch she found nearby.

The blunt force trauma ruptured Barbara’s small intestine, requiring emergency surgery.

The forensic pathologist who performed her autopsy said Barbara died of bronchopneumonia and acute chronic peritonitis. She determined that both were consequences of a “traumatic rupture of the small intestine” caused by the blunt force injury.

Barbara also had end-stage liver disease, and while it was a significant contributing factor, it was not a direct cause of her death, the forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy testified in 2020.

Superior Court Justice Helen Pierce said in her sentencing that Mr. Bushby’s fatal attack was motivated by a hatred of women and disregard for their lives.

Justice Pierce said while there was no evidence Mr. Bushby knew the Kentner sisters were Indigenous on the night of Jan. 29, 2017, it was proven beyond a reasonable doubt that he was motivated by hate toward women.

“Your actions have signalled to Indigenous people across Canada that they cannot expect to be safe, and that their lives are not valued,” she said.

Indigenous leaders from Northern Ontario said greater consideration has to be given in parole board risk assessments that involve Indigenous victims.

“There has to be a review on this particular case,” Deputy Grand Chief Anna Betty Achneepineskum of Nishnawbe Aski Nation said Monday.

In its August decision, the board said it determined “a release on full parole now will not pose undue risk and the release will contribute to the protection of society by facilitating [Mr. Bushby’s] reintegration back into society as a law-abiding citizen.”

Mr. Bushby was previously granted day parole in 2023, allowing him to live at his mother’s home in Thunder Bay, but the parole board revoked his release the following year.

At the time, the board said it found Mr. Bushby had violated several terms of his day parole, including a prohibition on consuming alcohol.

Mr. Bushby had failed a breathalyzer test during a traffic stop, the board said. He had also failed to remain at the scene after he reversed a car into another vehicle, and was a suspect in a car theft investigation, the parole board said in the decision.

He also got a new tattoo of a Confederate flag, which the board said was widely linked to “racist ideologies.”

Mr. Bushby, however, said he fell asleep and didn’t know what the tattoo artist was doing until the piece was done and questioned whether it was relevant to his case.

He also cut a swastika into a correctional facility’s lawn in August, 2025, according to the parole board’s decision.

stories.title: In Rochester, N.Y., businesses and officials defy Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming ‘stunt’
stories.summary: Residents oppose the removal of a name that is interwoven with businesses and landmarks throughout the region
stories.author: Matthew Frank
stories.content:
Don’t talk about politics in the boat.

Since Leandro DaSilva launched Ontario Boat Charters in Rochester, N.Y., six years ago, that has been the rule aboard his vessels.

The 49-year-old has been boating on the lake since he was 13. The water became a place where he could leave the stress of life on the shoreline. He named his boat company after the lake to share his love of it with others.

But after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order last week to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” Mr. DaSilva said he’s worried that the once-peaceful water his business relies on is now tied to political controversy.

“Any time you bring politics into anything, it’s going to divide people, and this new name will divide people more,” he said.

Canadians have swiftly condemned Mr. Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, which straddles the border between Canada and the United States, as an attack on Indigenous culture and an imposition of American nationalism on a lake whose name hasn’t changed in nearly 400 years.

Across the water in Rochester, located 150 kilometres southeast of Toronto, Americans are also opposing the removal of a name that is interwoven with businesses and landmarks throughout the region.

The city council of Rochester issued a proclamation on Friday to maintain Lake Ontario’s name and defy the President’s executive order. The proclamation called the “stunt” a distraction from other issues Americans face, including housing and the economy.

“To ‘change’ the identity of this lake, after centuries of being known by a single name, is as childish as it is futile,” the proclamation stated.

Asked to comment on Rochester’s proclamation, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said the lake’s new name reflects its heritage and place in the U.S.

“As the president said, the majority of the great lake’s volume sits in United States territory,” she said in an e-mail.

Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

Rochester city council president Miguel A. Meléndez Jr., who brought the proclamation forward, said the name “Lake America” disrespects the people who know Lake Ontario and its Indigenous history.

The lake’s name originated from an Iroquois word meaning “beautiful lake” or “sparkling water.” French explorers initially used other names such as Lac Frontenac, but Lake Ontario became most commonly used on maps.

Mr. Meléndez said the city council needed to take a stand against Mr. Trump because the water is critical to peoples’ livelihoods and Canada is Rochester’s best neighbour.

“It’s something we shouldn’t be picking fights over at this point, and it was important for us to stand up and say something,” he said in a Monday interview.

While the relationship between Canada and the U.S. will need repair, Mr. Meléndez said, he hopes the bond across the water will stay strong and outlast one president’s decisions.

On its website, the city refers to Lake Ontario as the “sweetwater sea.”

Rochester and Toronto once shared a direct connection through a ferry that travelled across Lake Ontario. A planned route between the two cities was first floated in 1979, according to The Globe and Mail’s archives.

In May, 2004, the ferry route was launched after Rochester bought a US$32-million boat. A month after operations began, two Globe reporters raced from Toronto to Rochester to see whether travel by water or land was faster. (The reporter travelling by car handily beat the one taking the ferry.)

But the ferry lost US$10-million in its first 10 months of operating and was ultimately shut down in 2006.

William Keeler, a librarian and archivist for the Rochester Historical Society, said the ferry helped bring the two cities closer together and was an example of cross-border co-operation during its brief existence.

But he also said losing the ferry illustrated Rochester’s shift away from relying on Lake Ontario for trade and instead using the nearly 200-year-old Erie Canal, which flows across upstate New York from Lake Erie to Albany.

Mr. Keeler said that Mr. Trump’s renaming of the lake is an insult to both Americans and Canadians.

“Trump is trying to add one more thing to his legacy,” he said. “The guy is an egomaniac.”

The name “Ontario” extended beyond the lake and has become a signifier for the region, he said. The town of Ontario, N.Y., is roughly 30 kilometres east of Rochester. Multiple beaches, hiking trails and businesses near the lake also incorporate the name.

When Matt Saxon, owner of Rochester-based screen-printing company Lake Ontario Press, saw Mr. Trump’s Friday executive order, he initially joked with customers that he would have to change his company’s name.

As the day went by, he got a flood of messages from customers asking for Lake Ontario-branded clothing to protest “Lake America” and preserve the original name.

On Saturday, he held a pop-up event inviting customers to have their own clothing screen-printed with Lake Ontario designs, and people lined up an hour before opening. Mr. Saxon said he printed at least 300 shirts – one of the best days his business has ever had.

“So many people wanted it,” he said. “There was no way I couldn’t do it. I was going to do something, but I didn’t think I’d be doing it that quickly.”

Mr. Saxon is already planning another event as demand for the designs continues, prompted in part by the lake’s name change starting to appear online.

Google updated its map on Saturday to show U.S. users the name “Lake America.” Canadian users still see Lake Ontario, while people in other countries are shown both names.

The web giant said in a brief statement Saturday that such updates “follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

On Monday, Mr. Trump also asked Apple to change the name on its maps app.

Regardless of what any map says, Mr. DaSilva said he will always refer to it as Lake Ontario. But he’s concerned that keeping “Ontario” in his company’s name will complicate his boating business with both names in use.

“This is something I have to think about, and I don’t want to spend my energy to change things,” Mr. DaSilva said. “Now, it’s really just a waste of time.”

With reports from the Associated Press

stories.title: ATV users open new trail in southern Bruce County
stories.summary: Terry Lamont has been discovering Bruce County’s fields and forests with his ATV since 2006.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Terry Lamont has been discovering Bruce County’s fields and forests with his ATV since 2006. “I put roughly 8000 km on a year on my ATV, and I volunteer with the club and help do trail maintenance. It’s good for your mind,” said Lamont.

“Let’s you get outside, enjoy the outdoors, away from all the other stuff that goes on in the world, and you can just get out and relax and have a good time.” Lamont is one of the first ATV enthusiasts to use a new 8-kilometre trail, constructed by the Huron Shores ATV club, spanning four concessions in Southern Bruce County.

“This trail, for a lot of years has been used unofficially by people. And it was getting fairly rundown. Not a lot of management and oversight on the trail,” said Tyler Jonston, president of the Huron Shores ATV Club. “So, we were prepared to take that on, in partnership with our other trail users and groups.

So, we’ll be monitoring the trail, and making sure that everybody’s safe and compliant, so they’ll be able to explore utilizing the trails.” Unofficial use of hiking trails by ATV users has, for years, caught the ire of local conservation authorities, and hiking groups, by causing ruts and damage.

More “sanctioned” places to ride, like the Sideroad 30 trail, should help reduce outcomes like that, caused by a small handful of ATV drivers. “We’ve cultivated some great relationships with the Municipality of Huron-Kinloss and with Bruce County, proving to them that the ATV club is a great trail partner in trail management and maintenance, as well as oversight for the trails to ensure that we have a safe place to ride,” said Johnston.

“It’s a sanctioned place to ride, so that all of our recreational users have a place that they can enjoy.” The new trail adds to more than 100 kilometres of trails stretching from Wingham to Port Elgin, maintained by the Huron Shores ATV club.

This new section, an important link, joining forest loops in Southern Bruce County together. “It’s a great thing to have it open. It helps connect all of our other group of trails down in this area, and keeps us off the main paved roads,” said Lamont.

“It allows our ATV users to connect to all our county forest trails down here in the region and gives us an opportunity to be able to do some more exploring down in Southern Bruce,” said Johnston.

stories.title: Increased speed limit takes effect between Windsor and Toronto
stories.summary: Highway travelers between Windsor and Toronto are able to move a little faster along Highway 401 as of Monday.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Highway travelers between Windsor and Toronto are able to move a little faster along Highway 401 as of Monday. The latest in a series of provincial speed limit increases has taken effect, raising the speed limit from 100 to 110 kilometres per hour along the stretch from Tilbury in the southwest to Toronto.

“It’s actually pretty nice. I didn’t realize it until you just said it, but I do remember seeing 110 speed limit,” said driver Ken Moore, who stopped for a break at the ONroute stop on Highway 401 east at Ingersoll, Ont. on Monday.

“The majority of the people on the highway travel at much higher speeds prior to the 110 increase,” said driver John Thomson, who also made a pit stop. While commercial transport trucks are already regulated with speed limiters set at 105 km/h, truck driver Manav says the new speed limit of 110 km/h gives truck drivers more breathing room.

“Trucks are heavy loaded, you know. On the downhill sometimes you cannot push the breaks too hard. So that is a good change for us,” he said. Marco Beghetto, media spokesperson for the Ontario Trucking Association, calls for consistent enforcement for all highway users.

“A portion of the truck population is abiding by the speed limiter rule at 105. A portion of the truck population is going to do what the cars are now allowed to do, which is a buck 20 plus. So yes, you’re going to have more vehicles doing a variation of different speeds, which I can see can be problematic,” he told CTV News.

“Any increase in speed is not an invitation to drive even more at an excessive speed,” said Derek Rogers, media relations coordinator for West Region OPP. Rogers says the higher speed limit will not change their job of keeping roads safe.

“Either driving too fast, or driving too fast for the conditions. So really, from an OPP perspective, it doesn’t change. Our focus is on responsible driving behaviour, and that focus remains in place,” he said. The final phase of speed limit increases for 2026 will take effect at the end of September.

The changes cover 938 kilometers in total, with 89 per cent of the province’s highway network up to 110 km/h. “The people who are going to exceed by a lot are still going to do it. I don’t see it having changed a lot. Just people are not getting speeding tickets as much now,” said driver Dave Perrotta.

stories.title: U.S. tariffs hit London Transit’s purchase of 29 new buses
stories.summary: Tariffs levied by the United States on some Canadian products increased the cost of each new bus purchased by London Transit by about $50,000 this year.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Tariffs levied by the United States on some Canadian products increased the cost of each new bus purchased by London Transit by about $50,000 this year. On Monday, the London Transit Commission (LTC) discussed unanticipated budget pressures stemming from changing trade policies in the U.S., and the ongoing conflict with Iran.

“We are monitoring the situation, trying to be prudent and fiscally responsible, but recognizing we do need some service enhancements,” LTC Chair Coun. Skylar Franke tells CTV News. In 2026, London Transit purchased 17 new buses to replace old vehicles being removed from service, plus 12 buses for service improvements.

The cost of each bus was budgeted to be about $1 million, but U.S. tariffs added $50,000 to the cost of each one, totaling almost $1.5 million. “Under the contract that we have with New Flyer, the buses are built partially in Canada, partially in the U.S.,” explains London Transit’s General Manager Kelly Paleczny.

“As a result, those tariffs are calculated the day the frame crosses the border.” The new tariffs are being included in future capital budgeting, including 24 buses that will be purchased in 2027. However, Paleczny suggests changes are coming to where buses are assembled.

“New Flyer has built a facility in Winnipeg so that they can now fully build a bus in Canada versus back-and-forth across the border,” Paleczny explains. “(It’s) in response to the Canadian demand and the need to mitigate those tariffs.” Franke points out that only two companies build buses in Canada, “If we’re taking a made in Canada approach, what does that look like for the (manufacturing) of busses?

Right now there’s very few places we can purchase busses from.” Meanwhile, the commission supported submitting a business case to the 2027 Municipal Budget requesting an additional $2 million to cover higher diesel costs related to the U.S. conflict with Iran, and to make some recent service improvements permanent.

Members also unanimously backed lobbying efforts seeking financial relief from the provincial and federal governments for public transit systems experiencing budget pressure from international issues outside their control.

Franke explains, “The transit commission, as well as staff, are going to be advocating to upper levels of government to try and figure out what they can do to assist us with trade wars and geopolitical international issues.”

Members also unanimously backed lobbying efforts seeking financial relief from the provincial and federal governments for public transit systems experiencing budget pressure from international issues outside their control.

Franke explains, “The transit commission, as well as staff, are going to be advocating to upper levels of government to try and figure out what they can do to assist us with trade wars and geopolitical international issues.”

stories.title: Cardinal Marc Ouellet wins lawsuit against woman who accused him of sexual misconduct
stories.summary: Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet has won his civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet has won his civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit. Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled that Paméla Groleau’s accusations against Ouellet are unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000. “The court finds that the allegations describing the four events cited by Ms. Groleau in the context of the class action are false,” he wrote in a decision released Monday. Groleau had accused Ouellet of touching her without consent on three occasions between 2008 and 2010, while she was training or working as a lay pastoral agent for the church. She also said she felt “hunted” by him at a fourth event, during which Ouellet moved across a room to come sit down next to her. Castonguay noted in his judgment that Groleau changed her story several times, including eventually saying that she only considered one of the alleged interactions to be a sexual assault. “Her allegations are unfounded to a point that, strategically, she decided to downgrade the three first events,” the judge wrote. Groleau testified in court to the incidents involving Ouellet that she felt were inappropriate, which all took place at church gatherings with other people present. The final alleged incident came in 2010, at an event celebrating a priest’s ordination, when Groleau said Ouellet slid his hand down her back to the top of her buttocks and left them there for “several seconds.” Castonguay concluded that her testimony “was neither credible nor reliable.” The allegations first surfaced in 2022 as part of a wider class-action lawsuit against the archdiocese of Quebec and dozens of its clergy or lay members. In response to being named in the class action, Ouellet launched a $100,000 defamation countersuit against Groleau, alleging that she damaged his reputation, honour and dignity. The judge said the damage to Ouellet “is amplified by the chosen vehicle, meaning that of a class action aimed principally at religious pedophiles, thereby equating Cardinal Ouellet, in the eyes of the ‘ordinary citizen,’ with that group of individuals.” Quebec Superior Court approved a $31.5-million out-of-court settlement for the class action earlier this month. In 2013, Ouellet was touted as a front-runner to replace former pope Benedict XVI, a role that went to former pope Francis. Ouellet headed the powerful Dicastery for Bishops, the Vatican office that oversees the selection of new bishops, from 2010 until his retirement in 2023. The news that he had been named in a class action created a media firestorm. The trial also heard from two other women who testified to having interactions with Ouellet that they felt were inappropriate. Castonguay ruled that their testimony was not pertinent to the question of whether Groleau had defamed Ouellet. He also concluded that Ouellet was “not the author of the gestures” described by one of the two women. The woman had testified that Ouellet had come up behind her and allegedly rubbed his pelvis against her behind as she prepared items for a mass in Montreal in 1992, but Castonguay said the evidence showed that the cardinal was not the person officiating masses at the time. Castonguay said the true impact of the allegations on Ouellet “is difficult to quantify,” and awarded him the $100,000 he’d been seeking. Ouellet has promised to donate the damages he’s awarded to organizations fighting against sexual abuse experienced by Indigenous people in Canada. Lawyers for Groleau did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ouellet’s lawyers said in a statement they were pleased the court had recognized he had suffered an injustice that would result in him getting compensation. “This judgment reaffirms a fundamental principle: even in the context of judicial proceedings, serious allegations must be based on accurate and relevant facts and advanced with the rigour required by their gravity,” said lawyer Dominique Ménard, in the statement. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026. stories.title: Montreal woman searches for cat last seen at Toronto Pearson airport
stories.summary: A Montreal woman says her cat escaped at Toronto Pearson airport and has not been found more than two weeks later.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Phil Carpenter
paragraphs: A Montreal woman is pleading for help finding her cat after the animal disappeared during a journey from Jordan to Canada more than two weeks ago.
Abir Batikhi says her seven-year-old cat, Caramel, was one of four cats travelling with her on a non-stop flight from Jordan on Aug. 17.
The Montreal resident says all four animals were secured in cages before departure. She however says that when she arrived in Montreal and collected the animals, one cage was empty.
“I received the four cages. One cat was missing,” Batikhi said.
2:29 ‘Pearson is a disaster’: Poilievre backs Toronto island airport expansion

After making inquiries, Batikhi says she was told Caramel had been seen in the cargo hold when the aircraft arrived at Toronto Pearson International Airport, where the flight stopped before continuing to Montreal.
She says airport officials informed her the cat escaped onto the airport ramp area near Terminal 3 and ran toward gates 29 and 30.
“That was the last reported sighting,” she said.
Since then, Batikhi has turned to social media in an effort to locate the missing pet.
“I post in all the groups on Facebook. Animal lovers, employees. I post a lot in Montreal and Toronto,” she said.
Batikhi, who has cared for Caramel since the cat was born, fears the animal May be hiding and struggling to survive.
“Because she’s scared, she will be hiding, starved. I don’t want her to die from starvation,” she said.
The animal shelter volunteer says she has been in contact with airport authorities repeatedly but remains frustrated that the cat has not been found.
“Please, I really want to know why they haven’t been able to trap her,” she said.
A spokesperson for Toronto Pearson said wildlife crews have been conducting daily sweeps of the airport grounds, setting humane live-capture traps and notifying ground crews to watch for the animal.
Dacia Rohlehr, CEO of pet transportation company Paws En Route, says incidents involving escaped animals during air travel are uncommon.
“There are about four million pets that travel annually, and out of those four million pets, about 0.01 per cent experience an issue,” Rohlehr said.
She says strict regulations are in place to reduce the risk of animals escaping during transport, including requirements that kennel doors be secured.
“The gate and the door have a zip tie and that is well secured as well, because you don’t want that to open during flight,” Rohlehr said.

Batikhi says the cages were secured with zip ties before departure from Jordan and inspected before the flight. She says she does not know whether Caramel escaped during the flight or after the aircraft landed.
“I just need to bring back my cat,” she said.

stories.title: For the first time in six years, the Port of Churchill shipped Canadian grain to Europe
stories.summary: Prairie grain is once again being shipped out of Churchill in northern Manitoba. Approximately 30,000 tonnes of Canadian durum wheat, supplied by Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods, is being loaded at the Port of Churchill and will be shipped to customers in Europe this week.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content: Churchill, MAN. – Prairie grain is once again being shipped out of Churchill in northern Manitoba. Approximately 30,000 tonnes of Canadian durum wheat, supplied by Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods, is being loaded at the Port of Churchill and will be shipped to customers in Europe this week. This marks the first shipment through the Port of Churchill since 2020, and is the first of three grain shipments expected out of the port this season, which will send more than 100,000 tonnes of grain to Europe. “Seeing Prairie grain once again moving through the Port of Churchill to European markets is an important milestone for Manitoba agriculture,” said Manitoba Agricultural Minister Ron Kostyshyn. “Our producers need more ways to reach customers around the world, and Churchill provides an important northern gateway that can help diversify our trade, strengthen our supply chains and create new opportunities for Manitoba and Western Canadian agriculture.” Grain shipments to the port were halted in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the failing rail line, which has now been largely completed. Chris Avery from Arctic Gateway Group (AGG), which owns and operates the port, says this will be the most diversified shipping season in the port’s history. “We’re very much open for business,” he said. “We’re once again a strategic asset to Canada, but that set of commodities is a mix of commodities. It’s critical minerals, potash, Arctic resupply. It’s many other goods as well.” Another vessel is set to arrive at the port this week, which will load zinc-concentrate and the first-ever shipment of potash, mined in Manitoba, by Potash and Agri Development Corporation of Manitoba (Padcom). Avery says AGG is also loading another resupply vessel this season destined for Nunavut, which he says shows how important of a role the port can play for the Arctic. stories.title: U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll stepping down after 18 months on the job: White House
stories.summary: is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: Washington — U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader during the Trump administration. No reason was given for the departure of Driscoll, who is a friend of Vice-President JD Vance, but tensions with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported. It marks the latest in a series of shakeups of the military leadership, with the Army especially seeing major upheaval. “Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added. A U.S. Army official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Driscoll submitted his resignation. The official did not provide additional details. The Pentagon referred questions to the Army. Driscoll’s resignation was reported earlier Monday by The Wall Street Journal. Hegseth suddenly ousted the service’s top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George, in April, while the Army’s commander in Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June. Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who has made a meteoric rise under Hegseth, took George’s place as the Army’s acting chief of staff. Under LaNeve, the service is pulling the plug on a drone modernization program that Driscoll had heralded. An Army unit based in Europe was building its own drones before LaNeve directed it to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion, officials said in August. Driscoll was a George ally and lamented his departure, along with both Republican and Democratic lawmakers. He told Congress in April that he and his family drove to George’s house following his resignation “and we all gave him a hug.” “That being said, the civilian leadership, the design of our system, is that they get to pick the leaders that they want,” Driscoll added. Driscoll is an Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vance, whom Driscoll met at Yale Law School. When nominating Driscoll in 2024, U.S. President Donald Trump called him “a disruptor and change agent.” As Army secretary, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world. The U.S. Senate confirmed him in February 2025, voting 66-28, following an Armed Services Committee hearing that was largely unconfrontational and focused on how the Army could modernize its systems, improve recruiting and beef up the military industrial base. Driscoll noted that his father and grandfather served in the Army and he vowed to be a secretary focused on the needs of soldiers. According to the Army, Driscoll served as an armor officer from August 2007 to March 2011, deploying to Iraq from October 2009 to July 2010. He also ran unsuccessfully in the Republican primary for a North Carolina congressional seat in 2020, getting about eight per cent of the vote in a crowded field of candidates. His departure comes after Hegseth ousted several other generals and admirals, including the head of the Navy. The Pentagon abruptly announced in April that Navy Secretary John Phelan was leaving the job, becoming the first head of a military service to depart during Trump’s second term. --- Ben Finley And Aamer Madhani, The Associated Press

stories.title: U.S. plan to develop Venezuelan oil adds urgency to Canada’s export diversification
stories.summary: Trump had said over the weekend that the deal puts Opec and Canada ‘on notice’
stories.author: Sophia Bertuzzi, Jeffrey Jones
stories.content:
A fractured trade relationship with the United States and potential surge in oil production in Venezuela could add urgency to Canada’s aims of expanding and diversifying its energy exports.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on the weekend that he had struck a deal to take majority control of Venezuela’s oil reserves, noting on social media that the deal puts the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and Canada “ on notice .”

The details are still unclear, but a flood of Venezuelan crude making its way to the U.S. market currently seems like a far-off proposition, and one fraught with risks. Indeed, Venezuela is an Opec member.

Still, the deal underpins the importance of Canada further reducing reliance on its dominant southern market – a years-long quest, analysts say.

That requires spending billions more dollars expanding pipeline capacity to the country’s coasts.

The recently expanded Trans Mountain system is currently the only pipeline network in Canada that transports Alberta crude oil to the West Coast, where it can be shipped overseas and sold at a premium to North American prices.

Before the expansion came online in May, 2024, Canada shipped about 97 per cent of its crude to the U.S. Since then, non-U.S. crude oil exports have steadily climbed from about 3 per cent to 15 per cent.

In the month of June, non-U.S. crude oil exports jumped nearly 27 per cent year over year, according to Statistics Canada’s latest energy statistics . More recently, that demand has been bolstered by Asian refineries scrambling to replace Persian Gulf crude as the Iran War effectively halted the flow of one-fifth of the world’s supply.

“If you are a big importer of oil, you’re seeing what’s going on in Iran, and you also saw what happened during the initial phase of the war in Ukraine. Those disruptions in global supply can hurt your economy very quickly,” Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said in an interview.

“A lot of those countries are trying to find new suppliers, partly to substitute for what they’re losing through the Iranian war, but also to ensure to have the optionality later on if there’s further disruption,” he added.

On Friday, Calgary-based Trans Mountain announced its network moved an average of 840,000 barrels of oil each day, running at 94 per cent of capacity during the second quarter of the year ending June 30th. Two-thirds of that was shipped to Asian refineries.

Canada and its energy industry have benefitted significantly from improved market access after the Trans Mountain expansion, but long-term competitiveness depends on being able to supply different markets rather than being captive to one, according to a TD Cowen report on Monday.

The report noted that Mr. Trump announced the Venezuelan oil deal a month before Ottawa’s Oct. 1 target for listing Alberta’s proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline as a project of national importance.

In July, the federal and Alberta governments announced Trans Mountain would take the lead on building and operating the one-million-barrel-a-day pipeline , running along roughly the same route as its existing system. The project is expected to cost up to $44-billion.

For now, Trans Mountain is in the process of making operational improvements that will boost the current pipeline’s capacity to 1.2-million barrels a day by the end of 2028, chief executive officer Mark Maki told The Globe and Mail.

In the meantime, Canada will continue to export about 4.5-million barrels a day to the U.S.

“We still don’t have the capacity to rotate fully away from the U.S.,” Mr. St-Arnaud said.

Shipping to Asia-Pacific markets is more profitable for Canadian oil producers, as exports are priced against the global Brent crude benchmark, which on Monday was trading at US$88 a barrel.

At home, Alberta producers sell to Canadian and U.S. refineries at the Western Canada Select price, which has recently been selling for a deeper discount to the North American West Texas Intermediate benchmark – as much as US$18.54 a barrel less than WTI as of Monday, compared with about US$12.50 a year ago.

The wider price spread could mean that Canadian oil shippers have filled up available space on the Trans Mountain Pipeline faster than expected when its expansion was completed in 2024, according to TD Cowen.

The lesson from the Venezuelan announcement is that market advantages are not guaranteed to last, the bank said.

With a report from Andrew Willis

Shipping to Asia-Pacific markets is more profitable for Canadian oil producers, as exports are priced against the global Brent crude benchmark, which on Monday was trading at US$88 a barrel.

At home, Alberta producers sell to Canadian and U.S. refineries at the Western Canada Select price, which has recently been selling for a deeper discount to the North American West Texas Intermediate benchmark – as much as US$18.54 a barrel less than WTI as of Monday, compared with about US$12.50 a year ago.

The wider price spread could mean that Canadian oil shippers have filled up available space on the Trans Mountain Pipeline faster than expected when its expansion was completed in 2024, according to TD Cowen.
The lesson from the Venezuelan announcement is that market advantages are not guaranteed to last, the bank said.

stories.title: Bare shelves at Alberta food banks as demand soar: ‘Very difficult year’
stories.summary: In the first six month the year, Food Banks Alberta distributed almost as much food as it did in all of 2025 — and the busiest months are yet to come.
stories.author: Jasmine King
paragraphs: Where pallets of food and supplies should be stacked high instead sit row after row of empty warehouse shelves.
Food banks across Alberta are sounding the alarm as some of their inventories reach dangerously low levels, making the organizations increasingly anxious as the holiday season approaches.
“This is the first time that we’ve encountered this level of scarcity within our warehouse,” said Darryl Burry, executive director of Food Banks Alberta.

The shelves at Food Banks Alberta are typically stocked with pallets upon pallets of donated products, piling all the way up to the roof of the warehouse. But right now, those same aisles are largely bare because of increased demand.
“Our goal here is to receive the donations of products that come from many corporate sponsors and supporters, and then we distribute that out to our network of food banks,” Burry said.
“Unfortunately, this month we have not received the same volume of donations and support as we normally would.”

The organization’s warehouse supplies 112 member food banks across the province. When a local food bank needs extra support, they place an order with Food Banks Alberta, who subsequently ships out the needed items.
In 2025, the association distributed 3.36 million pounds of food province-wide.
Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.
Demand increased so much this year, it distributed nearly 90 per cent of its total 2025 volume in the first six months of this year alone — with the busiest months still to come.
In August, the volume sent out ran 32.8 per cent higher than in August 2025.
Food Banks Alberta says statistics provided by Food Bank Canada’s 2025 HungerCount show Alberta recorded more than 210,000 average monthly food bank visits — a nearly 22 per cent jump from 2024.

“Most of the people walking through our members’ doors are working people and families trying to make ends meet,” Burry said. “They are our neighbours, our co-workers and the children sitting beside our children at school.
“Nobody in this province should have to choose between rent and groceries.”
While the 2026 HungerCount numbers won’t be released until October, projections indicate there’s been yet another significant jump in those accessing food banks in Alberta.
1:59 Food banks call for EI reform as food insecurity trends upward
When it comes to this summer, Burry says they have shipped more food out faster than donations came in.
“We’ve got about 350 pallets worth of product that we are short for the coming month of September,” Burry said.
Food Banks Alberta isn’t the only group noticing unprecedented demand; so is Edmonton’s Food Bank.
The organization supports more than 43,000 people monthly through its hamper program and the need is growing.

“We’re seeing higher levels of demand, and that can be in part for a large variety of reasons. However, we’re always trying to match that community demand as well,” said Haley Grinder, communications and media coordinator with Edmonton’s Food Bank.
“It does seem like this is a very, very difficult year for Albertans.”
2:05 Business Matters: Food inflation in Canada expected to remain elevated
The food bank says when demand outpaces supply, like it’s on track to do again this year, they have to spend some of their own funding to keep up and inflation makes it even harder.

“Last year, Edmonton’s Food Bank spent $3.9 million on food purchases. We anticipate being higher than that — approximately $2 million more on food purchases — just to offset the lack of donations and our buying power,” Grinder said.

“2026 obviously has been a year of immense challenges, there’s no doubt about that. Inflation, everything that’s going on in the world right now that has that trickle-down effect, and we’re definitely feeling that — so every little bit counts.”
As we head into the busiest season of the year for food banks in the province, they’re hoping for some additional help from Albertans.
“This is the first time that we’ve encountered this level of scarcity within our warehouse,” Burry said.
“It’s going to become a huge challenge as food banks want to make their orders, and we simply don’t have the product to be able to provide them.”

stories.title: Government officials are in Nepal to support search for missing Canadians, Anand says
stories.summary: Floods killed some 800 people and left roughly 3,000 missing in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The federal government has 10 officials on the ground in Nepal to support Canadians affected by flooding, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Monday.

In a statement posted on social media, Anand said the officials, which include a member of the RCMP, are working to locate missing Canadians and support affected families.

“Our priority is to locate Canadians and permanent residents and confirm their safety while offering support wherever and whenever possible,” she said.

Flash flooding killed some 800 people and left roughly 3,000 missing, after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

Anand said on social media on Saturday that one Canadian who was previously unaccounted for had been found safe.

She said Monday that 30 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing, a number she says May change as the government gets more information.

“We recognize with empathy the profound impact that this situation is having on families and communities across our country,” said Anand. “We remain in direct contact with all affected families through designated points of contact within each family and through a collective meeting with them today.”

The federal government has said it will provide $5-million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal.

Global Affairs Canada said in a statement Monday that officials are engaging with trekking companies, hospitals, local police, rescue centres, airlines and other Canadian travel industry partners to gather information, establish contact and help account for affected Canadians.

The department said the deputy high commissioner of Canada to India is one of the 10 officials in Kathmandu.

“Canadian officials are working closely with Nepalese and Chinese counterparts, as well as international partners including the Five Eyes, France, Japan, Italy and Singapore, to share information and support efforts to locate and assist Canadians,” said Global Affairs Canada.

The department said the RCMP has deployed a liaison officer to Nepal to offer assistance and help determine needs for on-the-ground support. It said the RCMP is also engaged through the Interpol network and has offered support with forensic equipment and expertise.

Canada’s travel advice for Nepal and China was updated Monday to advise against non-essential travel to affected areas due to the damage caused by severe flash flooding and mudslides and the ongoing risk of further flooding.

stories.title: Alvinston Arena Floor Fund almost halfway to goal after help from London Knights exhibition game
stories.summary: The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze. The facility, built in 1977, is reaching its end of life with critical repairs needed to the rink floor and refrigeration room.
stories.author: Brent Lale
paragraphs: The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze. The facility, built in 1977, is reaching its end of life with critical repairs needed to the rink floor and refrigeration room. With pinholes in the pipes, the municipality needed to be proactive when it came to the only ice surface in the community.

“It would be shut down for a couple of weeks if you have a major catastrophe,” said Dave Ferguson, mayor of Brooke-Alvinston. “If that’s the middle of February or hitting a playoff time, it’s going to just wreck everything.

So, when you can plan ahead and the ice came in, the cement came in and the boards on budget and on time. That is phenomenal for the small community,” said Ferguson. Work began on the arena floor project back in May and continues to progress.

“The quotes came back at $1.1 million,” said Ferguson. “The grant from Ontario (Ontario community Sport and Recreation Infrastructure Fund) is half of 2 million, so we could get up to $1 million of grant money matched dollar for dollar.

This was cost effective when the tenders came in and when you’re able to include the boards in it, the total project would be about $1.5 million. Half from the government, half from the township.” With roads and bridges to pay for, the Municipality did not want to include the repair costs on the tax bill of the 2,350 residents.

They started the Alvinston Arena Floor Fund (Aaff) immediately and with sponsors, and private donors included, they are making a significant dent in the goal. “We’re at about $450,000 so far,” said Jill Joris, fundraising manager for Brooke-Alvinston.

“Our goal is $1 million. We have some deals in the works as well, so hopefully those will pan out.” A major boost came this weekend when the London Knights approached the Municipality about hosting an exhibition game to help raise money for the Aaff.

With the arena under construction, the neighbouring community of Watford allowed them to host the game free of charge. The 650 tickets were snapped up quickly with the game being played in the hometown of Knights forward, Evan Van Gorp.

“Everywhere I went I just knew pretty much everybody because of the small town,” said Mike Van Gorp, Evan’s father. “Everybody was coming up and talking to me and Melissa and the atmosphere was just great.” One reason the game was so exciting was to see that calibre of play in a small venue.

“Everyone is so close to the ice and it is a very small ice surface,” said Mike. “A lot of the comments were, ‘I can’t believe how fast it is’ and how ‘great the players are and how skilled they are to make decisions in such a small rink like that’.

It was pretty cool.” With help from Sarnia-Lambton Tourism, additional fan-friendly activities were held around the arena hours prior to puck drop. “There were tons of fans in the stands,” said Joris. “We had a few at the watch party as well.

There were a silent auction and raffle and the donations for that were incredible. My heart grew three sizes that day.” Small-town arenas are not just skating and hockey. They host the fall fair, baseball and even the rodeo.

The hope is that the donations from the Aaff will prolong the life of the building for generations. “We replaced the cement and we’re going to do the boards next spring,” said Ferguson. “The ice pad and the boards will be all freshly redone by this time in 2027.”

stories.title: Lake Ontario merchandise grabs attention on both sides of the border
stories.summary: Branded hats and T-shirts are selling fast as Canadians and Americans alike spend to show support
stories.author: Arisa Valyear
paragraphs: Since U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America , there has been a surge in interest in Lake Ontario-themed merchandise from shoppers on both sides of the border.

Google searches for Lake Ontario shirts in Canada peaked around Aug. 30, three days after Mr. Trump signed the executive order to rename the body of water, and audiences looking for Lake Ontario hats, tees and other items have reached what the search engine labels as “breakout” status – a phrase meaning interest in the search term has grown by a margin of more than 5,000 per cent compared to a previous period, such as the prior week.
Searches for Lake Ontario T-shirts are also at breakout level in the United States, with peaks occurring on Aug. 27 and 30.

Clothing retailers and e-commerce sites are taking notice. Province of Canada, a Toronto-based company offering a variety of Canadian-themed selections (including an exclusive Heated Rivalry sweater ), released a Lake Ontario quarter-zip sweater on Friday and saw strong interest from consumers.
“Customers are specifically looking for made-in-Canada products,” said Allison Piccininni, Province of Canada’s product and operations manager, in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

Like all of the company’s merchandise, the item is manufactured in Canada. It’s available for pre-order at $128, and Ms. Piccininni said they’ve already sold hundreds, with about 75 per cent of orders coming from Ontario, and the next-highest from British Columbia. The company will donate 15 per cent of each sale to Indigenous charity Indspire .

The light grey sweater, which has the words “Lake Ontario” printed in blue text on the front, has a cheeky online description that hints at the ongoing strife between Canada and the U.S. : “Some names are already pretty good.”
“We can see Lake Ontario from our office, so it feels very relevant. It’s not just a trend we’re trying to jump on,” Ms. Piccininni said.

While the retailer currently isn’t shipping to the U.S. (a decision they made in July to mitigate tariff-related cross-border shipping issues), Ms. Piccininni said they’ve fielded a number of inquiries from shoppers in America, who are either expats or Canadian supporters.

In Calgary, Connor Curran, co-owner of the Canadian-made custom apparel brand Local Laundry, said he’s already sold about 100 of his company’s Lake Ontario T-shirts . “Alberta and Ontario are where most of the sales are coming from, and then B.C. and Manitoba,” Mr. Curran said in an interview with The Globe. “Albertans are proud of the name Lake Ontario, and we’re proud Canadians as well.”

The T-shirt – a light blue offering with the words “Lake Ontario Canada” printed in white text on the front – launched on Local Laundry’s website Friday and is available for pre-sale for $55. “Lake Ontario doesn’t need a rebrand,” reads the description.

The item, which is entirely made in Canada, is an opportunity for the company to support the Canadian economy, Mr. Curran said. “Our milling facility is in Toronto, our dyeing is done in Ajax, our cutting and sewing is done in Scarborough and then the items are shipped to Calgary where we decorate and print them.”

In the United States, particularly in areas along the shores of Lake Ontario such as Rochester, N.Y., interest in Lake Ontario-branded merch is also high. A post in a Rochester subreddit titled “Where to get Lake Ontario Merchandise?” received nearly 400 interactions and more than 100 comments, with users mostly listing Rochester-based businesses that supply the requested items.

One user pointed to Pretty Apothecary , a Rochester-based gift shop and home goods store that sells Lake Ontario caps, stickers, candles, patches and more. The store’s owner, Mike Pretty, said by Saturday morning they were completely sold out of their Lake Ontario inventory. “There’s been a big surge in interest and there’s a lot of pride surrounding the lake,” he told The Globe in an interview.
Mr. Pretty said the lake-themed merchandise was always decently popular with customers, but now eager buyers are entering the shop asking: “What do you have that’s Lake Ontario?”

Given the surge in interest, Mr. Pretty said he’s already filled about 50 pre-orders, and he’s going to be restocking his collection of themed patches, stickers, candles and caps. He’s also expanded his hat offerings from one design to three to meet demand. Mr. Pretty said the restocked merchandise should hit shelves within the next few weeks, and that the patches will be available again in early October.

Lake Ontario Press , a Rochester-based screen-printing shop run by Matt Saxon, also saw an influx of customers looking to support the Lake Ontario cause. He said interested buyers have been contacting him non-stop, and that on Saturday, the shop printed some 300 Lake Ontario-themed items for patrons.
“I had customers waiting an hour out the door and we ended up staying open an hour later just to finish up,” the business owner said.

stories.content:
Since U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America , there has been a surge in interest in Lake Ontario-themed merchandise from shoppers on both sides of the border.

Google searches for Lake Ontario shirts in Canada peaked around Aug. 30, three days after Mr. Trump signed the executive order to rename the body of water, and audiences looking for Lake Ontario hats, tees and other items have reached what the search engine labels as “breakout” status – a phrase meaning interest in the search term has grown by a margin of more than 5,000 per cent compared to a previous period, such as the prior week.

Searches for Lake Ontario T-shirts are also at breakout level in the United States, with peaks occurring on Aug. 27 and 30.

Clothing retailers and e-commerce sites are taking notice. Province of Canada, a Toronto-based company offering a variety of Canadian-themed selections (including an exclusive Heated Rivalry sweater ), released a Lake Ontario quarter-zip sweater on Friday and saw strong interest from consumers.

“Customers are specifically looking for made-in-Canada products,” said Allison Piccininni, Province of Canada’s product and operations manager, in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

Like all of the company’s merchandise, the item is manufactured in Canada. It’s available for pre-order at $128, and Ms. Piccininni said they’ve already sold hundreds, with about 75 per cent of orders coming from Ontario, and the next-highest from British Columbia. The company will donate 15 per cent of each sale to Indigenous charity Indspire .

The light grey sweater, which has the words “Lake Ontario” printed in blue text on the front, has a cheeky online description that hints at the ongoing strife between Canada and the U.S. : “Some names are already pretty good.”

“We can see Lake Ontario from our office, so it feels very relevant. It’s not just a trend we’re trying to jump on,” Ms. Piccininni said.

While the retailer currently isn’t shipping to the U.S. (a decision they made in July to mitigate tariff-related cross-border shipping issues), Ms. Piccininni said they’ve fielded a number of inquiries from shoppers in America, who are either expats or Canadian supporters.

In Calgary, Connor Curran, co-owner of the Canadian-made custom apparel brand Local Laundry, said he’s already sold about 100 of his company’s Lake Ontario T-shirts . “Alberta and Ontario are where most of the sales are coming from, and then B.C. and Manitoba,” Mr. Curran said in an interview with The Globe. “Albertans are proud of the name Lake Ontario, and we’re proud Canadians as well.”

The T-shirt – a light blue offering with the words “Lake Ontario Canada” printed in white text on the front – launched on Local Laundry’s website Friday and is available for pre-sale for $55. “Lake Ontario doesn’t need a rebrand,” reads the description.

The item, which is entirely made in Canada, is an opportunity for the company to support the Canadian economy, Mr. Curran said. “Our milling facility is in Toronto, our dyeing is done in Ajax, our cutting and sewing is done in Scarborough and then the items are shipped to Calgary where we decorate and print them.”

In the United States, particularly in areas along the shores of Lake Ontario such as Rochester, N.Y., interest in Lake Ontario-branded merch is also high. A post in a Rochester subreddit titled “Where to get Lake Ontario Merchandise?” received nearly 400 interactions and more than 100 comments, with users mostly listing Rochester-based businesses that supply the requested items.

One user pointed to Pretty Apothecary , a Rochester-based gift shop and home goods store that sells Lake Ontario caps, stickers, candles, patches and more. The store’s owner, Mike Pretty, said by Saturday morning they were completely sold out of their Lake Ontario inventory. “There’s been a big surge in interest and there’s a lot of pride surrounding the lake,” he told The Globe in an interview.

Mr. Pretty said the lake-themed merchandise was always decently popular with customers, but now eager buyers are entering the shop asking: “What do you have that’s Lake Ontario?”

Given the surge in interest, Mr. Pretty said he’s already filled about 50 pre-orders, and he’s going to be restocking his collection of themed patches, stickers, candles and caps. He’s also expanded his hat offerings from one design to three to meet demand. Mr. Pretty said the restocked merchandise should hit shelves within the next few weeks, and that the patches will be available again in early October.

Lake Ontario Press , a Rochester-based screen-printing shop run by Matt Saxon, also saw an influx of customers looking to support the Lake Ontario cause. He said interested buyers have been contacting him non-stop, and that on Saturday, the shop printed some 300 Lake Ontario-themed items for patrons.

“I had customers waiting an hour out the door and we ended up staying open an hour later just to finish up,” the business owner said.
