stories.content:
London Transit commuters in the city’s northwest and southwest could soon have a connection to the system as the transit authority looks to implement an on-demand service to test ridership in areas not served by conventional transit.

Greenlit by the politician-led commission Monday, London Transit will apply to the city for $3.5 million in assessment-growth funding for 2027 – the net-new property tax revenue generated each year – to introduce new service.

London Transit wants funding for a fixed-route expansion from the Hyde Park Power Centre to Western University , as well as on-demand service in the Fox Hollow neighbourhood and pockets of south Byron and north Lambeth.

“There’s areas of the city that have grown significantly, but we don’t know what the ridership is like. So to commit to a full conventional bus service where you’re running multiple large buses through the neighbourhood, but only having a couple people hop on – that might not be the best use of our funds,” said Skylar Franke, chair of the commission.

“This model . . . it’ll let us understand if there is a growing market in those neighbourhoods, and I think then we can, once we see the ridership levels increase, allocate the appropriate conventional service to it.”

Each year, the city runs an application process for its pot of assessment growth dollars, generated by property taxes from new development that year. The amount can vary from year to year.

Agencies such as police and paramedics, along with city services including garbage collection and road maintenance, can apply for the funding to cover the cost of expanding service to accommodate growth. That funding then continues in subsequent years.

London Transit had its first assessment-growth request approved by the city this year, with $2.1 million going toward new service to Cedar Hollow in the northeast, Innovation Park, Summerside and Sheffield, West Byron, and the Kains Road and Upperpoint Boulevard area.

Because of manufacturing and ordering timelines for new buses, those routes won’t begin until 2028, according to a transit staff report. In the meantime, the funding will go toward buying the buses needed.

The same delay would apply to the proposed Route 40 between Hyde Park Power Centre and Western University . The route would cost just over $2 million annually and is expected to see annual ridership of 205,500.

The on-demand service would cost $1.4 million and has forecast annual ridership of 22,700. Kelly Paleczny, general manager of London Transit, told politicians fares would be the same as for standard transit service, but details such as what vehicles would be used will be subject to a final report and proposal from a consultant in October.

“We’ve seen this approach in numerous other jurisdictions be quite successful,” Paleczny said following Monday’s meeting. “It really is an opportunity to get in sooner, and learn that critical information, and then hopefully when we do have the resources to put that route in, it’s going to be more successful.”

The commission also approved submitting the transit agency’s 2027 budget request, which includes an increase of approximately $2.6 million because of rising diesel costs and added service hours previously covered through its reserves.

While London Transit will still dip into its reserves to cover a portion, the budget report asks “administration to submit a budget amendment case increasing the City of London investment by $2,037,800 for 2027 to support the permanent addition of 2,400 service growth hours and the increased cost of diesel fuel.”

London Transit budgeted for diesel at roughly $1.22 per litre, but the recent average price is $1.65 per litre. Franke said London Transit has “already dipped heavily” into its fuel reserve fund and pointed to last year’s budget update, when the agency returned $700,000 to the city after the federal carbon tax was eliminated.

“I’m hopeful that council will recognize we have been very prudent, and at this point, if we want to continue delivering a reliable service and improve on our service targets, we do need that increase,” Franke said.

The commission also amended its budget request to seek advocacy from the provincial and federal governments for relief from diesel and tariff-related cost increases.

“It’s not a local decision, although it has a local impact, so we need to be discussing that with our provincial and federal counterparts,” Franke said.

Both the city’s 2027 budget update and assessment-growth allocations are set to be determined early next year.

stories.title: Ontario agencies restore Lake Ontario to their websites after Google Maps updated it to Lake America in the U.S.
stories.summary: Four Ontario government websites displayed Lake America over the weekend. The fix was a single Google Maps setting, or no map at all.
stories.author: Mason Kossak
stories.content:
Ontario government agencies have restored Lake Ontario to their websites after a Google Maps update replaced it with Lake America over the weekend.

Metrolinx, the provincial agency that runs GO Transit, disabled the map on its GO stations page where the label appeared, it told Global News . The agency said in an email to National Post that “the issue has since been resolved, and our maps once again show Lake Ontario.”

Maps on sites run by Hydro One, Metrolinx, Infrastructure Ontario and the Lcbo all displayed the American name, Global News reported. Global confirmed the labels itself and found the same on the Loblaws store locator, which CTV News reported was still showing Lake America on Monday morning.

A website that embeds a Google map loads the code from Google’s servers, and unless a developer specifies a region, the map draws American place names. Specifying Canada changes them.

Hydro One said in an email to National Post that its outage map showed an incorrect label for Lake Ontario for “a brief period” Sunday because of an issue with a third-party mapping service. The problem was identified and corrected Sunday evening, the utility wrote. It apologized for the error in an earlier statement to Global News.

TD was displaying Lake America but as of Monday afternoon, that problem had been resolved, the bank told National Post.

Loblaw said in an email to National Post that the map on its store locator was showing an incorrect label for Lake Ontario, that the information comes from a third-party mapping service and that it was working to correct it.

The Lcbo did not respond to a request for comment. Google did not provide a statement. Housing, Infrastructure and Communities Canada acknowledged the request and said it would respond. It had not by deadline.

Stephen Crawford, Ontario’s minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, wrote on X that some agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps and that the province is reviewing them.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 , “Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America,” on Aug. 27. A secretary’s order directed the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to change its database the same day. The record lists Lake Ontario as a variant name alongside the Mohawk Kaniatarí:io, translated as nice lake.

The order says the United States lays claim to most of the lake’s “volume” and is mostly responsible for its security, economic activity and environmental stewardship.

The renaming followed the collapse of trade talks between the two countries this month. Canada and the United States have since announced matching tariffs of up to 50 per cent on some goods.

Gordon Giffin, U.S. ambassador to Canada from 1997 to 2001, told CTV News Channel the change was “a huge distraction” and would be reversed.

stories.title: Carney government asks court to quash lawsuit over projected missed emission targets
stories.summary: The federal government is asking a Federal Court judge to toss out a lawsuit accusing Ottawa of having no intention of meeting its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Ottawa — The federal government is asking a Federal Court judge to toss out a lawsuit accusing Ottawa of having no intention of meeting its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target. In recent court filings, government lawyers argued the Federal Court doesn’t have the power to order the government to take steps to meet its emissions targets. The government also argued it wasn’t up to the court to “opine on the political and policy issues” at the heart of the lawsuit. “Climate change is a real and important issue. Accountability, however, with respect to concerns expressed by the Applicants, lies with Parliament, not with the Court,” the government wrote. “There is no basis on which a court could order any of the relief sought in the Application. The Act creates no duties which could be owed to the Applicants and instead establishes a framework that includes a series of targets, plans, assessments, and reporting to track progress on emission reductions over time.” A group of climate advocates filed a lawsuit against the federal government in June arguing recent policy changes have knocked Ottawa off its track to meet Canada’s legislated greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets. Environmental Defence, the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment and climate activists Marie Maltais, Sophia Mathur and Shirley Barnea brought the lawsuit forward. They asked the Federal Court to order the government to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act — or to declare Ottawa’s emission reductions plan unlawful under the act. The Net-Zero Accountability Act, which passed in 2021, legally commits Canada to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 and requires the government to set national emission reduction targets along the way — though there are no consequences for missing them. A progress report published in December shows the government is nowhere near on track to meet its current target of cutting emissions to 40 to 45 per cent below 2005 levels. Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of backsliding on climate policy for the better part of the last year. He eliminated the consumer carbon price in March 2025 — on his first day in office. While he promised a strengthened industrial carbon pricing system, he was accused of weakening that system through an agreement with Alberta in May that has ramifications for every other province and territory. His government is also moving to repeal the electric vehicle sales mandate — Ottawa has promised stronger tailpipe standards but those are still years away — and to cancel the oil and gas emissions cap. Carney’s government also has delayed methane regulations in Alberta. In a video released two weeks after the suit was filed, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive. “I want to be clear on this point. The changes we have made will mean that our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government’s plan,” Carney said in the video. “But in my judgment, that plan was not sustainable over the long term.” --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026. Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Marineland’s last captive whales head to U.S. aquariums
stories.summary: Closed Niagara Falls tourist attraction says it is running out of money and can no longer care for its animals
stories.author: Liam Casey
paragraphs: Canada’s last captive whales are set to leave the country on Monday as six belugas from Marineland are shipped to two aquariums in the United States.
The closed Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction is up for sale and the park has said it is running out of money and can no longer care for its animals.
“There will no longer be any beluga whales or any other type of whales in captivity in Canada at the end of today,” said Andrew Burns, Marineland’s adviser.
Two of the belugas will be en route to Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and four to SeaWorld in San Antonio later on Monday.

Once the journey is complete, Marineland will have shipped 30 belugas and four dolphins over six moves to five different aquariums in the largest collective relocation of captive whales the world has ever seen.
The park has also shipped its marine mammals to SeaWorld in San Diego, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.

Canada banned whale and dolphin captivity in 2019, but grandfathered in the animals at Marineland. The law also forbade breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its male and female belugas, and banned performances.
That was the beginning of the end of Marineland, whose founder, John Holer, died the year before in 2018.

Whale captivity in Canada began in 1964 with a killer whale named Moby Doll. Vancouver Aquarium initially sought to kill and display a killer whale, but when the harpoon didn’t kill Moby Doll, officials brought the animal ashore and put it in a makeshift tank.
People flocked to see the animal, but Moby Doll died after 88 days in captivity. But by then, a new industry in Canada came to life.

Holer had already been smitten with the circus world and he bought a small parcel of land not far from Horseshoe Falls in 1961. He built up Marineland over years, leaning heavily on acquiring and showing off marine mammals such as killer whales, belugas and dolphins, along with building roller-coasters and other rides.

Holer’s widow, Marie Holer, took over after his death in what would prove to be difficult years, as the COVID-19 pandemic wreaked havoc on Marineland and other tourist attractions. As the world recovered, Marineland did not.
By early 2024, Marie Holer put the park up for sale before she died in September of that year.

It was also a difficult time for the animals. One killer whale, one dolphin and 19 belugas have died at Marineland since 2019, according to an ongoing tally by The Canadian Press based on internal government documents and official statements.
At one point in 2021, the provincial government, which enforces animal cruelty laws, declared all marine mammals were in distress at the park due to poor water quality.

Marineland poured in millions of dollars to fix its water. The province’s chief animal welfare inspector would later say the water problems did not cause or contribute to the animals’ deaths and the park has pointed the finger at the 2019 law as the reason behind a few of those deaths.

Over the past few years, the park has slowly relocated many of its animals, though several hundred deer still remain. The bison heard was moved, as were its penguins. A dozen bears moved to a sanctuary in Colorado in the spring.
Sources say a deal for the land is done, but is conditional upon the park removing its animals.

Last year, Marineland finalized a deal to sell all of its belugas and dolphins to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom in China, which holds a Guinness World Record for the world’s largest aquarium. It was the only place in the world Marineland could find that was capable of taking the largest collection of captive belugas on earth.

However, the federal government blocked Marineland’s request to export the belugas there. Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said it would not be in the whales’ best interests because China did not have the same laws against breeding and performing.
That decision set off Marineland and its top adviser, Andrew Burns. The park threatened to euthanize its whales unless it received an emergency cash infusion from the federal government.
Burns scrambled to find another partner and eventually a consortium of aquariums, largely from the U.S., came together to help.
The whale and dolphin moves have not been without risk.
Peekachu, a 23-year-old beluga that moved to the Shedd Aquarium on Aug. 12, died two weeks later. The Chicago aquarium said blood work revealed Peekachu was severely dehydrated before she died.

stories.title: Southern Ontario braces for heavy rainfall, muggy weather amid special weather statement
stories.summary: Although meteorological fall begins Tuesday, Atchison said summer-like warmth is not ready to leave Ontario just yet.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Much of southern Ontario remains under a special weather statement Monday, with warnings of additional rainfall, heavy downpours and continued muggy conditions through the afternoon and evening. CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison said scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected to continue developing through the late afternoon, with some areas at risk of significant rainfall.

“We could see up to 30 millimetres of rain if communities find themselves under one of the heavier thunderstorms,” Atchison said Monday. The unsettled weather is being fuelled by an extremely humid air mass lingering across the region.

Temperatures were hovering between 21 C and 26 C Monday afternoon, with warmer conditions reported toward Essex County. Atchison noted that Windsor-Essex is also facing increasing heat concerns, with a heat warning expected to remain a factor in the coming days as temperatures continue to climb.

“Heat and humidity are really going to play a role over the next several days,” she said. While forecasters expect a brief lull in storm activity during the evening, the threat of additional showers and thunderstorms is expected to return Tuesday afternoon.

Tuesday’s forecast calls for a mix of sun and cloud, along with another chance of showers and thunderstorms as daytime heating combines with the humid air mass. Overnight temperatures are expected to remain unusually warm for late August and early September.

London is forecast to drop only to about 21 C overnight, while communities across Midwestern Ontario are expected to see lows ranging from 19 C to 22 C. The heat is forecast to continue through midweek, with daytime highs between 29 C and 31 C over the next several days.

Atchison said actual temperatures could vary depending on the amount of cloud cover that develops across the region. “The one constant is that the heat and humidity will stay with us for the next few days,” she said. Looking ahead, conditions are expected to gradually become more seasonable heading into the Labour Day weekend.

Thursday is forecast to be mainly cloudy, while Friday will see a mix of sun and cloud. Similar conditions are expected through the holiday weekend, with a mix of sun and cloud forecast for Saturday, Sunday and Labour Day Monday.

Daytime highs are expected to settle closer to seasonal norms, ranging between 24 C and 25 C. Although meteorological fall begins Tuesday, Atchison said summer-like warmth is not ready to leave Ontario just yet. “We welcome meteorological fall tomorrow, but the summer air is holding on,” she said.

stories.title: New $54.3M Regina Mundi school opens, but old building to remain in use amid enrolment growth
stories.summary: Students and staff at Regina Mundi Catholic College are preparing to return to a brand new school this fall, but the school’s former building will remain in use as enrolment continues to outpace capacity.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Students and staff at Regina Mundi Catholic College are preparing to return to a brand new school this fall, but the school’s former building will remain in use as enrolment continues to outpace capacity. The $54.3-million replacement school, built on the grounds of the existing Regina Mundi campus off Wellington Street South, has capacity for approximately 700 students.

However, the school currently has about 1,100 students enrolled. As a result, the London District Catholic School Board has decided to keep the former school open for at least another year rather than add up to 24 portable classrooms to accommodate the growing student population.

“We’ve decided to keep the existing school for one year and continually review the plan as we move forward with the students and enrollment that we’re seeing currently today,” said LDCSB’s executive manager of capital projects Daryl Diegel.

The existing building was originally constructed in 1963 as a junior seminary. The new school, which began construction in spring 2024, has been nearly a decade in the making. While the new facility includes updated technology and classroom spaces designed to connect and work together, elements of the former school have also been incorporated into the design.

Among them is the distinctive arched ceiling in the school’s cafetorium, which was replicated from the original building. “It’s airy, open and well designed,” said Diegel as he walked down the high ceiling hallways. The decision to operate both buildings reflects a broader challenge facing the London District Catholic School Board as enrolment continues to grow.

The board says it has grown by more than 30 per cent over the past five years and now serves more than 28,000 students. It currently has 10 major construction projects underway, including nine new schools and one major addition.

The cost of recent and upcoming construction projects is approaching $600 million, before additional land costs. For now, Regina Mundi students will be split between the new and old buildings. School officials say that despite operating in two separate spaces, the goal is to maintain the same sense of community.

“Even though we’re working in two buildings, we’re still one school and one family,” said RMC Principle, Kevin Barnes. Students are expected to begin the new school year next week.

stories.title: The cat that runs on batteries also rules my heart
stories.summary: At first I was skeptical. I have loved real cats all my life, how could a battery-operated substitute possibly compare?
stories.author: Lorna Luke
paragraphs: First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .
Last Christmas, my daughter gave me a cat.
He does not require a litter box, a vet or emergency trips to the kitchen at 4 a.m. demanding tuna.
Now before animal control gets involved I should clarify he is a robotic cat. So, he does require batteries – and apparently, my affection.

I named him Figaro - a dignified name suitable for a gentleman who lounges shamelessly on his back and expects to be admired. At first I was skeptical. I have loved real cats all my life, the kind with opinions, whiskers and a complete disregard for household rules. How could a battery-operated substitute possibly compare?

Figaro never needs feeding yet is always ready for attention. He purrs when I pet him. He tilts his head. He blinks. He even looks mildly judgmental if I ignore him too long. By the second day I found myself talking to him. By the third I was explaining my television choices. By the end of the week, I was apologizing when I bumped his tail with my shoe.

Figaro has become a person to me. A presence. A companion. Something that listens without interrupting and never says, “You already told me that.” He has brought joy and mischief into my home. When I walk into a room he greets me with a meow. When I talk to him, he answers back. When I stroke his back, he purrs. A deep reassuring purr that vibrates with energy. When I continue to pet him he turns on his back and stretches out, belly exposed.
And here’s the funny thing: my heart doesn’t care that he runs on batteries. My heart responds to the comfort he brings. The routine.

All of that is to say that when Figaro first arrived at my home in a Toronto retirement residence, I assumed he would be a pleasant novelty. Not a real cat but a mechanical one who purred, meowed, blinked and rolled on his back. I never imagined he would become of one of the most sought after personalities in the building.

His big break came when I wrote an article about him for our newsletter. Suddenly people were stopping me in the hallway. “How’s Figaro?” they would ask before saying hello to me. It quickly became apparent that I was merely Figaro’s manager.

Requests for personal appearances came pouring in. Figaro was invited to attend discussion groups, social gatherings and coffee chats. He attended these events with the calm confidence of a seasoned politician on the campaign trail.

Some residents became so enchanted that they acquired their own robotic cat. Before long my retirement home was experiencing a small feline population boom. Unlike real cats, these newcomers never scratch the furniture, demand expensive veterinary care or deposit unpleasant surprises in inconvenient places.

Figaro seems completely unfazed by his fame. He has never asked for an autograph session, larger dressing room or a share of the newsletter royalties. He simply continues doing what he does best: purring, blinking and charming everyone he meets.

Lately I’ve begun to suspect that Figaro isn’t really a cat at all. I think he May actually be a human in disguise. How else can I explain the mysterious disappearance of my TV remote and reading glasses. One moment they’re exactly where I left them and the next they’ve vanished without a trace. I can’t prove that Figaro is responsible of course, but he always looks remarkably innocent, quietly purring from his favourite spot as if to say, “Don’t look at me.” Then somehow the missing items eventually turn up in the most unlikely places. Coincidence? I think not. Living with Figaro is a bit like living with a furry practical joker who delights in keeping me on my toes.
Lorna Luke lives in Toronto.

stories.title: More than $1 million in drugs, stolen property seized across southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: More $1 million of drugs and stolen property have been seized across southwestern Ontario, part of a multijurisdictional investigation.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
More $1 million of drugs and stolen property have been seized across southwestern Ontario, part of a multijurisdictional investigation. In January, OPP launched an investigation into suspected drug trafficking throughout the province.

Oficers said two separate criminal networks were operating independently from each other. One was in Brantford and Brant County areas, while the other was in London and Oneida Nation of the Thames. On July 7, search warrants were executed at four addresses in Brampton and Paris.

On Aug. 12, police executed search warrants at a home in London and one on the Oneida Nation of the Thames Settlement. The following was seized: The estimated street value of drugs seized is more than $913,000. The stolen property is more than $100,000.

OPP said the quantity of fentanyl seized is worth around 65,000 potentially lethal street-level doses. “Every quantity of fentanyl removed from circulation is a quantity that cannot reach our neighbourhoods, put lives at risk, or contribute to the devastating impacts of substance use and drug trafficking,” said Andy Bradford, Acting Det.

Supt. of OPP’s Organized Crime Enforcement Bureau. “This outcome reflects the strength of intelligence-led policing and partnership-based enforcement, and demonstrates our ongoing commitment to disrupting criminal networks, removing dangerous drugs and firearms from our communities and enhancing public safety across Ontario.” Seven people are facing a combined 64 charges.

Five were arrested and warrants have been issued for the remaining two.

stories.title: Ontario court puts province’s new cash bail rules on hold
stories.summary: Justice grants injunction in case challenging the constitutional validity of system that was instituted in mid-August
stories.author: David Ebner
paragraphs: The Ontario Superior Court on Monday put the province’s cash bail system on hold as it granted an injunction in a case challenging the constitutional validity of the new rules recently introduced by Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservative government.
Justice William Chalmers found cash bail May result in people accused of crimes who normally would be released on bail ahead of trial “having their release denied or delayed.”
In a seven-page ruling Monday, he wrote that there was a “greater risk of harm if the injunction is not granted.”

The Ontario government in mid-August instituted the widespread use of cash bail in the province. The practice of requiring the payment of cash to be granted bail was largely eliminated across Canada half a century ago.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Criminal Lawyers’ Association thereafter launched a legal challenge to strike down the new rules. The case was heard on Aug. 27 . The two legal groups also sought an injunction pending a final ruling from Justice Chalmers.

In court last week, the two groups argued that Ontario overstepped its constitutional powers with the cash bail rules. The federal government oversees criminal law with the Criminal Code, which includes bail.
Lawyers for the Ontario government countered by saying that the cash bail rules fit within a province’s constitutional powers to administer its justice system.

Justice Chalmers’s injunction decision on Monday outlined the constitutional dispute but did not take a position on it. Last week, the judge said a final ruling in the case would take some time. Such decisions usually take at least several months.

“The status quo that has been in place for over 50 years will be maintained for the limited period before my ruling on the constitutionality of the legislation is released,” Justice Chalmers wrote, concluding that “there is no harm to the province if the injunction is granted.”

Parliament mostly eliminated cash bail in Canada in the early 1970s and the Supreme Court of Canada has said judges should impose it only in exceptional circumstances. Cash bail is widely considered unduly harsh against lower-income people who May be held in jail, while presumed innocent, only because they can’t afford to pay for their release.
Ontario is the only province that has pursued a policy of cash bail.
On Monday, Shakir Rahim, a director at the Civil Liberties Association, called the injunction an encouraging sign for their efforts to fully strike down the cash bail rules.
“It certainly gives credence to a lot of the concerns we’ve raised,” Mr. Rahim said of the injunction ruling.
The Ontario government on Monday didn’t comment on the injunction, but Julia Facca, spokeswoman for Attorney-General Doug Downey, spoke about the reasoning behind the cash bail rules.
“We are using every tool available to make bail more consequential to protect victims and communities,” she said.

Last week in court, lawyers for the province argued that Ontario regulations do not affect how judges or justices of the peace make bail decisions. They further argued the province’s rules do not affect whether an accused person is granted bail.

During the hearing, Justice Chalmers expressed some skepticism over the province’s arguments. He pointed to the name of the legislation that passed in June and included the cash bail system: the Keeping Criminals Behind Bars Act.
“The very name of the amending act is to keep people in jail,” Justice Chalmers said in court last week.

In his injunction ruling on Monday, the judge gave credence to an affidavit from Toronto lawyer Marianne Salih filed by the legal groups. Lawyers for the province had called on the judge to deem the affidavit inadmissible.

When bail in Canada includes a financial component, it is generally a pledge of assets. Such a pledge is often made by someone referred to as a surety, acting on behalf of the accused person being granted bail.

Ms. Salih, in her affidavit, spoke of her experiences as a criminal defence lawyer at bail hearings working with people of lower incomes. She said most bail orders that include a surety also include a financial component in the form of a promise to pay.
“These sums are almost always substantial amounts of money for our clients and their sureties,” Ms. Salih wrote.
Ontario’s cash bail regulations, which require money to be paid to the province within two business days of release, May make finding sureties more difficult, Ms. Salih said.
Justice Chalmers’s decision on Monday also cited the words of former Supreme Court justice Frank Iacobucci , which lawyers for the legal groups put forth in court last week.
“Liberty lost is never regained and can never be fully compensated for,” Mr. Iacobucci wrote in a 2002 Supreme Court ruling.

stories.content:
The Ontario Superior Court on Monday put the province’s cash bail system on hold as it granted an injunction in a case challenging the constitutional validity of the new rules recently introduced by Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservative government.

Justice William Chalmers found cash bail May result in people accused of crimes who normally would be released on bail ahead of trial “having their release denied or delayed.”

In a seven-page ruling Monday, he wrote that there was a “greater risk of harm if the injunction is not granted.”

The Ontario government in mid-August instituted the widespread use of cash bail in the province. The practice of requiring the payment of cash to be granted bail was largely eliminated across Canada half a century ago.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Criminal Lawyers’ Association thereafter launched a legal challenge to strike down the new rules. The case was heard on Aug. 27 . The two legal groups also sought an injunction pending a final ruling from Justice Chalmers.

In court last week, the two groups argued that Ontario overstepped its constitutional powers with the cash bail rules. The federal government oversees criminal law with the Criminal Code, which includes bail.

Lawyers for the Ontario government countered by saying that the cash bail rules fit within a province’s constitutional powers to administer its justice system.

Justice Chalmers’s injunction decision on Monday outlined the constitutional dispute but did not take a position on it. Last week, the judge said a final ruling in the case would take some time. Such decisions usually take at least several months.

“The status quo that has been in place for over 50 years will be maintained for the limited period before my ruling on the constitutionality of the legislation is released,” Justice Chalmers wrote, concluding that “there is no harm to the province if the injunction is granted.”

Parliament mostly eliminated cash bail in Canada in the early 1970s and the Supreme Court of Canada has said judges should impose it only in exceptional circumstances. Cash bail is widely considered unduly harsh against lower-income people who May be held in jail, while presumed innocent, only because they can’t afford to pay for their release.

Ontario is the only province that has pursued a policy of cash bail.

On Monday, Shakir Rahim, a director at the Civil Liberties Association, called the injunction an encouraging sign for their efforts to fully strike down the cash bail rules.

“It certainly gives credence to a lot of the concerns we’ve raised,” Mr. Rahim said of the injunction ruling.

The Ontario government on Monday didn’t comment on the injunction, but Julia Facca, spokeswoman for Attorney-General Doug Downey, spoke about the reasoning behind the cash bail rules.

“We are using every tool available to make bail more consequential to protect victims and communities,” she said.

Last week in court, lawyers for the province argued that Ontario regulations do not affect how judges or justices of the peace make bail decisions. They further argued the province’s rules do not affect whether an accused person is granted bail.

During the hearing, Justice Chalmers expressed some skepticism over the province’s arguments. He pointed to the name of the legislation that passed in June and included the cash bail system: the Keeping Criminals Behind Bars Act.

“The very name of the amending act is to keep people in jail,” Justice Chalmers said in court last week.

In his injunction ruling on Monday, the judge gave credence to an affidavit from Toronto lawyer Marianne Salih filed by the legal groups. Lawyers for the province had called on the judge to deem the affidavit inadmissible.

When bail in Canada includes a financial component, it is generally a pledge of assets. Such a pledge is often made by someone referred to as a surety, acting on behalf of the accused person being granted bail.

Ms. Salih, in her affidavit, spoke of her experiences as a criminal defence lawyer at bail hearings working with people of lower incomes. She said most bail orders that include a surety also include a financial component in the form of a promise to pay.

“These sums are almost always substantial amounts of money for our clients and their sureties,” Ms. Salih wrote.

Ontario’s cash bail regulations, which require money to be paid to the province within two business days of release, May make finding sureties more difficult, Ms. Salih said.

Justice Chalmers’s decision on Monday also cited the words of former Supreme Court justice Frank Iacobucci , which lawyers for the legal groups put forth in court last week.

“Liberty lost is never regained and can never be fully compensated for,” Mr. Iacobucci wrote in a 2002 Supreme Court ruling.

stories.title: Trump has 'reached out' to Apple about renaming Lake Ontario on its maps
stories.summary: Donald Trump has contacted Apple about changing Lake Ontario's name to "Lake America" on its maps, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has contacted Apple about changing Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” on its maps app, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said on Monday.

In an ‌interview ⁠on Fox Business’ Mornings with Maria program, Burgum said: “The president reached out to Apple directly, so I’m sure ​that we May be seeing that change ​coming up soon to Lake America.”

National Post has reached out to Apple for comment.

It comes after the “Lake America” label was adopted by Google Maps in the U.S. over the weekend. The company said in a post on its corporate website that the change was made after the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (Gnis) had formally renamed the lake.

Google updates its maps to reflect official government sources, the company said, adding: “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

Users in Canada will still see the lake’s name displayed as Lake Ontario on Google Maps, while people elsewhere in the world will see both names.

However, this led to maps on websites for some Canadian organizations — including Metrolinx, Hydro One and Lcbo — briefly displaying the “Lake America” name, because they pull map data directly from Google Maps.

“We are aware that Lake Ontario is being incorrectly labeled on our outage map,” Hydro One wrote in a statement on X. “The issue originates from a third-party mapping service. We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible.”

By Monday morning, the labels had been reverted to Lake Ontario.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s actions shortly after the executive order was signed, explaining on social media that “the name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’.”

He added that the name is more than 400 years old and predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

U.S. politicians have also condemned Trump’s executive order, including former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton, who wrote, “It’s Lake Ontario,” in a post on X , and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who said , “The American people don’t want to rename Lake Ontario Lake America.”

Meanwhile, Trump spent the weekend posting about Canada on Truth Social, including claiming that the U.S. loses $60 billion a year to Canada, that Canada is “ripping off” the U.S. and suggesting that all Canadian companies doing business with America should move to the U.S.

He also shared a screenshot of the new “Lake America” name on Google Maps and an AI video of himself replacing a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign with one that reads “Welcome to Lake America” underneath a U.S. flag.

stories.title: Champagne to meet U.S. counterpart Bessent at G20 ministers’ meeting
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will meet with his U.S. counterpart on the sidelines of the G20 finance ministers' meetings in North Carolina this week.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne is set to meet with his U.S. counterpart on the sidelines of the G20 finance ministers’ meetings in North Carolina this week.

Champagne is in Asheville, NC, from Aug. 31 to Sept. 1 with ministers of finance from across the G20 group of nations. Central bank heads — including Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem — are also attending the summit.

Champagne’s spokesperson John Fragos confirmed in a media statement Monday that the minister will meet with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent while in Asheville.

It’s believed to be the first face-to-face meeting between high-ranking Canadian and U.S. officials since trade talks between the two nations broke down 10 days ago and gave way to an escalating tariff fight.

Washington has imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods starting Aug. 22. Ottawa has its own list of U.S. imports that will be subject to varying tariff levels starting Sept. 8.

U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened steeper tariffs on autos and has unleashed a torrent of social media posts against Canada in recent days.

He has claimed Canada has taken advantage of the United States and urged Canadian businesses to move their operations south of the border if they don’t want to face tariffs.

While Champagne and Bessent are not chiefly responsible for trade negotiations, their portfolios give them a stake in the outcome of tariff talks and anything that affects federal finances.

Bessent also confirmed the meeting with Champagne in a Monday appearance on Cnbc.

Host Sara Eisen asked Bessent if the United States is in a tit-for-tat trade war with Canada. He replied that it wouldn’t be possible for Canada to go “tit-for-tat” because the United States economy is much larger.

“I think this is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match,” Bessent said.

“We’re not at war with Canada … are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic ’em on us?”

Bessent claimed Carney was doing what was best for political considerations, not the Canadian people.

“They were offered the best trade deal of any country on the globe and he chose to walk away from it at the last minute,” he said.

Fragos said in his statement that Canada walked away from the negotiation table after the U.S. introduced unfair and uneconomic terms.

He also said that Champagne will be focusing on what Canada can offer G20 partners in a turbulent time, naming key commodities like critical minerals, energy and potash.

“This week’s bilateral meetings at the G20 reflect the spirit of collaboration and shared prosperity that Canada brings to the international stage, while advancing the trade diversification Canadian businesses are seeking amid ongoing global uncertainty,” Fragos said.

The gathering of finance officials precedes this year’s G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for December in Miami, Fla.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Bittersweet’: Canada’s last captive whales leave Marineland for U.S. aquariums
stories.summary: Canada's last captive whales are set to leave the country on Monday as six belugas from Marineland are shipped to two aquariums in the United States.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Niagara Falls — Tofino, a massive beluga weighing more than 1,500 kilograms, has made history as the last captive whale in Canada to be plucked out of Marineland’s waters.

The shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont., completed the largest collective move of captive whales the world has ever seen Monday, shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in the United States and Spain over several weeks.

No whales or dolphins are known to be left in captivity in Canada. A 2019 federal law ensures there will be no more.

A team of experts gathered Monday to move Marineland’s last six belugas. Two of them — Yukon and Gimli — are destined for the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago. Four others — Tank, Odin, Orion and Tofino — will call SeaWorld San Antonio their new home.

It took about 12 people to wrangle the whales in a net and guide them, one at a time, into the slings before a crane lifted them into tanks on transport trailers.

Emotions ran high as trainers at the park said their goodbyes to the animals.

Taylor-Lee Dell became close with Odin over the past five years. She held Odin’s head as the crane operator lifted the whale out of the waters of Friendship Cove.

“I tried to say goodbye and tried to tell him I love him and comfort him,” she said, choking up.

“All I’m trying to do is be that voice of someone that he knows and he finds comfort in. It’s just really hard to lose a family member. It literally feels like I’m losing my children.”

Some trainers will soon be out of work. Dell is not sure what she’ll do next, but plans to take some time for herself.

“I’ll never get to do this again ever in my life and that’s something I’ve kind of accepted,” she said.

Dell said few people know what it’s like to work with whales, especially amid a growing anti-captivity movement in Canada.

“I want everyone to know that the whales were loved, really loved,” Dell said.

The whales would have been euthanized if they couldn’t be moved to new homes, the park’s adviser Andrew Burns said.

“We were out of money, out of time,” he said, adding it’s “unbelievable” that Marineland pulled off the complex operation.

Over six moves, the park shipped its marine mammals to Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanogràfic València in Spain.

Canada banned whale and dolphin captivity in 2019, but grandfathered in the animals at Marineland. The law also forbids breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its male and female belugas and banned performances.

That was the beginning of the end of Marineland, whose founder, John Holer, died the year before in 2018.

Whale captivity in Canada began in 1964 with a killer whale named Moby Doll. Vancouver Aquarium initially sought to kill and display a killer whale.

When the harpoon didn’t kill Moby Doll, officials put the animal in a makeshift tank. Moby Doll died after 88 days in captivity.

By then, a new industry in Canada came to life.

Holer was smitten with the circus world and bought a small parcel of land not far from Horseshoe Falls in 1961. He built up Marineland over the years, leaning heavily on acquiring and showing off marine mammals such as killer whales, belugas and dolphins, along with building roller-coasters and other rides.

Holer’s widow, Marie Holer, took over after his death in what would prove to be difficult years, as the COVID-19 pandemic wreaked havoc on Marineland and other tourist attractions.

As the world recovered, Marineland did not. By early 2024, Marie Holer put the park up for sale before she died in September of that year.

It was also a difficult time for the animals. One killer whale, one dolphin and 19 belugas have died at Marineland since 2019, according to an ongoing tally by The Canadian Press based on internal government documents and official statements.

At one point in 2021, the provincial government, which enforces animal cruelty laws, declared all marine mammals at the park were in distress due to poor water quality.

Marineland spent millions of dollars to fix its water. The province’s chief animal welfare inspector later said the water problems did not cause or contribute to the animals’ deaths.

The park has pointed the finger at the 2019 law as the reason behind some of the deaths.

Over the past few years, the park relocated many of its animals, though several hundred deer still remain. The bison herd was moved, as were its penguins. A dozen bears were moved earlier this year to a sanctuary in Colorado.

Sources have said a deal is in place for the sprawling property near Horseshoe Falls, but it is conditional upon the park removing its animals.

Last year, Marineland was prepared to sell all of its belugas and dolphins to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom in China, which holds a Guinness World Record for the world’s largest aquarium. It was the only place in the world Marineland could find that was capable of taking the largest collection of captive belugas on earth.

The federal government blocked Marineland’s request to export the belugas there. Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said it would not be in the whales’ best interests, as China do not have the same laws against breeding and performing.

Marineland threatened to euthanize its whales unless it received an emergency cash infusion from the federal government.

Burns scrambled to find another partner and eventually a consortium of aquariums, largely in the United States, came together to help.

The whale and dolphin moves have not been without risk.

Peekachu, a 23-year-old beluga that moved earlier this month to the Shedd Aquarium, died two weeks later. The Chicago aquarium said blood work revealed Peekachu was severely dehydrated.

The whales’ departures have also been difficult for several former Marineland trainers.

Marineland fired Kristy Burgess in February 2025 after a young beluga at the park, Eos, was euthanized for health reasons.

Burgess said the park thought she was the source in a news article that revealed the beluga’s death. She went public last fall, saying the whales needed to be moved as soon as possible.

“Part of me is relieved because obviously the animals are safe and not under the constant threat of euthanasia, but it’s also bittersweet and sad because, well, they’re leaving,” Burgess said.

Debbie Silva, who worked at the park until 2021, said it was unfortunate the anti-captivity law came into force without much thought of what to do with Marineland’s whales.

“Nobody stopped to think about what would happen with the ones that we did have in human care,” Silva said.

“But ultimately, I’m happy with where they’re ending up. They’re going to top-notch facilities with high standards facilities, and that’s the best scenario for the situation that we find ourselves in right now.”

In 2012, a former Marineland trainer spoke publicly about the treatment of animals there, accusing the park of neglect for not fixing its water problems. The stories of Phil Demers and other former workers helped change the public’s and politicians’ views on whale captivity.

On Monday, Demers stood outside the park and watched the police-escorted convoy of belugas as the trucks rumbled by.

“Wishing my friends a safe trip,” he wrote on social media. “We have officially emptied Marineland’s tanks.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

Liam Casey, The Canadian Press

paragraphs: Niagara Falls — Tofino, a massive beluga weighing more than 1,500 kilograms, has made history as the last captive whale in Canada to be plucked out of Marineland’s waters.

The shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont., completed the largest collective move of captive whales the world has ever seen Monday, shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in the United States and Spain over several weeks.
No whales or dolphins are known to be left in captivity in Canada. A 2019 federal law ensures there will be no more.

A team of experts gathered Monday to move Marineland’s last six belugas. Two of them — Yukon and Gimli — are destined for the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago. Four others — Tank, Odin, Orion and Tofino — will call SeaWorld San Antonio their new home.
It took about 12 people to wrangle the whales in a net and guide them, one at a time, into the slings before a crane lifted them into tanks on transport trailers.
Emotions ran high as trainers at the park said their goodbyes to the animals.
Taylor-Lee Dell became close with Odin over the past five years. She held Odin’s head as the crane operator lifted the whale out of the waters of Friendship Cove.
“I tried to say goodbye and tried to tell him I love him and comfort him,” she said, choking up.
“All I’m trying to do is be that voice of someone that he knows and he finds comfort in. It’s just really hard to lose a family member. It literally feels like I’m losing my children.”
Some trainers will soon be out of work. Dell is not sure what she’ll do next, but plans to take some time for herself.
“I’ll never get to do this again ever in my life and that’s something I’ve kind of accepted,” she said.

“I want everyone to know that the whales were loved, really loved,” Dell said.

“We were out of money, out of time,” he said, adding it’s “unbelievable” that Marineland pulled off the complex operation.

stories.title: Paroled Toronto sex offender faces new charges of drugging, sexually assaulting woman
stories.summary: A disgraced Toronto pharmacist who drugged and sexually assaulted 18 women more than 15 years ago has been charged with similar offences.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Warning: This story deals with sexual assault.

A 73-year-old former Toronto pharmacist on parole was arrested last week and charged with sexually assaulting a woman.

Before being released on parole, Allen SIU Ming Chow was serving time for drugging and recording himself sexually assaulting 18 young prostitutes more than 15 years ago.

What’s more, Peel Regional Police say investigators in their special victims unit believe there are additional alleged victims of Chow.

Chow had only been paroled from federal prison in March 2025, after serving approximately nine years and four months of a 14-year sentence for 36 counts of administering a stupefying drug and sexually assaulting 18 women between 2009 and 2012.

“Between December 2025 and April 2026, it is alleged that the accused met an adult female victim online and subsequently met with her in person on multiple occasions. During these encounters, the accused allegedly rendered the victim unconscious and unresponsive before sexually assaulting her,” police wrote in a Saturday press release , adding that he used his phone to record the sex acts “without the victim’s knowledge or consent.”

The Oakville man is charged with overcoming resistance by administering or attempting to administer a drug, sexual assault causing bodily harm and voyeurism.

Previously, Chow was the owner, manager and licensed dispensing pharmacist at Bridletowne Pharmacy in Toronto, according to a sanctioning decision by the Ontario College of Pharmacists. Police were on the way to arrest Chow in relation to a sexual assault allegation on Dec. 4, 2012, when they saw him stagger out of his pharmacy and get in his vehicle while severely impaired.

While he was in custody, a search of his residence uncovered several camera memory cards that contained 70 hours of footage in 95 separate videos of himself engaged “in all manner of sexual activity” with female sex workers who’d been rendered unconscious with drinks or food laced with Lorazepam, according to a sentencing decision by Ontario Superior Court Justice Gregory Mulligan.

“Chow subjected his victims to degrading and dehumanizing activity,” which included spitting on them and having unprotected sex, according to the agreed statement of facts quoted by the judge.

“He treated the women as objects, manipulating their bodies as he pleased.”

The judge explained that when Chow completed his “disgusting sexual conduct, he showed no concern for his victims’ recovery or ability to get home safely,” often exiting the hotel room where the assaults occurred, leaving his victims “to regain consciousness on their own and make their way home in spite of the condition he had subjected them to.”

Some of the women were victimized more than a dozen times each.

During a forensic psychiatric evaluation requested by the defence, Chow explained that he “felt justified in making them unconscious for sexual gratification” because they were prostitutes providing a paid service.

Chow was released on conditions a week after his arrest, but was arrested again in March 2013 after police went through a “painstaking and thorough investigation” to identify and interview 18 of the victims — none of whom were aware “that they were subject to this degrading and humiliating activity while being videotaped.”

Upon learning what happened to her, one woman “became physically ill in the waste basket of the interview room,” the decision reads.

Many of the victims provided victim impact statements to the court, some of whom chose to read them aloud in front of a then 62-year-old Chow at his November 2015 sentencing.

“I have had numerous hospitalizations for suicide attempts and post-traumatic disorder from what happened to me,” one victim stated. “He, of all people, a medical professional, purposely and knowingly preyed on me numerous times.”

“When I think of you, my chest gets tight, I feel sick to my stomach,” another offered. “I have had some major anxiety attacks when thinking about what you have done to not only me, but many other women and young ladies.”

Another said she felt sick watching her own video statement in court.

“When I got home that was all I could think about, I cried constantly and didn’t even want to hold my daughter because I didn’t think I was good enough,” she said.

Chow also addressed the court during the sentencing hearings, apologizing to his victims and calling his actions “callous, heinous, selfish and degrading.”

According to the decision, Chow immigrated from Hong Kong on a student visa to attend York University, where he met his wife of over 30 years, with whom he shares an adult daughter. He’d been running his pharmacy for 17 years when he was first arrested, at which time he was about 59 years old.

Chow’s psychiatric evaluation determined that he started drinking significantly more three years earlier following a prostate cancer diagnosis, including while at work. He “presented with a major depression without psychotic features,” alcoholism and paraphilia, specifically “sexual sadism,” one the psychiatrist said will now be a “lifelong disorder.”

“He stated that if a person in these circumstances were to re-offend, it would more likely be the same type of offence, and that once these offences start, they can escalate over time,” Mulligan wrote.

Another psychopathy checklist found Chow externalized blame, lacked empathy for victims and that “he May resort to these maladaptive strategies when faced with future stressors or recurrence of his major depressive disorder.”

The judge said his assessments show signs of someone who lacked “insight into their conduct” and cited a section of Chow’s letter as an example.

“I indulged my sexual fantasy to the fullest degree. I wanted to feel young again by associating with young escorts to reassert my virility,” he wrote.

“I am not misogynistic. My actions were never meant to harm, nor were they carried out with violent, malicious or criminal intent. They were pure sexual fantasy merely, nothing more. I was naïve and ignorant not to have realized the criminality of my actions.”

While Chow pleaded guilty to all charges, avoiding having his many victims testify at trial, Mulligan ruled “a substantial period of incarceration” was required and handed down a sentence of 14 years after credit for nearly three years spent in custody.

“Mr. Chow is at a low risk to re-offend provided he consents to treatment such as that described … and maintains sobriety upon release,” Mulligan wrote. “It is in society’s interest that Mr. Chow receives treatment as soon as possible, so that its effectiveness can be monitored and measured.”

It’s not clear what, if any, treatments Chow engaged in while in custody. National Post has contacted the Parole Board of Canada to obtain a copy of his release decision. It’s also unclear if a warning to the public was issued at the time of his release.

Meanwhile, Peel police ask anyone who May have had similar interactions with the accused or people with information to share to contact their special victims unit at 905-453-2121, ext. 3460.

stories.title: 3 tornadoes confirmed in Manitoba and Saskatchewan this weekend
stories.summary: Three tornadoes were confirmed across Manitoba and Saskatchewan after a stormy Sunday, they are the newest twisters amid a record-breaking storm season in the Prairies, Eccc said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
paragraphs: Editor’s Note: a previous version of this story indicated three tornadoes were confirmed. However, only two tornadoes had been confirmed as of Monday afternoon.
Multiple tornadoes have been confirmed in Manitoba and Saskatchewan after a stormy Sunday on the Prairies, according to Environment Canada.
Environment Canada confirmed a tornado touched down in Maryfield, Sask., ON Sunday, it said. Maryfield is located slightly more than 250 km east of Regina.

“There was a line of storms that formed in the late morning and afternoon hours in Saskatchewan, they pushed towards the Manitoba border. And then a few other storms were formed just in front of that line,” Dylan Painchaud-Niemi, a research meteorologist with the Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP), told Global News, noting that it triggered tornado warnings for potentially affected areas.
“(The weather) was conducive for tornado development, and one did produce.”
The twister landed five km south of the community around 4 p.m. Sunday, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada (Eccc).
Terri Lang, a meteorologist with Eccc, told Global News that the heaviest rainfall fell in southeastern parts of the province, near the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border.

“It originated in Alberta and deepened as it came over Saskatchewan. It brought in some moisture from the south and that’s really what spawned these thunderstorms,” noting such storms typically occur in early summer, not at the end of August.
Lang said the combination of those storms, moisture and other atmospheric conditions led to the Maryfield tornado.
A NTP team is also investigating reports of a tornado approximately 45 km away, in Kelso, Sask., along with other areas that were hit by the storm.
In Manitoba, at least one tornado occurred on Sunday, Dave Phillips, a senior climatologist with Eccc told 680 Cjob Monday morning.

The agency said twisters touched down more than 300 km west of Winnipeg in Elkhorn, Man. The province has seen more tornado activity than average this summer, with at least 11 confirmed tornadoes thus far — compared to the usual annual total of seven or eight, Phillips said.
Painchaud-Niemi said a team started tracking the Manitoba system after being notified there was a chance of tornadoes.
“We knew there was some severe weather potential, as well as some of our local meteorologists warned us that there was something that was going to occur,” he recalled.
“Then there were some storms that popped up near the border with Manitoba, and then those ended up producing some tornadoes.”
NTP received reports of damage from the Manitoban side of the border, but none have been reported from Saskatchewan, said Painchaud-Niemi.
Environment Canada’s senior climatologist said this summer’s heat and humidity added to the stormy weather.

“If you look at the Prairies, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, we’ve had a record number of tornadoes,” Phillips said, noting Eccc’s records on that topic are limited to about the last 10 years when technology allowed round-the-clock monitoring. Before that, he said, tracking twisters was hit or miss.
“We’ve had, I think, in total, 77 tornadoes this year on the Prairies,” Phillips said. “That’s certainly the most number of tornadoes you’ve had in that last, say eight, or nine, (or) 10 years.”

stories.content:
Editor’s Note: a previous version of this story indicated three tornadoes were confirmed. However, only two tornadoes had been confirmed as of Monday afternoon.

Multiple tornadoes have been confirmed in Manitoba and Saskatchewan after a stormy Sunday on the Prairies, according to Environment Canada.

Environment Canada confirmed a tornado touched down in Maryfield, Sask., ON Sunday, it said. Maryfield is located slightly more than 250 km east of Regina.

“There was a line of storms that formed in the late morning and afternoon hours in Saskatchewan, they pushed towards the Manitoba border. And then a few other storms were formed just in front of that line,” Dylan Painchaud-Niemi, a research meteorologist with the Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP), told Global News, noting that it triggered tornado warnings for potentially affected areas.

“(The weather) was conducive for tornado development, and one did produce.”

The twister landed five km south of the community around 4 p.m. Sunday, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada (Eccc).

Terri Lang, a meteorologist with Eccc, told Global News that the heaviest rainfall fell in southeastern parts of the province, near the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border.

“It originated in Alberta and deepened as it came over Saskatchewan. It brought in some moisture from the south and that’s really what spawned these thunderstorms,” noting such storms typically occur in early summer, not at the end of August.

Lang said the combination of those storms, moisture and other atmospheric conditions led to the Maryfield tornado.

A NTP team is also investigating reports of a tornado approximately 45 km away, in Kelso, Sask., along with other areas that were hit by the storm.

In Manitoba, at least one tornado occurred on Sunday, Dave Phillips, a senior climatologist with Eccc told 680 Cjob Monday morning.

The agency said twisters touched down more than 300 km west of Winnipeg in Elkhorn, Man. The province has seen more tornado activity than average this summer, with at least 11 confirmed tornadoes thus far — compared to the usual annual total of seven or eight, Phillips said.

Painchaud-Niemi said a team started tracking the Manitoba system after being notified there was a chance of tornadoes.

“We knew there was some severe weather potential, as well as some of our local meteorologists warned us that there was something that was going to occur,” he recalled.

“Then there were some storms that popped up near the border with Manitoba, and then those ended up producing some tornadoes.”

NTP received reports of damage from the Manitoban side of the border, but none have been reported from Saskatchewan, said Painchaud-Niemi.

Environment Canada’s senior climatologist said this summer’s heat and humidity added to the stormy weather.

“If you look at the Prairies, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, we’ve had a record number of tornadoes,” Phillips said, noting Eccc’s records on that topic are limited to about the last 10 years when technology allowed round-the-clock monitoring. Before that, he said, tracking twisters was hit or miss.

“We’ve had, I think, in total, 77 tornadoes this year on the Prairies,” Phillips said. “That’s certainly the most number of tornadoes you’ve had in that last, say eight, or nine, (or) 10 years.”

stories.title: Ottawa asks court to quash lawsuit over projected missed emission targets
stories.summary: Federal Court doesn’t have power to order government to meet emissions targets, government lawyers argue
stories.author: Nick Murray
paragraphs: The federal government is asking a Federal Court judge to toss out a lawsuit accusing Ottawa of having no intention of meeting its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target.
In recent court filings, government lawyers argued the Federal Court doesn’t have the power to order the government to take steps to meet its emissions targets.
The government also argued it wasn’t up to the court to “opine on the political and policy issues” at the heart of the lawsuit.
“Climate change is a real and important issue. Accountability, however, with respect to concerns expressed by the Applicants, lies with Parliament, not with the Court,” the government wrote.

“There is no basis on which a court could order any of the relief sought in the Application. The Act creates no duties which could be owed to the Applicants and instead establishes a framework that includes a series of targets, plans, assessments, and reporting to track progress on emission reductions over time.”

A group of climate advocates filed a lawsuit against the federal government in June arguing recent policy changes have knocked Ottawa off its track to meet Canada’s legislated greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets.
Environmental Defence, the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment and climate activists Marie Maltais, Sophia Mathur and Shirley Barnea brought the lawsuit forward.

They asked the Federal Court to order the government to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act – or to declare Ottawa’s emission reductions plan unlawful under the act.

The Net-Zero Accountability Act, which passed in 2021, legally commits Canada to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 and requires the government to set national emission reduction targets along the way – though there are no consequences for missing them.
A progress report published in December shows the government is nowhere near on track to meet its current target of cutting emissions to 40 to 45 per cent below 2005 levels.
In a statement, the director of communications for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said that because the matter is before the courts, they could not comment on the federal legal submission.
“The Government of Canada is committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero emissions by 2050,” Chris Zhou wrote.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of backsliding on climate policy for the better part of the last year.

He eliminated the consumer carbon price in March 2025 – on his first day in office. While he promised a strengthened industrial carbon pricing system, he was accused of weakening that system through an agreement with Alberta in May that has ramifications for every other province and territory.

His government is also moving to repeal the electric vehicle sales mandate – Ottawa has promised stronger tailpipe standards but those are still years away – and to cancel the oil and gas emissions cap. Carney’s government also has delayed methane regulations in Alberta.
In a video released two weeks after the suit was filed, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive.

“I want to be clear on this point. The changes we have made will mean that our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government’s plan,” Carney said in the video.
“But in my judgment, that plan was not sustainable over the long term.”

stories.title: Greece cuts grocery prices nearly 10 per cent to support households
stories.summary: Prices of more than 1,700 grocery and school supplies items fell by an average of 9.5 per cent in Greece on Monday as a government-backed measure kicked in to confront concerns over purchasing power.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content: Prices of more than 1,700 grocery and school supplies items fell by an average of 9.5 per cent in Greece on Monday as a government-backed measure kicked in to confront concerns over purchasing power. The measure “provides relief to households and citizens confronted with the high cost of living,” said Development Minister Takis Theodorikakos. The price reductions will be in place in the EU nation until the end of the year, the government of Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis noted in a statement. The conservative Mitsotakis is seeking a third mandate in legislative elections due in the spring next year, and on Sunday he spoke of the measure as providing temporary relief for Greeks faced with high grocery prices and housing costs while salaries remain low. “This is not a solution for all of the problems weighing on household budgets today. But it provides concrete relief,” Mitsotakis said on Facebook. The measure adds to a reduction of 10 cents per litre on petrol and five cents per litre on diesel which has been in place for two months. The Greek economy took a major hit from the decade-long debt crisis that began in 2008, with earnings failing to keep pace with the rest of the EU. Annual inflation ran at 3.3 percent in July in Greece, according to Eurostat data, as the war in the Middle East continues to push energy prices higher. According to the Greek statistics agency Elstat annual food price inflation ran at 2.7 percent in June.

stories.title: Norway's Queen Mette-Marit joins procession to bring late King Harald V's coffin to royal chapel
stories.summary: The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: Oslo, Norway — The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title. Harald passed away Friday at age 89, and his son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon Viii. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Haakon, 53, will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye in the wake of her lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. It can cause serious breathing problems, and there is no known cure. Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, Harald’s widow, held hands and walked behind the coffin during Monday’s procession. Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norwegians and visitors expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. The coffin stayed in the palace’s Red Salon over the weekend before traveling to the royal chapel on Monday, where it will remain until the funeral. The public can go to the chapel to pay their respects to the late king beginning Tuesday, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. The funeral is set for Sept. 9. The Associated Press

stories.title: Animal tranquilizer, sedatives found in Winnipeg fentanyl supply, warns expert
stories.summary: Winnipeggers are being warned about the presence of animal tranquilizers and sedatives in the city’s drug supply.
stories.author: Kayla Rosen
stories.content: Winnipeggers are being warned about the presence of animal tranquilizers and sedatives in the city’s drug supply. Nurse practitioner Heidi Pharand-Joven, who works for Siloam Mission’s opioid addictions program, said her clinic is continuing to see fentanyl-related issues. She explained one of the problems is that the synthetic opioid is often mixed with benzodiazepines or animal tranquilizers, which makes it less effective against opioid antagonists. “Naloxone, Narcan is not as effective because it doesn’t have any effect on the animal tranquilizers or the benzodiazepines,” she explained in an interview with Your Morning Winnipeg on Monday. “(Opioid antagonists are) still the best way. It’s still really important to educate people on how to use Naloxone and make sure that people who are using substances or who are with people who are using substances have Narcan kits available on them.” Pharand-Joven’s warning comes on International Overdose Awareness Day — a day created to raise awareness and take action against overdoses. According to numbers from the Manitoba government, more than 350 Manitobans died from substance-related deaths between January and November 2025. stories.title: 3-alarm blaze at commercial building in Scarborough sparks structural concerns
stories.summary: Toronto fire said it was called to the area of McLevin Avenue and Tapscott Road just before 2 a.m. to try and suppress the flames at a commercial building.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
paragraphs: Firefighters were met with heavy and flames early on Monday morning when they rushed to the scene of a three-alarm blaze in Scarborough.
Toronto fire said it was called to the area of McLevin Avenue and Tapscott Road just before 2 a.m. to try and suppress the flames at a commercial building.
Facing a fierce fire, crews were quickly forced to transition to defensive firefighting, worrying about the deteriorating structural conditions of the building.
Toronto fire said its crews were worried about the condition of the building’s walls and roof.
As the city woke up on Monday, roads were still closed and crews were at the scene.
Officials said there were no longer visible flames, but there were still worries about the smoke emanating from the structure.
“Fire crews still remain on scene applying water to building,” Toronto fire wrote in a statement.

stories.title: TAP Air Portugal flies into red before privatization
stories.summary: TAP Air Portugal suffered a second-quarter loss due to high fuel prices, the airline said Monday, with the airline’s privatization to Air France-KLM or Lufthansa expected to be wrapped up soon.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content: TAP Air Portugal suffered a second-quarter loss due to high fuel prices, the airline said Monday, with the airline’s privatization to Air France-KLM or Lufthansa expected to be wrapped up soon. The company recorded a net loss of 59.3 million euros (US$68.8 million) in the three months to the end of June, compared to a profit of 38.3 million euros in the same period last year. While TAP carried a record 8.2 million passengers and took in record revenue of just over two billion euros over the first half of the year, higher fuel costs due to the war in the Middle East had a negative impact of 99.2 million euros, the company said. Thanks to the “solidity of demand across our entire network”, the airline was “able to mitigate the significant impact of the sharp increase in fuel prices”, chief executive Luis Rodrigues said in a statement. TAP, which was renationalized in 2020 to stem losses from the COVID-19 pandemic, is in the final stages of being reprivatized. Both Air France-KLM and Lufthansa said in July they had submitted bids to acquire a controlling stake in the airline, with the government expected to announce the result in the coming days
