stories.title: An upcoming election could produce modern Germany's 1st far-right state governor
stories.summary: An election in eastern Germany on Sunday could produce the first far-right state governor in the country’s post-World War II history as Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his unpopular national government struggle to dispel what he calls “widespread moroseness.”
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: Moeser, Germany — An election in eastern Germany on Sunday could produce the first far-right state governor in the country’s post-Second World War history as Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his unpopular national government struggle to dispel what he calls “widespread moroseness.” Several polls show a large lead for the anti-migration Alternative for Germany, or AfD, ahead of the election to the state legislature in Saxony-Anhalt. Taking control of a state government would be the biggest prize in the party’s 13-year history, a political shock to Germany and at least a symbolic blow to Merz. Breaking a taboo “If AfD wins the election and forms the government, that would be kind of breaking a taboo in Germany,” said Wolfgang Merkel, a political science professor with the WBZ Berlin Social Science Center. Modern Germany so far has been “an exception” in Europe in having no radical right-wing party governing at the national, state or big-city level, he added. Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union has led Saxony-Anhalt, a region west of Berlin that’s among the country’s less prosperous and is home to 2.1 million of Germany’s 83.5 million people, since 2002. But it faces strong headwinds. In last year’s national election, AfD achieved the best postwar showing by a far-right party, with 20.8 per cent of the vote. It became Germany’s biggest opposition party. It was stronger in the ex-communist east, including Saxony-Anhalt. And with Merz’s government struggling to convince voters it can turn around a stubbornly slow economy, it has gained in national polls as it harnesses discontent with issues beyond its signature theme of curbing migration. AfD sees a ‘historic opportunity’ In Saxony-Anhalt, AfD is seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature. That would overcome the so-called “firewall” of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with AfD, whose regional branch is one of several classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a proven right-wing extremist group. AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism. AfD’s campaign slogan is “Everything is possible.” “This is a historic opportunity that we have here in Saxony-Anhalt,” its candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, told The Associated Press at a campaign event in the small town of Moeser, where supporters lined up to meet the charismatic 35-year-old over beer and sausages. “We will write history here.” Among his top priorities, Siegmund lists “the deportation of people who are illegal, a deportation offensive and above all dropping the incentives for why people come here and exploit our social system.” He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about “disinformation.” AfD’s first and so far only head of a county administration was elected in 2023 in neighbouring Thuringia state. A state administration would be a far bigger prize, fueling the party’s ambitions of further gains and one day governing at the national level. Germany’s 16 states have extensive powers, for example in overseeing security matters and running the education system. In Saxony-Anhalt, AfD wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn’t permitted in Germany. It pledges to ban schools from officially raising the rainbow flag and ensure they fly the national flag. It opposes taxpayers’ money being “given away” to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn’t a matter state governments can decide. “No one here needs to be afraid, quite the contrary,” Siegmund said. “Every honest person in Saxony-Anhalt will benefit from an AfD-led government.” Opponent says an AfD government would mean isolation Siegmund’s main opponent, incumbent governor Sven Schulze from Merz’s CDU, told the AP at his party’s offices in Magdeburg, the state capital, that AfD “wants the past back” and the state would face “isolation” with AfD in power. He pointed to major progress made in strengthening Saxony-Anhalt’s economy and bringing down unemployment since Germany was reunited in 1990. The far right, he said, effectively “doesn’t want to have anyone here who was born abroad and lives and works here.” With many immigrants working in hospitals and companies, for example, that would be “a huge problem for Saxony-Anhalt,” he said. “AfD does one thing — it describes problems,” said Schulze, who said that he won’t work with the party and his own CDU is “100 per cent” behind him. “But it never has a solution for a problem.” AfD’s chances of governing are uncertain even if it does become by far the strongest party. If it doesn’t win an absolute majority, Merkel said he doesn’t see it governing for lack of any potential coalition partner. That likely would leave Schulze trying to cobble together some kind of alliance with multiple smaller parties to his left. That would leave many people saying that “they are clinging to power,” Merkel said. Merz needs progress on reforms It remains unclear how an AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt would affect the national government, particularly if Merz’s CDU and its coalition partners, the centre-left Social Democrats, fare poorly in elections Sept. 20 in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, another eastern state. Merkel said he believes Saxony-Anhalt is too small to have “any particular impact.” But a significant loss of votes would amplify a narrative that the traditional big parties are in decline. Merz’s government needs to prove its ability to reform Germany and so far lacks “visible successes,” Merkel added, noting that “when the economy isn’t running, basically all areas of politics are infected.” Merz sought to spread optimism after his Cabinet met last week to underline its determination to push through reforms. “We must get out of this climate of glumness and anger,” he said. “Together, we must shake off this widespread moroseness that has long paralyzed our country.” Geir Moulson And Fanny Brodersen, The Associated Press

stories.title: Voting under way in three federal by-elections
stories.summary: Elections are being held in the Quebec riding of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano
stories.author: The Canadian Press staff
paragraphs: Voting was underway Monday in federal byelections in Quebec, B.C. and Ontario taking place under the shadow of an intensifying trade war with the United States.

Elections Canada reports that thousands have already cast votes in advance polls in the three byelections. It estimates that 11,800 advance ballots came in for Beaches-East York, 11,000 for Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and 16,700 for North Vancouver-Capilano.
All eyes are on what could be a close race in rural Quebec. Conservative Richard Martel resigned his seat in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord to sit in the Senate.
Martel won a tight three-way race in 2025, beating the Liberal and Bloc Québécois candidates by about 1,500 votes.
McGill University political science professor Daniel Béland says if the Tories can’t hold on to the Quebec seat, it will add to the narrative that Pierre Poilievre’s leadership is in trouble.
The area is home to the aluminum industry and other sectors wrapped up in the ongoing trade war with the U.S. The Liberals are fielding a well-known dairy farmer, Daniel Gobeil, as their candidate.

The Conservatives are running Régis Gaudreault, a retired lawyer and former law professor at Cégep de Chicoutimi, while the Bloc is running Caroline Dubé, who previously worked for Mario Simard, the Bloc MP for the neighbouring federal riding of Jonquière.
Byelections in the Toronto riding of Beaches-East York and in North Vancouver-Capilano are being held to replace former cabinet ministers Nate Erskine-Smith and Jonathan Wilkinson.
Wilkinson resigned his seat in June to take up a diplomatic posting in Europe.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley is running for Wilkinson’s former Vancouver seat. His Conservative opponent Stephen Curran is a commercial lawyer who came second to Wilkinson in 2025. Stephen Tweedale, a provincial party staffer, is running for the NDP.

In Toronto, Erskine-Smith is now running for a city council seat in October’s municipal election. He resigned his federal seat to seek an Ontario Liberal party nomination for a provincial byelection, which he failed to win.

Erskine-Smith’s former constituency office manager, Tanveer Shahnawaz, is running for the Liberals there. Shannon Devine, a labour leader who ran there in the 2025 election, is once again the NDP candidate. Local restaurant owner Jim Syrbos is running for the Conservatives.
Polls close in Ontario and Quebec at 9:30 p.m. ET, while B.C.’s polls close at 7 p.m. PST.

stories.title: Ontario woman questions $500 fee to transfer family's medical records to new doctor
stories.summary: Ontario woman questions $500 fee to transfer family's medical records to new doctor CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 31, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
Ontario Medical Association recommends fees be 'reasonable'
When Melissa Snider found a new family doctor closer to her home in Denfield, Ont., she was happy at the thought of no longer travelling to London for medical visits.
The relief turned to shock however when her former family doctor quoted Snider $100 per person to transfer her records, along with those of her husband and their three children, to a new physician.
"It was quite surprising to me that transferring medical records for a family of five would cost me $500," said Snider, whose kids are all under the age of nine.

"My kids are all healthy so it would just be vaccine records for them, and my husband and I are pretty healthy too, so our records themselves would not be very extensive. Half a grand in this economy is just not doable for something so silly."

Snider said she had previously paid around $35 for the service. She asked a Facebook group for moms if others have been in this situation. She said she received a variety of responses, with some saying their doctor did it for free, and others saying they had to pay varying fees.
Access to personal health information and related fees is governed
Personal Health Information Protection Act and not c
overed by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (Ohip), according to
the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (Cpso).

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records May include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, said Cpso spokesperson Laura Zilke.
The Information Privacy Commissioner recommends a $30 fee for electronic transfers, according to the Ontario Medical Association, which sets out recommended fees in its
Physicians’ Guide to Uninsured Services.

In some cases, doctors May charge $30 for the first 20 pages and then $0.25 per extra pages, but all other methods of reproducing records should be charged for at cost, the guidance states. This can include clerical labour costs, toner and paper costs, equipment, and storage space.

policy requires that fees be reasonable, reflect cost recovery, and be commensurate with the nature of the service provided, including factors such as the materials used, the time required to prepare the records, and the direct cost of sending them."

Primary Care Electronic Medical Record , where patient records are integrated onto one accessible system.

The electronic record aims to provide clinicians with a more complete view of a patient’s health history, improving coordination across the health system and reducing delays caused by missing records. It also
seeks to save patients money in transfer fees, unnecessary medical tests and lab work.

The province is currently in a procurement phase but Varughese said officials have consulted with family physicians and he's hopeful this will simplify the process for doctors and patients.
As for Snider, she plans to provide her new doctor with a verbal medical history and not pay the hefty transfer cost.

stories.title: Federal byelection polls open for voters in Quebec, Toronto, Vancouver
stories.summary: The federal byelections are taking place under the shadow of an intensifying trade war with the United States.
stories.author: News Staff
paragraphs: Voting is underway in three federal byelections taking place Monday under the shadow of an intensifying trade war with the United States.
All eyes are on what could be a close race in rural Quebec, where Conservative Richard Martel resigned his seat in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord to sit in the Senate.
Martel won a tight three-way race in 2025, beating the Liberal and Bloc Québécois candidates by about 1,500 votes.
McGill University political science professor Daniel Béland says if the Tories can’t hold on to the Quebec seat, it will add to the narrative that Pierre Poilievre’s leadership is in trouble.
Elections are also on in the Toronto riding of Beaches-East York and in North Vancouver-Capilano to replace former cabinet ministers Nate Erskine-Smith and Jonathan Wilkinson, respectively.
Wilkinson, a former cabinet minister, decided to take a new appointment as Canada’s ambassador to the European Union.

In the Beaches-East York riding, which is considered a Liberal stronghold, the seat was once held by Nate Erskine-Smith, who originally had said that he wanted to run for the provincial leadership but is instead running for Toronto City Council in the Oct. 26 municipal elections being held across Ontario.
“I honestly have no idea how it’s gonna go, but I feel like Beaches-East York is usually a pretty Liberal-NDP riding so we’ll see,” said one person who cast their ballot during advance voting.

“I always say if you don’t vote, you don’t get to complain. It’s always nice to get a chance to have your say and put a vote in for who you want to see in the party or in leadership, and try and steer the city in a way that you want,” another voter said.
Elections Canada reports that thousands cast votes in advance polls — with 11,800 advance ballots in Beaches-East York, 11,000 in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and 16,700 in North Vancouver-Capilano.
Voting on election day ends at 9:30 p.m. ET in the Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and Beaches-East York ridings, and 10 p.m. ET in North Vancouver-Capilano.
The federal Liberals need to win just one of the three ridings in order to maintain their majority control in the House of Commons. According to the party standings , it has 170 seats.

stories.title: Emergency physicians say this summer’s patient levels are unprecedented
stories.summary: Health care system is no longer on the brink of collapse but caving in before our eyes, an ER doctor says
stories.author: Alanna Smith
paragraphs: Emergency physicians in major cities across Canada say they can usually catch their breath during the summer months. But this year has been unlike any other with patient levels in some cities reaching highs never seen before.

Doctors who spoke with The Globe and Mail had difficulty pinning this summer’s rush to any single issue. It’s the symptom, they said, of hospital overcrowding, an aging population, more medically complex patients, limited access to other health care supports – and the list goes on.

Then there are unique factors in certain provinces, such as a measles outbreak that has sickened hundreds this year in Manitoba. Or the wildfire smoke that suffocated Ontario in July and led to a spike in respiratory-related emergency department visits.
Kirk Magee, an emergency physician at the Qeii Health Sciences Centre in Halifax, said this summer has been noticeably different.
“Many days you walk through the waiting room and it feels like it’s January,” he said, recalling a recent shift when he saw patients who had been waiting for more than 15 hours.
“That’s horrific even in the middle of influenza season, but I’ve never ever seen that before at this time of year.”

During the summer, EDs expect to see an increase in trauma cases linked to such activities as boating, quadding or sports. But overall patient volumes tend to dip as respiratory illnesses slow down and people head off on vacation, though the trend has been slimming in recent years.

Dr. Magee said the summer surge is a predictable outcome of hospital overcrowding, which leaders in the health care system have been sounding the alarm over for years. Hallway medicine is now the norm in congested EDs across Canada.

Noam Katz, an ER doctor at St. Boniface Hospital in Winnipeg, said the health care system is no longer on the brink of collapse but caving in before our eyes. “This is the end state of what people have been warning everybody about for years,” he said.

Research released by the Canadian Institute for Health Information in June, which covered parts of 2024 and 2025, showed that one in 10 patients spent more than 14 hours waiting for care in Canadian EDs. Those requiring admission sometimes waited three times longer.

Staffing is also a constant challenge. Another study , published in July, found that nearly half of the 410 ED physicians surveyed by the Canadian Medical Association last year had reduced their clinical hours and roughly 20 per cent had taken time away from working in EDs.
Real-time, public data on patient volumes are limited across Canada. While the Canadian Institute for Health Information does track these metrics, not all hospitals provide data.

In Alberta, internal provincial data provided to The Globe shows there were 7,485 emergency inpatients (EIP) who were waiting for a hospital bed on July 26. This is an eight per cent increase from the July count last year, a 96 per cent jump from five years ago and 176 per cent rise from 2016.

The data show the problem is particularly acute in Edmonton where there were 5,118 EIPs in July, a 37 per cent increase from the previous year. In January, major hospitals in the capital called on Alberta to declare a formal emergency due to overcrowding; the province didn’t do so.
Paul Parks, president-elect of the Alberta Medical Association’s emergency medicine section, said there is no more elasticity in the health system.

He warned that patients will continue to die in a similar manner to Prashant Sreekumar, who died last December after eight hours in an Edmonton ED. The risk also rises for disabilities and other suboptimal outcomes.
“More and more people are going to be in our waiting rooms, are going to be sitting hours and hours suffering in pain with no care and some May die because of it.”
Despite politicians across Canada having committed to improving ED overcrowding, emergency physicians say provincial governments are falling short on their promises.

Vancouver emergency physician Kaitlin Stockton said doctors asked British Columbia to create a working group and commit to a four-step framework to improve health care delivery. She said the province declined.

The framework asked the province to establish transparent performance targets, mandate public reporting of utilization and performance metrics, use an accountability framework and create an independent oversight body to audit performance.

“I don’t want to hear any more about how much money is being spent on what. I don’t care. I want to know the outcomes,” Dr. Stockton said. “The only people who are being held accountable are frontline providers.”

Michael Herman, an Ottawa-based emergency physician, stressed that ED overcrowding is “not ordained from heaven” but the result of poor policy choices from hospitals, health authorities and governments.
He said better data collection and accountability measures must be implemented to help understand and solve the issues plaguing EDs: “If you don’t take a temperature, you can’t find a fever.”

Losing the seasonal reprieve is also bad for staff morale, especially heading into the busy viral season. He said ED staff have left because the tempo is unrelenting and expects others will do the same.
Quebec, too, has not escaped the summer phenomenon.

Montreal-based emergency physician Judy Morris said the reason EDs are clogged extend well beyond the department’s walls. She stressed that there are not enough community supports, such as long-term care and addiction treatment beds.
“If the appropriate facilities to adequately treat these patients would exist, they wouldn’t have to come to the ER,” she said, adding there is “no end in sight.”

stories.content:
Emergency physicians in major cities across Canada say they can usually catch their breath during the summer months. But this year has been unlike any other with patient levels in some cities reaching highs never seen before.

Doctors who spoke with The Globe and Mail had difficulty pinning this summer’s rush to any single issue. It’s the symptom, they said, of hospital overcrowding, an aging population, more medically complex patients, limited access to other health care supports – and the list goes on.

Then there are unique factors in certain provinces, such as a measles outbreak that has sickened hundreds this year in Manitoba. Or the wildfire smoke that suffocated Ontario in July and led to a spike in respiratory-related emergency department visits.

Kirk Magee, an emergency physician at the Qeii Health Sciences Centre in Halifax, said this summer has been noticeably different.

“Many days you walk through the waiting room and it feels like it’s January,” he said, recalling a recent shift when he saw patients who had been waiting for more than 15 hours.

“That’s horrific even in the middle of influenza season, but I’ve never ever seen that before at this time of year.”

During the summer, EDs expect to see an increase in trauma cases linked to such activities as boating, quadding or sports. But overall patient volumes tend to dip as respiratory illnesses slow down and people head off on vacation, though the trend has been slimming in recent years.

Dr. Magee said the summer surge is a predictable outcome of hospital overcrowding, which leaders in the health care system have been sounding the alarm over for years. Hallway medicine is now the norm in congested EDs across Canada.

Noam Katz, an ER doctor at St. Boniface Hospital in Winnipeg, said the health care system is no longer on the brink of collapse but caving in before our eyes. “This is the end state of what people have been warning everybody about for years,” he said.

Research released by the Canadian Institute for Health Information in June, which covered parts of 2024 and 2025, showed that one in 10 patients spent more than 14 hours waiting for care in Canadian EDs. Those requiring admission sometimes waited three times longer.

Staffing is also a constant challenge. Another study , published in July, found that nearly half of the 410 ED physicians surveyed by the Canadian Medical Association last year had reduced their clinical hours and roughly 20 per cent had taken time away from working in EDs.

Real-time, public data on patient volumes are limited across Canada. While the Canadian Institute for Health Information does track these metrics, not all hospitals provide data.

In Alberta, internal provincial data provided to The Globe shows there were 7,485 emergency inpatients (EIP) who were waiting for a hospital bed on July 26. This is an eight per cent increase from the July count last year, a 96 per cent jump from five years ago and 176 per cent rise from 2016.

The data show the problem is particularly acute in Edmonton where there were 5,118 EIPs in July, a 37 per cent increase from the previous year. In January, major hospitals in the capital called on Alberta to declare a formal emergency due to overcrowding; the province didn’t do so.

Paul Parks, president-elect of the Alberta Medical Association’s emergency medicine section, said there is no more elasticity in the health system.

He warned that patients will continue to die in a similar manner to Prashant Sreekumar, who died last December after eight hours in an Edmonton ED. The risk also rises for disabilities and other suboptimal outcomes.

“More and more people are going to be in our waiting rooms, are going to be sitting hours and hours suffering in pain with no care and some May die because of it.”

Despite politicians across Canada having committed to improving ED overcrowding, emergency physicians say provincial governments are falling short on their promises.

Vancouver emergency physician Kaitlin Stockton said doctors asked British Columbia to create a working group and commit to a four-step framework to improve health care delivery. She said the province declined.

The framework asked the province to establish transparent performance targets, mandate public reporting of utilization and performance metrics, use an accountability framework and create an independent oversight body to audit performance.

“I don’t want to hear any more about how much money is being spent on what. I don’t care. I want to know the outcomes,” Dr. Stockton said. “The only people who are being held accountable are frontline providers.”

Michael Herman, an Ottawa-based emergency physician, stressed that ED overcrowding is “not ordained from heaven” but the result of poor policy choices from hospitals, health authorities and governments.

He said better data collection and accountability measures must be implemented to help understand and solve the issues plaguing EDs: “If you don’t take a temperature, you can’t find a fever.”

Losing the seasonal reprieve is also bad for staff morale, especially heading into the busy viral season. He said ED staff have left because the tempo is unrelenting and expects others will do the same.

Quebec, too, has not escaped the summer phenomenon.

Montreal-based emergency physician Judy Morris said the reason EDs are clogged extend well beyond the department’s walls. She stressed that there are not enough community supports, such as long-term care and addiction treatment beds.

“If the appropriate facilities to adequately treat these patients would exist, they wouldn’t have to come to the ER,” she said, adding there is “no end in sight.”

stories.title: Mountie killer in Saskatchewan tells court forfeiting truck to Crown unreasonable
stories.summary: In 2009, a jury convicted Curtis Dagenais of first-degree murder for shooting constables Robin Cameron and Marc Bourdages.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Saskatoon - A man sentenced to life in jail for killing two Mounties in a chase involving his blue pickup truck went to court Monday to try to get the vehicle back.

Curtis Dagenais argued that his 1986 GMC 1500 – smashed, dented and pockmarked with bullet holes – is his and still holds value for its parts.

“It’s unreasonable (for the Crown to keep it),” Dagenais, 61, said as he appeared by video in the courtroom of Justice Daryl Labach.

It has been 17 years since a jury convicted Dagenais of first-degree murder for shooting constables Robin Cameron and Marc Bourdages in 2006. He was also convicted of attempted murder for wounding Const. Michelle Knopp.

In July 2006, Dagenais was in the GMC truck when officers went to arrest him in Spiritwood, northwest of Saskatoon, after a report of a domestic dispute. He sped off and the resulting police chase on country roads ended with an RCMP vehicle ramming into the side of his truck. A shootout followed.

Dagenais had testified the officers shot at him first, so he grabbed a rifle under his truck seat and blindly returned fire to save his own life. The Crown argued at trial that it was Dagenais who surprised the Mounties with gunfire and that he lied in court to get away with murder.

Court had previously heard Dagenais was flagged as a police hater.

Dagenais received three life sentences without eligibility of parole for 25 years. For the past 20 years, his truck has been stored at RCMP headquarters in Regina.

At Monday’s hearing, prosecutor Scott Bartlett told court the truck’s windows are broken and the doors dented. It’s also pockmarked with bullet holes, he added.

“I can’t imagine (Saskatchewan Government Insurance) would ever allow it to be registered. It could never pass an inspection,” Bartlett told court. “It simply has no value.”

Asked why the Crown wants the truck forfeited, Bartlett said in a later interview the vehicle has been stored long enough. He added he has no control over what would happen to the vehicle should it be surrendered.

A section of the Criminal Code that deals with forfeiture says “offence-related property” can be disposed of.

RCMP said in a statement it will continue to maintain possession of the truck until given direction by the courts to dispose of it.

The Crown had originally sought to have the convicted killer’s truck forfeited in June 2021.

Bartlett told court the forfeiture case was tied up due to Dagenais seeking support from Innocence Canada, a non-profit group that helps exonerate people who believe they’re not guilty.

Bartlett said he didn’t hear from Innocence Canada until this year, and that the group told him it would not be representing Dagenais.

He said Dagenais was previously given an adjournment in June to sort out his case for Monday’s hearing.

“It hasn’t been accomplished,” he told court. “I’m looking for a reason for us to believe that if we adjourn it one more time, that something would be different.”

Dagenais told court he is trying to get a meeting with a lawyer. Labach adjourned the case to Oct. 19 to give Dagenais more time to find one, but said he won’t grant another extension.

“My patience,” he said, “is starting to wear a little thin.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

– By Jeremy Simes in Regina

stories.title: Why things can get tricky when apartment buildings are 'condominiumized'
stories.summary: Why things can get tricky when apartment buildings are 'condominiumized' CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 31, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: 15 hours ago
Kipps Lane buildings have had long elevator breakdowns, 4 weeks with no hot water
An aging north London apartment complex where tenants recently went four weeks without hot water was converted from rental apartments to condos in 2021 and marketed to investors.
The ownership structure, one real estate expert says, can become problematic when older apartment buildings are converted to condos, particularly when maintenance and repair costs rise.

"Once they are condominiumized, after a few years the underlying problems start to rear their heads and you are faced with major repairs," said Ron Butler, a mortgage broker who discusses the condo market on his
Butler was speaking generally to CBC News about the practice of converting older apartment buildings into condos, not about the Kipps Lane property specifically.

The six multi-storey buildings, collectively known as Riverfront Towers, contain about 700 units. The units were sold to individual investors after the City of London approved the condo conversion in 2021. Sireg Management took over management of the buildings after the conversion.
The buildings have had maintenance issues that prompted complaints from tenants to the city over the past year.
In addition to the l engthy delay in restoring hot water this summer, tenants at 750 Kipps Ln. told CBC News they felt trapped in their units while waiting weeks for both elevators to be repaired.
Those problems and others prompted Acorn, a tenants' rights group, to hold a tenants' meeting in the lobby of 756 Kipps Ln. on Wednesday evening.
Acorn's Jordan Smith met with tenants who shared stories of what he described as "extreme neglect," including moisture problems in walls and pest infestations.

"The overall disrepair, it's egregious," said Smith. "The four weeks without water, that's vital service but it's just the tip of the iceberg. They've got every kind of repair needed you can imagine."
In a statement to CBC News, Sireg Management said it has carried out numerous repairs since taking over the Kipps Lane buildings and is continuing to address outstanding issues.
"We recognize that some repairs have taken longer than residents, and frankly we ourselves, would have preferred," the statement said.
The company said several factors, including worker availability and the supply of parts and equipment, can affect how quickly repairs are completed.
The company also said it has reached out to the city about a possible partnership.

"Our objective is to find practical ways to expedite necessary capital improvements, improve the quality of life for existing residents and preserve housing affordability over the longer term," the statement said.

In a statement, the city said its housing team met with Sireg to discuss an application through its Dollars to Doors program. However, the city said, "the funding request does not meet the program's current guidelines."
The program provides loans and financial incentives to help stimulate the creation of new, affordable rental housing.

A section of Sireg's website called Simple Investor markets the former rental units as condos for investors to purchase and rent out. Sireg manages the rentals on behalf of the owners, a business model the company says can create "generational wealth" for investors through a "hands-off approach to real estate investing."
The website says Sireg manages properties for more than 1,800 investors, with about $1.3 billion in assets under management.
It also says hundreds of thousands of rents have been paid out and "not one rent has been missed."
"This shows the reliability of our model," the website says.
Sireg president Todd C. Slater has a Simple Investor
YouTube channel where he discusses the real estate and rental market. The company also promotes in-person workshops, webinars and coaching sessions about real estate investing.
Butler said prospective investors should proceed carefully when considering units in older apartment buildings that have been converted to condos.

Butler said borrowing costs have risen in recent years, while rents have softened. At the same time, the cost of replacing or repairing big-ticket items such as roofs, elevators and parking structures can put downward pressure on investors' profits.

"Eventually there's more pressure on the landlord to try to increase rents," said Butler. "Then there is this difficulty of living in a place where the elevators never work, where there are leaks or other problems. It's problematic for everyone."
Mark Bhalla is vice-president of policy at the Condominium Authority of Ontario, an organization that works to promote well-managed condos through education and training programs.

Bhalla said condo rules require boards to consult experts when creating estimates of the long-term costs of managing a building. Condo corporations must also collect enough fees from owners to build a reserve fund to cover expected future repairs.

The condo owners, rather than tenants, pay those fees. Rentals in apartments converted to condos continue to be governed by Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, which limits annual rent increases in older buildings.
Butler said there can be an important difference between a condo board made up largely of owners who live in the building and one made up of investors who live elsewhere.
"It's just about, 'Can I make enough rent to make a profit on this unit?' They are divorced from the actual participation in the building."

stories.title: This 102-year-old Toronto man's recent Bell scare exposes risks in Canada's unregulated end to landlines
stories.summary: Bell says man's issue was an equipment breakdown, but impending end to landlines in his Swansea neighbourhood highlight the risks in the shift away from copper to fibre.
stories.author: Diana Zlomislic
stories.content:
On a recent Thursday night in west-end Toronto, a passerby noticed an elderly man sitting on a concrete stoop outside his home at 9:30 p.m., clutching a cane, inconsolable in the dark.

The stranger stopped to help.

The man, who is 102 years old, had waited hours for a Good Samaritan.

The Bell landline at his Swansea home, his literal lifeline to the world, died suddenly and he didn’t know what to do. The stress so overwhelmed him that his words, to the stranger, sounded like gibberish . He was speaking a Slavic language from his youth.

Figuring out how to help seemed impossible until the Samaritan flashed his cellphone and the man recited a phone number he knew by heart.

Annie Pejovich Chant answered.

Pejovich Chant, the man’s daughter and a realtor who gathers weekly with a klatsch of neighbourhood seniors to chew over their personal headlines, had a hunch about what happened.

Earlier this month, Bell Canada had circulated a letter to homes across Swansea warning customers it was in the process of replacing the aging copper network that powers the company’s landlines.

“This means that effective Nov. 4, 2026, we will be shutting down your current Bell home phone service,” the company’s letter states. “If you do not take action by this date, your service will be disconnected.”

Pejovich Chant couldn’t figure out why Bell appeared to act pre-emptively in her dad’s case. He received his own warning letter Aug. 4 with the November deadline still months away. (The answer, she would soon learn, was a bit more complicated.)

“This is totally unacceptable for all the seniors in Toronto who have a landline,” Pejovich Chant wrote in an email to me. She asked the Star to not name her father to protect him from telemarketing scams.

Pejovich Chant’s father is among a growing number of seniors aging in place who rely on a medical emergency device that plugs into a phone jack. Pushing a wearable button sends a distress signal through the landline to a 24/7 monitoring station.

Pejovich Chant wondered how many other seniors were quietly losing their lifelines.

A blind spot in emergency response

Telecommunications companies are deactivating legacy copper lines without notifying emergency alert providers. Connect America, parent company of Lifeline Canada, confirmed this critical gap in Canada’s telecom network transition.

“At this time, we have not received direct proactive notifications or co-ordinated transition plans from major telecommunications providers regarding copper-network decommissioning,” Aaron Nye, COO of Connect America, wrote in an email to the Star.

Nearly 40 per cent of Lifeline’s Canadian subscribers still rely on traditional landline connections to transmit life-saving signals to monitoring centres, Nye confirmed.

While other countries have decommissioned aging copper networks for technological and economic reasons, they’ve taken greater care in ensuring the process protects vulnerable citizens like Pejovich Chant’s dad and her coffee mates.

Canada’s hands-off approach has elicited concern and criticism from consumer advocacy groups and even from within the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (Crtc).

“In many countries, a regulatory framework is established to oversee and manage copper decommissioning,” writes Bram Abramson, a Crtc commissioner, in a 2024 policy decision order. “Not in Canada. Here, copper decommissioning has proceeded without active regulatory oversight.”

Canada’s approach, Abramson adds, “shifted certain risk costs from those conducting the decommissioning — where other regulatory frameworks might place them — onto those impacted by it.”

The downside of fibre phone lines

For more than a century, traditional copper phone lines carried their own low-voltage electrical current straight from a telecom company’s central utility office. If an ice storm brought down the power grid across an entire city, an old-fashioned landline kept working.

Fibre optic cables transmit data using pulses of light, not electricity. Because light cannot carry power, a fibre landline relies on an electrically powered modem inside the customer’s home to convert those light pulses into a dial tone.

During a power outage, the modem shuts off and the landline dies unless homeowners source, install and maintain their own Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) or backup battery.

Bell Canada sells a portable one on its website for $299.99. It promises up to nine hours of backup power for a modem.

Abramson appears to be the only one within the Crtc actively warning the public of the risks of retiring copper landlines — “that lifeline for so long.”

“When Canadians think of landline voice,” he wrote in a 2026 policy order , “they often assume it continues to work when household power fails. For generations that expectation reflected how the network was engineered and regulated.”

As these trusted telephone networks fade, so must consumers’ assumptions about the reliability of the modern landline, he noted.

“The service has changed,” Abramson writes. “Especially where phone lines remain a service of last resort, the public deserves a clearer discussion of how.”

‘The ultimate euphoria’

The rush to decommission copper networks began more than a decade ago.

In 2011, early Crtc proceedings discussed the shortcomings of the technology and noted telecom companies should supply an eight-hour, in-home backup battery to subscribers. That provision, however, was never written into the official rule book as a mandatory condition.

At a 2016 telecom conference, former BCE chief financial officer Glen LeBlanc explained the financial rationale behind shifting to fibre optics. Converting premises to fibre was projected to slash technician dispatches by 40 to 50 per cent.

“The great savings — the ultimate euphoria — is when you can shut down your copper network,” LeBlanc said. “That’s where I think you see the telco of tomorrow.”

Problem ‘an isolated equipment issue’

Fast forward to today, Pejovich Chant escalated her dad’s landline emergency to Bell executive management. I also reached out to Bell senior media relations manager Elise Von Scheel who confirmed in an email that Pejovich Chant’s father’s neighbourhood is scheduled to lose its legacy copper infrastructure this fall. She added that his particular disconnection was caused by a faulty aging copper connector.

“This was not a proactive decommissioning of the service by Bell,” von Scheel told the Star, “but rather an isolated equipment issue that was repaired and the connection subsequently restored.”

Pejovich Chant told me she asked the Bell technician if the company could install a fibre line while keeping the copper line as a backup. She said she was told they’ll look into it. She also asked if Bell could supply and install a backup battery for her father to keep the fibre line working during a power outage. She said she was told such requests are approved on a case-by-case basis.

“In rare scenarios,” von Scheel shared in an email to the Star, “Bell has occasionally provided assistance in securing a one-time UPS backup when a customer’s medical monitoring device was only compatible with a copper network.”

Von Scheel said Bell is “continuing conversations with the customer to support a transition to fibre.”

The Star, simplified

I asked the Crtc for an interview with Abramson and if it could explain its hands-off approach on copper decommissioning.

“Commissioners speak through their decisions,” Crtc spokesperson Megan McLean wrote in an email, rejecting my request.

“The Crtc is taking a number of actions to address service outages and ensure Canadians are connected to the services they need,” McLean added. “This includes an ongoing proceeding that aims to help make telecommunications networks more resilient and reduce outages.”

Last Friday, Pejovich Chant’s father opened his mail to find a second notice from Bell Canada, warning him he was on the verge of losing his home phone service, for which he pays $70 monthly.

Pejovich Chant is frustrated by the regulator’s apparent indifference and hopes public pressure will compel the Crtc and telecom companies to re-evaluate their approach here.

“There aren’t many opportunities in life to make a difference,” she says. “I think this is one of them.”

stories.title: He warned Doug Ford’s government this hospital locks people in ‘horrific’ isolation. The province called one hospital exec — then did nothing
stories.summary: Psychiatrist Dr. John Bradford warned the province in 2018 about “horrific conditions" at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
paragraphs: The Ontario government has been aware for at least eight years of serious concerns about a psychiatric hospital’s practice of keeping patients in isolation for prolonged periods of time, the Star has learned — a practice that was recently found to be akin to torture .

Documents filed in a proposed class action lawsuit also reveal that when the Ministry of Health looked into Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care’s use of long-term seclusion, officials did not visit the facility and spoke to only one hospital executive over the phone before deciding no further action was necessary.
Leading experts have described the hospital’s practice as “egregious,” “abusive” and unlike anything seen in other North American facilities.

The ministry’s actions, or lack thereof, almost a decade ago are being described by critics — including the former Waypoint psychiatrist who brought his concerns to the government — as a “missed opportunity” to help seriously mentally ill patients who have been kept in isolation at Waypoint for sometimes years and in at least one case, decades .

The ministry “had the opportunity to intervene and force Waypoint to correct course back then,” said lawyer Anita Szigeti, an expert on mental health law who has several clients in long-term seclusion at Waypoint, the province’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital, located on Georgian Bay in Penetanguishene.

The hospital has consistently refused to divulge how many patients are being kept in long-term seclusion, but it was revealed during an Ontario Review Board hearing earlier this month that there are at least 11 secluded patients just in the 20-bed unit where Azevedo is kept.

An independent assessment filed during the hearing concluded that seclusion would fall under the United Nations’ definition of solitary confinement, and that secluded patients at Waypoint are being kept in conditions that the UN has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings. Waypoint’s CEO, Dr. Nadiya Sunderji, has said the hospital “categorically” disagrees with those findings.

The records outlining the concerns that were brought to the government’s attention in 2018, and the ministry’s subsequent probe in 2019, were filed as part of a proposed class action against the hospital by Toronto firm Rochon Genova on behalf of several plaintiffs who have been kept in long-term seclusion.
It’s a missed opportunity that has cost a lot of people their freedom

The courts declined to certify the matter as a class action, concluding that the decision to seclude a patient is an individualized process and plaintiffs alleging wrongdoing would have to bring individual claims.

The office of Health Minister Sylvia Jones did not respond to the Star’s request for comment for this story; Jones’ ministry has not responded to any requests from the Star regarding its coverage of seclusion at Waypoint.

The concerns were raised in December 2018 — a few months after Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservative government came to power — by forensic psychiatrist Dr. John Bradford, one of the world’s leading experts in forensic psychiatry who briefly worked at Waypoint.
“I was concerned about the serious and irreversible harm that patients would suffer in confinement,” Bradford said in an affidavit filed in court.
He said that patients were being confined for long periods of time in “horrific conditions, the likes of which I have never seen in any other psychiatric hospital in Ontario.”

In an interview with the Star this month, Bradford said he felt his concerns were taken seriously by the ministry. However, he didn’t have the full picture about what the ministry did with those concerns until this summer, when he viewed the other records filed in the proposed class action.
Bringing concerns to government

Bradford worked for decades as the clinical director of the forensic psychiatry program at what was then the Royal Ottawa Hospital, and is a past chair of the examination board for forensic psychiatry of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada.

He worked at Waypoint between 2016 and 2017. He resigned after his concerns about the prolonged use of seclusion went unaddressed after raising them with the hospital’s senior executives, including then-CEO Carol Lambie.

People being in seclusion for long periods of time, even years, “was very, very foreign to me in any of my previous psychiatric experience,” Bradford told the Star. “I’d seen similar situations in correctional facilities, but never in a health care facility.”

He decided to raise his concerns externally. He first went to the Ontario Human Rights Commission, where he felt they took the issues seriously, but Bradford was worried about their lack of power to compel Waypoint to do anything.

He and another Waypoint psychiatrist decided to go instead to the provincial government. They had a meeting in December 2018 with then-assistant deputy health minister, Tim Hadwen. Bradford recalled there was also a lawyer from the attorney general’s office and a representative from the local health integration network at the meeting. He said the main focus was the “abusive” prolonged seclusion.

Bradford understood that there were limits to what the ministry could do. Waypoint, at the time operating under a different name, was divested from the Ontario government in 2008 along with other psychiatric facilities, meaning the government was no longer responsible for the day-to-day operation of the hospital.

But Waypoint was still a public Catholic hospital, and the health minister retained some discretionary powers, such as issuing directives to the hospital’s board or appointing inspectors to review the hospital’s operations.
“If my concerns were correct, and I believed they were, then I believed that those were things the ministry could consider,” Bradford said.
Inside the ministry’s probe
Cochrane and another ministry official, Ragaven Sabaratnam, were tasked with looking into Bradford’s concerns.

In an affidavit filed in May 2023, Cochrane said they conducted interviews “with management staff at Waypoint,” as well as with the psychiatric patient advocate office, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario and the North Simcoe Muskoka local health integration network. Waypoint also shared some of its policies with them.

They brought the results of the interviews to Hadwen, who “determined that there was no need for the minister of health to exercise” any of the discretionary powers “because Waypoint had policies and procedures in place to address clinical care for its patients,” Cochrane says in her affidavit.
No further steps were taken, she said.
Hadwen communicated the outcome to Bradford in an April 2019 email, one in a series of emails filed in court.
Horrific conditions, the likes of which I have never seen in any other psychiatric hospital in Ontario.
“After reviewing the information made available to us, we are confident that Waypoint has implemented changes to address the concerns you raised,” Hadwen wrote.
He said that the ministry’s work included speaking with representatives — plural — of Waypoint.

In fact, only one Waypoint representative — then-vice-president of clinical services Rob Desroches — was interviewed, over the phone. Cochrane confirmed this when she was cross-examined on her affidavit by the plaintiffs’ lawyers in the proposed class action, when asked if her Waypoint interviews were with any of the senior executives named as defendants in the lawsuit.
“The interview was with Mr. Desroches,” she said.
The lawyer followed up: “So it was a single interview?”
Cochrane replied that it was. She said the interview would have been “definitely less than two hours.”

A summary of the January 2019 call with Desroches shows the ministry officials asked him six questions, three of which were about seclusion. The first question sought clarification on the hospital’s reporting policies and practices around seclusion.

Desroches said the hospital was in the midst of revamping some of its procedures, which would include clinical managers creating daily, weekly, and monthly reports about seclusion that would go up to vice presidents for review.

He said “several initiatives have been put in place” to reduce the use of seclusion and that an unnamed expert had been brought in from the United States to provide training on safety and the use of seclusion.

He said Waypoint had also requested additional funding to hire more people to escort patients out of seclusion more often; as the Star reported last week, the hospital is still struggling to bring all secluded patients out for seclusion relief on a daily basis due to staffing shortages.
In response to another question, Desroches said there had been no third-party review conducted specifically on the use of long-term seclusion.
‘That is not an investigation’
Back in 2019, Bradford was pleased with Hadwen’s response.

“I sincerely appreciate you taking our concerns seriously and acting on these concerns,” Bradford wrote in an email. “I appreciate you taking action in the name of quality of care and respect for the human rights of the patients detained at Waypoint.”
Hadwen then forwarded Bradford’s response to Cochrane — “Reasonably positive,” Hadwen wrote.
Cochrane, in turn, forwarded the response to other ministry staff, writing: “FYI — Hopefully we can close this file now.”
Bradford said he was dismayed when he saw the emails for the first time this summer.

In the years since Bradford’s warning, Waypoint has continued to lock patients up in long-term isolation. By 2019, Hamblett would have already been in continuous seclusion at Waypoint for almost 14 years. He’s still in seclusion to this day.
“I’m still not sure what to make of it,” Bradford said of Cochrane’s email. “It sounds as though they thought the matter was over. I took them at face value that they had sorted things out.”

Bradford said he had no idea the ministry had only spoken to one representative at Waypoint, nor that officials had not gone into the facility, “which would have been, in my mind, the most basic part of intervening,” Bradford said.
“I think there’s a big difference between hearing someone talking about policies and procedures and actually seeing how they implement them.”
Cochrane has been involved in conducting a secret review of the forensic mental health system, which the Star first reported in April.

Cochrane wrote to Szigeti, the lawyer, asking if she would participate in a “confidential discussion” about the system and requesting that she sign a nondisclosure agreement. “We believe your input will make an important contribution to informing advice to government,” Cochrane wrote.

Szigeti declined to participate as she refused to sign the NDA. The Star subsequently filed a freedom of information request for the terms of reference of the review, but was told that “no responsive records were located.”
Szigeti said in an interview this month that she shares Bradford’s concerns about the ministry’s actions in 2019.
“That is not an investigation,” she said. “That’s a phone call to ask basic questions — ‘In your opinion, are you doing everything right?’”
She said it appears that the magnitude of the problem of long-term seclusion was not revealed to the ministry during their questioning, “but it should have been.”
“If this had been properly investigated back in 2018-19 and the institution had been forced to correct course, then Camelott Hamblett May have been released from seclusion,” she said.
And Azevedo, who has been held in seclusion since 2021, May have never been placed in isolation in the first place.
Bradford said he also can’t shake the thought of Hamblett and whether his situation would have improved had things been done differently almost a decade ago.
“It’s an enormous period of somebody’s lifetime,” he said.

stories.content:
The Ontario government has been aware for at least eight years of serious concerns about a psychiatric hospital’s practice of keeping patients in isolation for prolonged periods of time, the Star has learned — a practice that was recently found to be akin to torture .

Documents filed in a proposed class action lawsuit also reveal that when the Ministry of Health looked into Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care’s use of long-term seclusion, officials did not visit the facility and spoke to only one hospital executive over the phone before deciding no further action was necessary.

Leading experts have described the hospital’s practice as “egregious,” “abusive” and unlike anything seen in other North American facilities.

The ministry’s actions, or lack thereof, almost a decade ago are being described by critics — including the former Waypoint psychiatrist who brought his concerns to the government — as a “missed opportunity” to help seriously mentally ill patients who have been kept in isolation at Waypoint for sometimes years and in at least one case, decades .

The ministry “had the opportunity to intervene and force Waypoint to correct course back then,” said lawyer Anita Szigeti, an expert on mental health law who has several clients in long-term seclusion at Waypoint, the province’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital, located on Georgian Bay in Penetanguishene.

The hospital has consistently refused to divulge how many patients are being kept in long-term seclusion, but it was revealed during an Ontario Review Board hearing earlier this month that there are at least 11 secluded patients just in the 20-bed unit where Azevedo is kept.

An independent assessment filed during the hearing concluded that seclusion would fall under the United Nations’ definition of solitary confinement, and that secluded patients at Waypoint are being kept in conditions that the UN has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings. Waypoint’s CEO, Dr. Nadiya Sunderji, has said the hospital “categorically” disagrees with those findings.

The records outlining the concerns that were brought to the government’s attention in 2018, and the ministry’s subsequent probe in 2019, were filed as part of a proposed class action against the hospital by Toronto firm Rochon Genova on behalf of several plaintiffs who have been kept in long-term seclusion.

It’s a missed opportunity that has cost a lot of people their freedom

The courts declined to certify the matter as a class action, concluding that the decision to seclude a patient is an individualized process and plaintiffs alleging wrongdoing would have to bring individual claims.

The office of Health Minister Sylvia Jones did not respond to the Star’s request for comment for this story; Jones’ ministry has not responded to any requests from the Star regarding its coverage of seclusion at Waypoint.

The concerns were raised in December 2018 — a few months after Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservative government came to power — by forensic psychiatrist Dr. John Bradford, one of the world’s leading experts in forensic psychiatry who briefly worked at Waypoint.

“I was concerned about the serious and irreversible harm that patients would suffer in confinement,” Bradford said in an affidavit filed in court.

He said that patients were being confined for long periods of time in “horrific conditions, the likes of which I have never seen in any other psychiatric hospital in Ontario.”

In an interview with the Star this month, Bradford said he felt his concerns were taken seriously by the ministry. However, he didn’t have the full picture about what the ministry did with those concerns until this summer, when he viewed the other records filed in the proposed class action.

Bringing concerns to government

Bradford worked for decades as the clinical director of the forensic psychiatry program at what was then the Royal Ottawa Hospital, and is a past chair of the examination board for forensic psychiatry of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada.

He worked at Waypoint between 2016 and 2017. He resigned after his concerns about the prolonged use of seclusion went unaddressed after raising them with the hospital’s senior executives, including then-CEO Carol Lambie.

People being in seclusion for long periods of time, even years, “was very, very foreign to me in any of my previous psychiatric experience,” Bradford told the Star. “I’d seen similar situations in correctional facilities, but never in a health care facility.”

He decided to raise his concerns externally. He first went to the Ontario Human Rights Commission, where he felt they took the issues seriously, but Bradford was worried about their lack of power to compel Waypoint to do anything.

He and another Waypoint psychiatrist decided to go instead to the provincial government. They had a meeting in December 2018 with then-assistant deputy health minister, Tim Hadwen. Bradford recalled there was also a lawyer from the attorney general’s office and a representative from the local health integration network at the meeting. He said the main focus was the “abusive” prolonged seclusion.

Bradford understood that there were limits to what the ministry could do. Waypoint, at the time operating under a different name, was divested from the Ontario government in 2008 along with other psychiatric facilities, meaning the government was no longer responsible for the day-to-day operation of the hospital.

But Waypoint was still a public Catholic hospital, and the health minister retained some discretionary powers, such as issuing directives to the hospital’s board or appointing inspectors to review the hospital’s operations.

“If my concerns were correct, and I believed they were, then I believed that those were things the ministry could consider,” Bradford said.

Inside the ministry’s probe

Cochrane and another ministry official, Ragaven Sabaratnam, were tasked with looking into Bradford’s concerns.

In an affidavit filed in May 2023, Cochrane said they conducted interviews “with management staff at Waypoint,” as well as with the psychiatric patient advocate office, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario and the North Simcoe Muskoka local health integration network. Waypoint also shared some of its policies with them.

They brought the results of the interviews to Hadwen, who “determined that there was no need for the minister of health to exercise” any of the discretionary powers “because Waypoint had policies and procedures in place to address clinical care for its patients,” Cochrane says in her affidavit.

No further steps were taken, she said.

Hadwen communicated the outcome to Bradford in an April 2019 email, one in a series of emails filed in court.

Horrific conditions, the likes of which I have never seen in any other psychiatric hospital in Ontario.

“After reviewing the information made available to us, we are confident that Waypoint has implemented changes to address the concerns you raised,” Hadwen wrote.

He said that the ministry’s work included speaking with representatives — plural — of Waypoint.

In fact, only one Waypoint representative — then-vice-president of clinical services Rob Desroches — was interviewed, over the phone. Cochrane confirmed this when she was cross-examined on her affidavit by the plaintiffs’ lawyers in the proposed class action, when asked if her Waypoint interviews were with any of the senior executives named as defendants in the lawsuit.

“The interview was with Mr. Desroches,” she said.

The lawyer followed up: “So it was a single interview?”

Cochrane replied that it was. She said the interview would have been “definitely less than two hours.”

A summary of the January 2019 call with Desroches shows the ministry officials asked him six questions, three of which were about seclusion. The first question sought clarification on the hospital’s reporting policies and practices around seclusion.

Desroches said the hospital was in the midst of revamping some of its procedures, which would include clinical managers creating daily, weekly, and monthly reports about seclusion that would go up to vice presidents for review.

He said “several initiatives have been put in place” to reduce the use of seclusion and that an unnamed expert had been brought in from the United States to provide training on safety and the use of seclusion.

He said Waypoint had also requested additional funding to hire more people to escort patients out of seclusion more often; as the Star reported last week, the hospital is still struggling to bring all secluded patients out for seclusion relief on a daily basis due to staffing shortages.

In response to another question, Desroches said there had been no third-party review conducted specifically on the use of long-term seclusion.

‘That is not an investigation’

Back in 2019, Bradford was pleased with Hadwen’s response.

“I sincerely appreciate you taking our concerns seriously and acting on these concerns,” Bradford wrote in an email. “I appreciate you taking action in the name of quality of care and respect for the human rights of the patients detained at Waypoint.”

Hadwen then forwarded Bradford’s response to Cochrane — “Reasonably positive,” Hadwen wrote.

Cochrane, in turn, forwarded the response to other ministry staff, writing: “FYI — Hopefully we can close this file now.”

Bradford said he was dismayed when he saw the emails for the first time this summer.

In the years since Bradford’s warning, Waypoint has continued to lock patients up in long-term isolation. By 2019, Hamblett would have already been in continuous seclusion at Waypoint for almost 14 years. He’s still in seclusion to this day.

“I’m still not sure what to make of it,” Bradford said of Cochrane’s email. “It sounds as though they thought the matter was over. I took them at face value that they had sorted things out.”

Bradford said he had no idea the ministry had only spoken to one representative at Waypoint, nor that officials had not gone into the facility, “which would have been, in my mind, the most basic part of intervening,” Bradford said.

“I think there’s a big difference between hearing someone talking about policies and procedures and actually seeing how they implement them.”

Cochrane has been involved in conducting a secret review of the forensic mental health system, which the Star first reported in April.

Cochrane wrote to Szigeti, the lawyer, asking if she would participate in a “confidential discussion” about the system and requesting that she sign a nondisclosure agreement. “We believe your input will make an important contribution to informing advice to government,” Cochrane wrote.

Szigeti declined to participate as she refused to sign the NDA. The Star subsequently filed a freedom of information request for the terms of reference of the review, but was told that “no responsive records were located.”

Szigeti said in an interview this month that she shares Bradford’s concerns about the ministry’s actions in 2019.

“That is not an investigation,” she said. “That’s a phone call to ask basic questions — ‘In your opinion, are you doing everything right?’”

She said it appears that the magnitude of the problem of long-term seclusion was not revealed to the ministry during their questioning, “but it should have been.”

“If this had been properly investigated back in 2018-19 and the institution had been forced to correct course, then Camelott Hamblett May have been released from seclusion,” she said.

And Azevedo, who has been held in seclusion since 2021, May have never been placed in isolation in the first place.

Bradford said he also can’t shake the thought of Hamblett and whether his situation would have improved had things been done differently almost a decade ago.

“It’s an enormous period of somebody’s lifetime,” he said.

stories.title: Ontario teacher contracts expire, with no deal in sight. What parents and students need to know
stories.summary: Negotiations have stalled at the outset, with disputes over what’s to be discussed where in a two-tier bargaining system.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
paragraphs: The school year is about to start — but teacher and support staff contract talks are nowhere near finished.
On Saturday — just two days before all agreements expire Monday — education unions took part in rallies held across the province. And they’re planning their own in-school day of solidarity Sept. 16.

While it is not unusual for negotiations to continue into the fall and new year, this time around they have stalled at the outset, with the province and most education unions duelling over what is to be discussed at central and local tables under Ontario’s two-tier bargaining system.
They now await labour board rulings, which could take weeks or months. With no strike votes taken as yet, and with no real talks, job action or strikes can’t happen anytime soon.
Balanced Day trades the traditional day for three 100-minute teaching periods split by two 45-minute “nutrition breaks.”

“It’s truly frustrating. We have been talking about bargaining for quite some time; we did ask to bargain early ,” said Joe Tigani, president of Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions, referring to a call by education labour leaders to begin talks last March instead of June.
“Our members are going into the fall knowing that we’re short-staffed” and under-resourced, he added. “Kids have less; workers have to do more with less.”

Under the province’s bargaining system, big-money items such as salaries and benefits are discussed between the unions, and the province and the association representing directors of education, with more administrative issues left for union locals and individual boards.

“At this early stage of bargaining, the first step is to determine what issues will be negotiated at central or local tables. Those decisions are still underway, with some unions choosing to bring this matter to the Ontario Labour Relations Board,” said Emma Testani, press secretary to Education Minister Paul Calandra.
“We respect their decision to do so and at all times are ready to continue discussions on the scope of central versus local issues before proceeding to the next stage of negotiations.”

Tigani hopes the labour board process “will be done in a reasonable time frame, which will allow us to get back to the table and engage in some meaningful conversation ... We will be looking ahead and planning for all eventualities into the fall and into the spring.”

He added, however, that “if the government continues to do everything they can to stall the process and not want to engage, then I guess we May have a look at other options to get them to engage in the bargaining process ... I mean, if it’s March of 2027 and the government still is trying to figure out a way to not bargain, I think we’re having a very different conversation.”
While the province is spending more on education, unions and school boards have argued it has not kept up with inflation most years, and doesn’t match their actual costs.
Students and their families joined the rally at Queen’s Park on Saturday.

But with $30.6 billion in core education funding this year, Testani said “our government continues to make historic investments in education to protect student learning, strengthen classrooms and ensure students and teachers have the supports they need to succeed.”
She said that funding increases since 2017-18 have hit 30.8 per cent, “outpacing inflation of 27.1 per cent over the same period.”
Rob Kristofferson, a labour studies expert and professor at Wilfrid Laurier University, said the decision on what is negotiated centrally and locally is important.

“They unions have talked about surplus and redundancy rules” around jobs, he said, “and they feel those issues can be very unique to local boards and are not suitable for centralization. I gather the government is going in the other direction.”

Kristofferson, who is also president of the Ontario Confederation of University Faculty Associations, said with the labour board decision “this could drag on for a few months before we get much indication which way it’s going to go.”

However, he added, “democracy can be messy and time-consuming, but it’s certainly a valuable thing that we need to preserve. We can’t just do everything in the sake of efficiency or uniformity; we need to have our local communities, parents and teachers locally who understand those environments much better than some remote government at Queen’s Park, and they should be participating in the decision making about their local institutions.”

For now, there is no threat of a strike or lockout hitting schools. Bargaining has to begin in earnest before the sides can apply for conciliation, and if no deal is reached after that, a no-board report can be issued allowing a strike or job action 17 days later.
The day of solidarity planned next month is expected to be like one held last spring, with union members sporting similar colours, or union leaders speaking publicly about the issues.
David Mastin, president of the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, says it’s a show of unity for all 275,000 teachers and education workers in the province.

stories.content:
The school year is about to start — but teacher and support staff contract talks are nowhere near finished.

On Saturday — just two days before all agreements expire Monday — education unions took part in rallies held across the province. And they’re planning their own in-school day of solidarity Sept. 16.

While it is not unusual for negotiations to continue into the fall and new year, this time around they have stalled at the outset, with the province and most education unions duelling over what is to be discussed at central and local tables under Ontario’s two-tier bargaining system.

They now await labour board rulings, which could take weeks or months. With no strike votes taken as yet, and with no real talks, job action or strikes can’t happen anytime soon.

Balanced Day trades the traditional day for three 100-minute teaching periods split by two 45-minute “nutrition breaks.”

“It’s truly frustrating. We have been talking about bargaining for quite some time; we did ask to bargain early ,” said Joe Tigani, president of Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions, referring to a call by education labour leaders to begin talks last March instead of June.

“Our members are going into the fall knowing that we’re short-staffed” and under-resourced, he added. “Kids have less; workers have to do more with less.”

Under the province’s bargaining system, big-money items such as salaries and benefits are discussed between the unions, and the province and the association representing directors of education, with more administrative issues left for union locals and individual boards.

“At this early stage of bargaining, the first step is to determine what issues will be negotiated at central or local tables. Those decisions are still underway, with some unions choosing to bring this matter to the Ontario Labour Relations Board,” said Emma Testani, press secretary to Education Minister Paul Calandra.

“We respect their decision to do so and at all times are ready to continue discussions on the scope of central versus local issues before proceeding to the next stage of negotiations.”

Tigani hopes the labour board process “will be done in a reasonable time frame, which will allow us to get back to the table and engage in some meaningful conversation ... We will be looking ahead and planning for all eventualities into the fall and into the spring.”

He added, however, that “if the government continues to do everything they can to stall the process and not want to engage, then I guess we May have a look at other options to get them to engage in the bargaining process ... I mean, if it’s March of 2027 and the government still is trying to figure out a way to not bargain, I think we’re having a very different conversation.”

While the province is spending more on education, unions and school boards have argued it has not kept up with inflation most years, and doesn’t match their actual costs.

Students and their families joined the rally at Queen’s Park on Saturday.

But with $30.6 billion in core education funding this year, Testani said “our government continues to make historic investments in education to protect student learning, strengthen classrooms and ensure students and teachers have the supports they need to succeed.”

She said that funding increases since 2017-18 have hit 30.8 per cent, “outpacing inflation of 27.1 per cent over the same period.”

Rob Kristofferson, a labour studies expert and professor at Wilfrid Laurier University, said the decision on what is negotiated centrally and locally is important.

“They unions have talked about surplus and redundancy rules” around jobs, he said, “and they feel those issues can be very unique to local boards and are not suitable for centralization. I gather the government is going in the other direction.”

Kristofferson, who is also president of the Ontario Confederation of University Faculty Associations, said with the labour board decision “this could drag on for a few months before we get much indication which way it’s going to go.”

However, he added, “democracy can be messy and time-consuming, but it’s certainly a valuable thing that we need to preserve. We can’t just do everything in the sake of efficiency or uniformity; we need to have our local communities, parents and teachers locally who understand those environments much better than some remote government at Queen’s Park, and they should be participating in the decision making about their local institutions.”

For now, there is no threat of a strike or lockout hitting schools. Bargaining has to begin in earnest before the sides can apply for conciliation, and if no deal is reached after that, a no-board report can be issued allowing a strike or job action 17 days later.

The day of solidarity planned next month is expected to be like one held last spring, with union members sporting similar colours, or union leaders speaking publicly about the issues.

David Mastin, president of the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, says it’s a show of unity for all 275,000 teachers and education workers in the province.
