According to a criminal complaint, the woman contacted law enforcement July 31 and reported concerning behaviour from Larson dating back to 2013. The woman told investigators she dated Larson for about two months in 2013 after meeting him through mutual friends. At the time, she lived in Madison and Larson lived in Fond du Lac. She described the relationship as intense and said Larson expressed an obsession with Ed Gein, death and gore. The relationship ended after Larson allegedly called her and said he was suicidal with a gun to his head. The woman moved to Canada later that year and did not give Larson her new address. She said Larson subsequently sent several letters to her mother’s home in Madison and continued trying to contact her in the years that followed. In a 15-page email sent in 2015, Larson allegedly told the woman he had tattooed “their symbol” and her initials on his body and wrote extensively about his inability to let go of their relationship. “My will to care about you is just too strong. I simply don’t let go, and I don’t forget,” Larson allegedly wrote. The complaint says Larson also told the woman he had kept numerous items from their brief relationship, including letters, an earring he said was still tangled with her hair, a pressed flower, cards and a voicemail. The woman told investigators the unwanted contact intensified again in 2025. In November, she received a handwritten card from Larson at her business office in Dane County. Larson allegedly acknowledged that she did not want to speak with him but wrote that he would continue trying to reach her until she responded, including potentially calling or “just knock[ing] on your door someday.” A month later, the woman received another card at her home address. The “Nightmare Before Christmas”-style card featured the phrase “Season’s Creeping” and included a letter in which Larson allegedly wrote about wandering around Madison and possibly encountering her. “That would be a memorable encounter, surely... I’ll keep my eyes open,” Larson allegedly wrote. The complaint says Larson ended the letter by referring to the woman’s husband and child by name. The woman told investigators that was especially distressing because she and her husband had been careful not to post information about their child on social media, and she did not know how Larson obtained her home address. Larson also allegedly filed complaints against the woman, who works as a therapist, with professional licensing boards. The woman told police Larson had never been her client. In one complaint, Larson allegedly accused her of refusing to provide “closure” over the relationship, which had ended more than a decade earlier. The woman told officers through tears that she “just wants this to stop” and said she feared what Larson might do next, including what could happen to her child. She later told detectives she “just wanted to disappear,” because that had been the only way Larson stopped contacting her. Investigators executed a search warrant Aug. 14 at Larson’s Fond du Lac County residence, where authorities reported finding an extensive collection of items related to murders, serial killers and the woman. At the bottom of the basement stairs, investigators reported seeing a grave rubbing bearing the name “Edward Gein.” Inside the basement were glass shelves containing memorabilia connected to several notorious killers, including 10 binders labelled “Edward Gein Book,” items purportedly from Gein’s grave or home and .22-caliber cartridges displayed with a sign claiming they were the same type used by the Zodiac Killer. Investigators also reported finding a jar accompanied by a sign claiming it contained a piece of John Wayne Gacy’s brain, a mummy and bottles labelled with names including arsenic, strychnine, cyanide and ricin. The complaint does not establish whether those labels accurately identified the objects or substances. Authorities also reported finding skeletal remains in a glass casket, a skull displayed in a glass case and additional skulls on shelves. The Fond du Lac County Sheriff’s Office said an anthropologist conducted an initial examination of the remains and determined many are likely ancient Native American remains. Authorities said additional testing is needed to determine more about their origin. Investigators also searched a padlocked room in the basement after a passcode Larson provided did not work and officers forced their way inside. Authorities described the room as a bedroom containing a lifelike silicone doll and what appeared to be a painting of a nude woman resembling the alleged stalking victim. Papers bearing the woman’s name were also found on the bed. One note allegedly described a plan to send letters under another person’s name and mail them from a different area to prevent the woman from immediately recognizing their origin. The writer also discussed heating the letters and envelopes to destroy fingerprints and DNA. Investigators reported finding five skulls and part of another skull on shelves in the room, two large bones arranged in the shape of a cross and what appeared to be a human jawbone on a dresser. They also found a tote and garbage bag containing numerous items allegedly connected to the woman, including letters, pressed flowers, bottles and a clay head investigators said appeared to depict her. Among the books discovered was one about a woman stalked for 13 years before being kidnapped and held in a soundproof storage container. Other books dealt with private investigation, finding information about people and the psychology of stalking. Investigators also recovered a 25-page collection of writings that repeatedly referenced the woman, her husband and their child. In one passage, the writer expressed anger over the woman’s life with her family and wrote about wanting “to take their skulls.” Assistant District Attorney David Olson highlighted that passage during a court hearing. “The defendant discusses aching to take the skulls of the person, who again in context, is the victim and her partner,” Olson said. Another passage described traveling to the woman’s home at night while dressed in black with gloves and a mask. The writer described circling the block, sitting outside the home with the vehicle’s lights and engine turned off and holding a machete while watching the house. The writer also described approaching the property, taking bags of garbage and wanting to experience the feeling again. The passage characterized the behaviour as “creepy, strange, stalker-ish, potentially dangerous,” but said it did not bother the writer. Larson’s attorney, Sara Christensen, emphasized during the hearing that the allegations have not been proven and questioned whether the writings reflected events that actually occurred. “We don’t know if there is anything that connects those writings to being an actual event or if they are just writings,” Christensen said. Christensen also said Larson has no prior criminal history, has lived in the same home for more than 20 years and has known his wife for more than 25 years. The judge described the allegations as “very disturbing,” while noting that they remain allegations. “It’s not normal behaviour for a rational person that’s alleged here,” the judge said. “I understand they’re just allegations.” Larson was given a $15,000 cash bond. Court records show he posted the bond and was released from custody. He is scheduled to return to court Sept. 11. By Adam Rife

stories.title: Trump's inner circle shrinks as senior White House officials resign ahead of midterms
stories.summary: Trump faces a growing White House staff exodus as key advisers depart ahead of the 2026 midterm elections in November.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
President Donald Trump is entering a critical stretch of his second term with a slew of resignations among his senior staff, forcing him to rely on an even smaller circle of aides.

Over the last month, Trump lost his chief spokesperson, his top legal adviser, a key national security adviser and his liaison to Capitol Hill. More senior officials are said to be weighing a potential exit over the next few months, according to people familiar with the matter.

While staff departures are typical before midterm elections, the departures of key aides such as White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt this month took some in the White House by surprise, according to a person familiar with the matter.

James Braid, White House director of legislative affairs and a longtime Trump aide, announced earlier this month his plans to quit in the coming weeks. Braid’s announcement came a week after Leavitt — another one of Trump’s most trusted advisers and fiercest defenders — said she would step down at the end of August. Their successors have not been announced.

White House deputy national security adviser Andy Baker, who had been personally involved in negotiations with Iran, and White House Counsel David Warrington have also departed and were replaced by existing administration officials.

The senior staff exodus comes at an already tumultuous time for Trump, who is struggling with foreign and domestic challenges — including some of his own making.

Republicans are facing the prospect of losing their congressional majorities in the November midterm elections, a result that could open his administration to subpoenas and investigations under a Democratic-led Congress.

As he enters the last two years of his final term, Trump faces historically low approval ratings, a shaky economy and an unpopular war in Iran that has roiled the global energy markets. He’s engaged in a fresh trade war with Canada and has lashed out at South Korea, another longtime U.S. ally.

The string of departures threatens to create a vacuum in Trump’s inner circle and finding replacements won’t be easy.

“If your vetting process the first go-round mandates that you have to claim that the 2020 election was stolen, then the pool of candidates was probably already small and getting smaller now,” said Marc Short, who served in the first Trump administration.

The administration expressed little outward concern over the outflow of aides.

“This movement is bigger than any one staff member, and the president’s mission to make America greater than ever before will continue unabated,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers.

Still, the loss of some of Trump’s closest advisers has left the White House without a clear succession plan in key offices. Braid, whose job was to press congressional Republicans on the president’s legislative agenda, has lost much of his staff over the last six months, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Though Leavitt plans to remain in Trump’s orbit, her absence in the communications office deprives the president of one of his most effective messengers to sell his domestic and foreign policies to skeptical voters.

Trump, however, is in no rush to replace Leavitt, according to a person familiar with the matter. In the meantime, the White House is weighing a plan to again rotate Cabinet officials through the briefing room as they did while she was on maternity leave earlier this year, the person said.

“This also is, without question, the hardest time to hire into an administration,” said Lisa Camooso Miller, a former Republican National Committee communications director. “The real question is, who’s going to fill these roles? Will they be the right people, and will they be people that the president listens to? It’s not so much about the vacancies, but who’s willing to go into the second two years of an administration that largely will face headwinds with a change in Congress.”

Post-midterm strategy

The administration has announced some key moves to boost its political operation and strategy ahead of the midterms.

In April, Trump announced deputy chief of staff James Blair would temporarily leave the White House to lead the president’s political operation. Earlier this summer, the White House brought back veteran advisers Jason Miller and Johnny DeStefano to focus on midterm messaging, Bloomberg previously reported.

Trump also tapped his cabinet secretary, Will Scharf, to replace Warrington as White House counsel, partly in preparation for the onslaught of congressional investigations should Democrats take control of the House, according to a White House official. Scharf was part of Trump’s legal team during his four years out of office and was one of the president’s lawyers in the election obstruction case.

Several other aides have left in recent months. Trump’s pardons attorney and staunch ally Ed Martin has announced his departure from the Justice Department. Abigail Jackson, a deputy White House spokeswoman, stepped down last month to take a job in the private sector. Emily Underwood, who worked under White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, left earlier this month to join a venture capital firm, according to a person familiar with her decision. Caleb Orr, a top adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is expected to replace her.

The remaining team will have their work cut out for them. In addition to resolving conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, some within the party are pushing the White House for fresh economic plans, including further tax cuts to expand the president’s signature tax and spending law.

The administration is expected to unveil economic-focused policy proposals in the coming weeks, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Trump has also told aides he wants to travel more frequently to stump for House and Senate candidates in the home stretch of the midterm campaign, the person said. Cabinet members have been traveling ahead of the midterms, and there has been internal competition among them to do so, the person said.

“I think it’s clear that the number one issue continues to be affordability and people feeling insecure in the current economy,” Short said. “There also has to be: Here’s what our candidates clearly laid out, and I’m less confident that American voters understand that right now.”

— With assistance from Jennifer A. Dlouhy and Josh Wingrove.

stories.title: Thousands of people escape reality at the Oxford Renaissance Festival
stories.summary: The Oxford Renaissance Festival (ORF) in Thorndale, Ont. brought thousands of people out into a world of imagination.
stories.author: Brent Lale
paragraphs: It’s an escape into a world of creativity. The Oxford Renaissance Festival (ORF) in Thorndale, Ont. brought thousands of people out into a world of imagination. At the Larp (Live Action Pole Playing) fight pit, guests were getting a chance to battle. “I love encouraging everybody to get out of their bubble and try something new,” said Karma, the voice of the fight pit.

“I can talk to you until I’m blue in the face, but nothings is going to give you the vision until you are able to see if for yourself with your own eyes.” All around the Thorndale Fairgrounds, people were dressed up. “I am a fawn today,” said Cade Collins, a cosplayer. “I made up this costume. Most of the pieces are made by me like my shirt and my vest and my bracers.

I love being at the Ren Fair and getting to dress up and see people and all sorts of cool outfits.” A few metres away, gun commander Mike Robertson was loading his cannon to fire. “This is the greatest,” said Robertson who owns the three-pound ball cannon from the 1990s. “This is this is something we do we do about 12 weekends a year and it’s super fun to even own a cannon.”

Back at the fight pit, Dustin Smith (AKA Wargn Magnamus) was helping with the Larp. He is a part of a group who travel to a 53-acre property near Watford, Ont. every weekend to Mixed Medieval Arts Larp. “Our very first year here, they thought we’d be sitting around a little table, giving up business cards, showing off a brochure, something like that,” said Magnamus.

“We ran around in a rat costume until they got somebody dressed in a rat catcher costume, and we just made that storyline up that every day is new here. Every day is something special.” Each year since 2013, the ORF has brought thousands of people to a place where they can enjoy a comedy show, food, drink, vendors or just mingle with pirates and fairies.
“People that want to escape this political, mundane world, to be able to come in to an age of fantasy, to an age of history, and be able to relive some of our culture,” said Magnamus.

stories.title: Danielle Smith to speak at Alberta Day celebration as referendum nears
stories.summary: Alberta officially became a Canadian province on Sept. 1, 1905, and various festivities were planned this weekend ahead of the province's birthday on Tuesday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith is set to speak in Calgary on Sunday afternoon at an event marking Alberta Day.

Alberta officially became a Canadian province on Sept. 1, 1905, and various festivities were planned this weekend ahead of the province’s birthday on Tuesday.

Smith’s speech at Calgary’s Heritage Park is set to come as the province’s separation referendum nears.

The premier has called a vote for Oct. 19 that will ask Albertans whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The premier has said she’s voting for the province to stay, and that hundreds of thousands of Albertans signed petitions in support of either separation or staying in Confederation.

She said their voices deserve to be heard.

Petitioners on both sides have pushed back against Smith’s approach.

Separatist leader Jeffrey Rath has accused Smith of betraying separatist UCP members, misleading Albertans and undermining the province’s interests in Ottawa.

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, accuse Smith of self-serving politics by calling the vote merely to placate restive separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

4:41 Alberta’s Smith advises Canada against ‘making threats’ to U.S. amid trade war

On Saturday, Alberta separatists converged outside the legislature in Edmonton, with many saying Alberta would be better off without Canada after having joined Confederation 121 years ago.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi held a “Vote for Canada” rally in Calgary, also on Saturday. During that rally, he called for the fall referendum to be put off amid the escalating trade war with the United States.

Earlier this week, Thomas Lukaszuk, organizer of the pro-federalist Forever Canadian petition, made a similar call.

Lukaszuk said he was writing on behalf of the more than 400,000 Albertans who signed his petition.

“We submit that this is not the time for unnecessary domestic conflict; this is the time for Albertans to stand together with our fellow Canadians and collectively rally against this unprecedented economic threat,” Lukaszuk wrote.

Smith was asked about the calls to postpone the referendum amid the trade tensions during a recent interview with CTV News, but didn’t say whether rescheduling the vote was on the table.

Instead, she compared the anger Canadians in Quebec and Ontario might be feeling toward Trump amid the trade war with the anger Albertans feel toward former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

Smith has said before separatists have a decade-long list of resentments with Trudeau over his energy and environmental policies.

“I would say that in the last 18 months, the new prime minister and I have done everything we can to reset the relationship,” she said during the interview.

“But when you cause that kind of damage, people get hurt. That’s what we’re seeing in Alberta right now. I don’t think that you solve problems by ignoring them. You solve problems by addressing it.”

She said she is working to explain to Albertans that Ottawa is working for them, and vice versa, and renewed her call for Albertans to vote to remain in Confederation.

stories.title: No danger to public after CN train derailment in Nova Scotia: officials
stories.summary: The company says the upright derailment happened around 5:30 p.m. Saturday in Truro, N.S., and the cause is under investigation. No leaks, fires or injuries were reported.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted August 30, 2026 2:04 pm

CN says there is no danger to public safety after 14 railcars derailed in central Nova Scotia.

The company says the upright derailment happened around 5:30 p.m. Saturday in Truro, N.S., and the cause is under investigation.

CN says three of the derailed railcars contained residue hydrogen peroxide, and they have been safely secured.

The railroad company says the other 11 railcars were carrying mostly “paper-related” products.

It says no leaks, fires or injuries have been reported.

A detour remains in place around the Queen Street railway crossing as of Sunday.

CN apologized to Truro residents for the inconvenience caused by the derailment, and thanked local emergency services for their help.

stories.title: Trump renaming Lake Ontario 'like something out of Saturday Night Live,' says Ford
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford wants to move past the Lake Ontario-Lake America matter and see a trade deal to let Canada and the U.S. prosper.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: Ontario Premier Doug Ford ridiculed President Donald Trump’s order changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, while expressing optimism that Canada and the U.S. would eventually overcome their differences on trade and tariffs.

Ford, who was part of a heated back-and-forth with Trump last week after talks over a U.S.-Canada trade deal broke down, said on Abc’s This Week on Sunday that the Great Lake’s name would stay despite Trump’s executive order to rename it.

“It was like something out of Saturday Night Live, when he signed a document saying ‘Change to Lake America,’” Ford said. “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue to be Lake Ontario.”
The premier expressed confidence that the two sides will overcome their dispute.
“God bless America. God bless Canada. We’ll get through this,” he said. “Let’s get a deal and let both countries prosper.”

Canada and the United States have been locked in an increasingly tense trade dispute that has led to tariff increases on both sides. Ford said he had advised Prime Minister Mark Carney that the most recent deal on the table would have been bad for Canada.

“I deal with the Leadership of many Countries, but I find Canada to be the worst. They are entitled no longer!” Trump said in a social media post on Sunday. Trump threatened further consequences last week if the U.S. neighbour and Nato ally didn’t “get in line.”
Ford said Trump’s actions were damaging the U.S. economy.

“There’s countries all over the world that want our uranium, our potash, our, you know, high-grade nickel and every other critical mineral. I’d rather sell it down to the U.S.,” he said. “If you work together, we’re going to create more opportunities, more jobs. If I can say, everyone’s feeling bullied by President Trump, and this is the worst thing he could do for the American economy.”

stories.title: Museum London karaoke night to turn favourite songs into stories of home
stories.summary: Londoners are being invited to reach into their musical past and perform a song during a karaoke night exploring culture and belonging at Museum London. Come As You Are Karaoke and CD Jewel Case Collage Night is inspired by Heart-shaped Box, a video installation featuring childhood footage of Toronto artist Zinnia Naqvi singing rock songs […]
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us May earn us a commission, which supports our work.

Londoners are being invited to reach into their musical past and perform a song during a karaoke night exploring culture and belonging at Museum London.

Come As You Are Karaoke and CD Jewel Case Collage Night is inspired by Heart-shaped Box, a video installation featuring childhood footage of Toronto artist Zinnia Naqvi singing rock songs with her older sisters in the mid-1990s.

“I think in all of my work, I try to sort of complicate the diasporic experience,” said Naqvi, a photographer and video artist who teaches part-time at Toronto Metropolitan University and the University of Toronto.

Naqvi was born in Canada after her parents and sisters immigrated from Pakistan. The footage shows three-year-old Naqvi learning the popular songs her teenage sisters had embraced while adjusting to life in Canada.

The installation examines how people can inherit traditions from their families while also claiming the language and popular culture surrounding them. Its title comes from the Nirvana song Naqvi sings in the video.

The work is featured in Biscuits and Empire: Reframing Colonial Photography, which pairs Naqvi’s family videos with photographs of British India found in Museum London’s collection.

The exhibition connects London’s former biscuit industry with colonial trade while contrasting historical photographs of India with a family recording itself on its own terms.

“There’s a different way of telling a story, and there’s a way of telling your own story,” said Zahra McDoom of Museum London. “That’s what I would like people to take away.”

McDoom found the 1940s photographs, taken in British India and later donated by London-based Somerville Industries, and invited Naqvi to create a contemporary response.

“Karaoke is really a release. I’m a big karaoke fan,” Naqvi said. “I like to go with my friends a lot because it can just be a really great way to express yourself and have fun.”

Visitors May perform any song that reminds them of home, childhood or an important period in their lives. The all-ages event, organized with Ontario Culture Days in collaboration with local karaoke group Queeraoke, also includes an activity in which participants decorate old CD jewel cases and create new cover art.

“It’s the perfect opportunity to soak in Zinnia’s and Zahra’s exhibition and then go belt out your song of choice,” said Sarah Munro, Museum London’s curator of engagement and outreach.

The event will be held in the museum’s Centre at the Forks, a glass-walled space overlooking the Thames River.

Munro said she hopes the night leaves visitors with “a greater appreciation for making the connection between art and history here at Museum London.”

What: Come As You Are Karaoke and CD Jewel Case Collage Night

When: Saturday, Sept. 26, from 6 to 8 p.m.

Where: Museum London, 421 Ridout St. N. (Centre at the Forks)

Admission: Pay what you can; a $10 donation is suggested

stories.title: Grand Bend man charged after fleeing OPP stop
stories.summary: A man from Grand Bend is facing multiple charges after allegedly fleeing a traffic stop and nearly striking pedestrians and police officers during two separate encounters with OPP on Friday.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
paragraphs: A man from Grand Bend is facing multiple charges after allegedly fleeing a traffic stop and nearly striking pedestrians and police officers during two separate encounters with OPP on Friday. The Lambton County OPP say the incident began just after 5 p.m. on Aug.

28 during a seatbelt enforcement campaign near Main Street and Kitchener Avenue in Grand Bend. Police say the driver fled after being stopped, nearly hitting several pedestrians as he left the area. According to the OPP, the vehicle then travelled to Oak Street, where officers were conducting a Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (Ride) spot check.

Police say the driver went through the checkpoint and nearly struck three uniformed officers. No injuries were reported. The suspect was later located and arrested. The suspect, 36, of Grand Bend, has been charged with three counts of assault with a weapon and one count of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle.

He also faces charges of failing to stop for police, failing to properly wear a seatbelt, making unnecessary noise, driving without a licence, and performing a stunt with a motor vehicle. Lambton OPP is asking anyone who witnessed the incident or has dashcam or surveillance footage from the area to contact police.

stories.title: Google changes Lake Ontario to Lake of America for Google Maps users in the U.S.
stories.summary: Following its 'long-standing policy,' Google will now display Lake America instead of Lake Ontario for Maps users in the U.S.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
paragraphs: Google has officially renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America on its Maps interface — at least for people using the app or website in the U.S.

On Saturday, the tech giant announced it had changed the name of the body of water, through which the border with Canada runs, to reflect the most recent update from the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (Gnis).
That change was initiated by an executive order signed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week, instructing the department of the interior to make it so.
“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” Google wrote.

What app users will see depends on their country location, as determined by their device’s operating system, SIM, network and current location. Desktop and other web viewers are presented information based on individual regional search settings or, failing that, the device’s location as determined by Google.

That means people in the U.S. should see Trump’s new moniker, Canadians will keep seeing the historically accurate name and the rest of the world will see both names, presented as “Lake Ontario (Lake America).”
National Post contacted Google’s country manager for Canada, Sabrina Geramia, for comment but was directed back to its statement.

In testing other web and app-based mapping services from a Canadian address, Apple Maps users continue to see Lake Ontario. A search for “Lake America” yields America Lake in Brule County, South Dakota and, curiously, Lake Ontario.

They followed up by creating an interface that lets users enter their own names for the lake to generate a map image, or have MapQuest create one at random, such as “Lake Oh Canada,” “Lake Double-Double,” and “Lake Not Erie.”
Their example, a shot at Trump’s Gulf of America renaming, was “Lake Are We Doing This Again?”
Some of the user replies included names like “Lake of Hormuz,” “Lake Epstein Files,” and “Lake Tariff Tantrum.”
There are other locations around the world where two places have the same name on Google Maps for users from outside those countries.

For instance, the British see the Falkland Islands while Argentinians see the South American island chain as Islas Malvinas. Everyone else gets the English name first, the other in parentheses. The same style applies to the long-disputed Persian or Arabian Gulf separating Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Also on Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford dipped his toes back into the debate by posting a video of himself lakeside next to a new billboard at the Fifty Point Conservation Area in Grimsby that reads “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” in both official languages.

“Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them,” Ford said in the 39-second clip in which he also accused the U.S. head of state of making the change because Canada is “standing up” for itself in the trade war with the U.S.

Trump appeared to fire back later Saturday afternoon, posting an AI-generated video of himself kicking over a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign along a shoreline and replacing it with one reading “Welcome to America” over the iconic intro to the Peer Gynt suite adapted by Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg. The music then switches to the Village People’s Ymca as Trump performs his signature dance moves.

Earlier in the day, he’d posted another AI-generated video of a marching army of Canadian geese with hair similar to Trump’s and holding machine guns in muscled human arms. The video, set to the theme song for the television show Hawaii Five-O, ends with the birds firing their weapons as fireworks soar overhead and the words “Lake America” appear.
The president aired further grievances against Canada on Truth Social Sunday, using the automotive industry as his foil.
In a longer post later, he claimed to have “revived, and indeed saved” the American car industry by way of tariffs.

“One of the Worst Abusers is Canada. I don’t want Canadian cars, I don’t want Canadian parts, I don’t want Canadian anything. They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” he wrote.
“They want to be treated like a State, but they aren’t one. I deal with the Leadership of many Countries, but I find Canada to be the worst.”
Ten minutes later, he invited Canadian companies “doing business with America” to relocate to the U.S.
The U.S. Department of State also waded into the hydronym conversation on X, sharing a screenshot from its website showing the U.S. consulate location in Toronto.
“It was brought to our attention that Lake America was erroneously labeled as Lake ‘Ontario’ on our website. We have corrected this mistake and apologize for deadnaming the lake.”

stories.content:
Google has officially renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America on its Maps interface — at least for people using the app or website in the U.S.

On Saturday, the tech giant announced it had changed the name of the body of water, through which the border with Canada runs, to reflect the most recent update from the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (Gnis).

That change was initiated by an executive order signed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week, instructing the department of the interior to make it so.

“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” Google wrote.

What app users will see depends on their country location, as determined by their device’s operating system, SIM, network and current location. Desktop and other web viewers are presented information based on individual regional search settings or, failing that, the device’s location as determined by Google.

That means people in the U.S. should see Trump’s new moniker, Canadians will keep seeing the historically accurate name and the rest of the world will see both names, presented as “Lake Ontario (Lake America).”

National Post contacted Google’s country manager for Canada, Sabrina Geramia, for comment but was directed back to its statement.

In testing other web and app-based mapping services from a Canadian address, Apple Maps users continue to see Lake Ontario. A search for “Lake America” yields America Lake in Brule County, South Dakota and, curiously, Lake Ontario.

They followed up by creating an interface that lets users enter their own names for the lake to generate a map image, or have MapQuest create one at random, such as “Lake Oh Canada,” “Lake Double-Double,” and “Lake Not Erie.”

Their example, a shot at Trump’s Gulf of America renaming, was “Lake Are We Doing This Again?”

Some of the user replies included names like “Lake of Hormuz,” “Lake Epstein Files,” and “Lake Tariff Tantrum.”

There are other locations around the world where two places have the same name on Google Maps for users from outside those countries.

For instance, the British see the Falkland Islands while Argentinians see the South American island chain as Islas Malvinas. Everyone else gets the English name first, the other in parentheses. The same style applies to the long-disputed Persian or Arabian Gulf separating Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Also on Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford dipped his toes back into the debate by posting a video of himself lakeside next to a new billboard at the Fifty Point Conservation Area in Grimsby that reads “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” in both official languages.

“Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them,” Ford said in the 39-second clip in which he also accused the U.S. head of state of making the change because Canada is “standing up” for itself in the trade war with the U.S.

Trump appeared to fire back later Saturday afternoon, posting an AI-generated video of himself kicking over a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign along a shoreline and replacing it with one reading “Welcome to America” over the iconic intro to the Peer Gynt suite adapted by Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg. The music then switches to the Village People’s Ymca as Trump performs his signature dance moves.

Earlier in the day, he’d posted another AI-generated video of a marching army of Canadian geese with hair similar to Trump’s and holding machine guns in muscled human arms. The video, set to the theme song for the television show Hawaii Five-O, ends with the birds firing their weapons as fireworks soar overhead and the words “Lake America” appear.

The president aired further grievances against Canada on Truth Social Sunday, using the automotive industry as his foil.

In a longer post later, he claimed to have “revived, and indeed saved” the American car industry by way of tariffs.

“One of the Worst Abusers is Canada. I don’t want Canadian cars, I don’t want Canadian parts, I don’t want Canadian anything. They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” he wrote.

“They want to be treated like a State, but they aren’t one. I deal with the Leadership of many Countries, but I find Canada to be the worst.”

Ten minutes later, he invited Canadian companies “doing business with America” to relocate to the U.S.

The U.S. Department of State also waded into the hydronym conversation on X, sharing a screenshot from its website showing the U.S. consulate location in Toronto.

“It was brought to our attention that Lake America was erroneously labeled as Lake ‘Ontario’ on our website. We have corrected this mistake and apologize for deadnaming the lake.”

stories.title: Dr. Brittany Graham named Grey-Bruce medical officer of health
stories.summary: Grey Bruce Public Health (Gbph) has announced That Dr. Brittany Graham has been appointed to the permanent position of Grey-Bruce’s Medical Officer of Health (MOH) and Chief Executive Officer of Gbph.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Grey Bruce Public Health (Gbph) has announced That Dr. Brittany Graham has been appointed to the permanent position of Grey-Bruce’s Medical Officer of Health (MOH) and Chief Executive Officer of Gbph. She has served as acting MOH since April 16, 2026.

The Board of Health for Gbph formally approved the appointment during its regular meeting on Aug. 28 “Dr. Graham has done an excellent job as Acting Medical Officer of Health, and we are thrilled to welcome her to the permanent position,” said Board of Health Chair Kenneth Craig.

The Board also announced that Dr. Eileen de Villa will serve as Acting Medical Officer of Health and CEO during Dr. Graham’s parental leave, which is set to begin on Sept. 8, 2026, and last until summer 2027. ““We are also fortunate that Dr. de Villa has agreed to serve as Acting Medical Officer of Health and CEO while Dr.

Graham is on parental leave. Dr. de Villa is a respected leader in public health who knows this organization and community well,” added Craig. “With a newly reconstituted Board and dedicated staff, the organization’s future is bright, and I look forward to contributing to its continued success when I return from leave,” Dr.

stories.title: Bodies of two missing swimmers found in Lambton County
stories.summary: OPP say the body of a missing swimmer has been recovered in Lambton County.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
OPP say the body of a missing swimmer has been recovered in Lambton County. The 66 year old from London was reported missing just before 3 p.m. Friday. They were last seen at the dock attached to an address on Canal Street in Grand Bend.

The Underwater Search and Recovery Unit with the Lambton Marine Unit located the body of the missing swimmer around 1:45 p.m. Saturday. No further details have been made available at this time. Additionally, OPP say a second, unrelated, missing swimmer in Lake Huron at the Pinery Provincial Park has been recovered.

Just before 3 p.m. Saturday, Lambton OPP received a report of another missing swimmer who was last seen at the Pinery Provincial Park beach. The OPP Marine Unit and Underwater Search and Recovery Unit recovered the body at approximately 8:20 p.m.

The deceased individual is a 36-year-old from Scarborough.

stories.title: With Canadians quietly lending a hand, a U.S. spy satellite-turned-telescope takes flight
stories.summary: Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could shed light on some of the deepest questions researchers have about dark energy and the universe
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Andrea Crespi was still a middle-school student in Italy when three American astronomers won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

Back then, the mystery of that acceleration – and the curious phenomenon called dark energy that powers it – seemed like an unsolvable problem.

Fast-forward 15 years and Mr. Crespi, now a graduate student at Ontario’s University of Waterloo, May be among those with the best shot yet at cracking the riddle of dark energy.

That exciting possibility moved a step closer to reality on Sunday morning with the successful launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Named after Nasa’s first chief astronomer, who helped usher in the era of astronomy in space, the telescope is now poised to explore some of the deepest questions that researchers have about the universe, with dark energy topping the list.

“It feels like an opportunity,” said Mr. Crespi about the launch. “Like we’re at the turning point of the story.”

Despite concerns that weather would postpone the early morning liftoff, conditions proved favourable enough for a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket to send the telescope roaring on its way at 7:26 a.m. ET.

The bus-sized observatory is now on a 100-day journey to L2, a point in space about 1.5 million kilometres away, where gravitational forces are balanced in a way that allows objects located there to easily maintain their position relative to Earth.

After a period of testing, the Roman telescope is expected to begin its epic survey of the universe in the coming months. Astronomers in the U.S. and around the world are anticipating a trove of data from the newly launched instrument and hoping for discoveries across a range of subfields.

“It’s going to be revolutionary,” said Jason Rowe, an astronomer at Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, who is part of the team that will be using the new telescope to probe the characteristics and distribution of alien solar systems around our galaxy.

Years in the making, the 10.5-tonne, US$4.3-billion satellite is Nasa’s third large-scale astronomical observatory in space – and the most unique in its purpose and history.

Nasa's new flagship astronomical observatory was launched into space from Florida on Sunday on a mission to probe some of the biggest mysteries in astrophysics and cosmology.

Whereas the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes were built to peer at tiny patches of sky to make their penetrating discoveries, Roman has a field of view that is roughly 100 times larger. Its forte is less about zeroing in on individual targets than it is looking at the universe in bulk – either by taking in the myriad of stars that make up the Milky Way, or by gazing out at the innumerable galaxies that lie beyond.

By seeing more, it will also have a better chance of spotting what is fleeting or rare, including supernovas and other short-lived phenomena.

“Our universe puts on spectacular cosmic displays every second, but they happen very quickly, so they often elude our telescopes,” said Julie McEnery, Nasa’s senior scientist on the project, during a press briefing on Saturday. “With Roman’s panoramic vision, we’ll not only catch these events, but we’ll see many at once.”

Fittingly for a telescope so well-suited for spying on the cosmos, the instrument’s primary mirror was originally meant to be used for spying on other countries.

Measuring 2.4 metres across, it is as large as the Hubble’s main mirror but has a much shorter focal length, which accounts for its more expansive view of the heavens.

When it was created more than two decades ago by a division of ITT Corporation, now part of L3Harris Technologies Inc., the mirror was to be used in a spy satellite. But when the satellite was cancelled in 2005, the exquisite mirror became a white elephant. In 2012, the National Reconnaissance Office, an agency of the U.S. military, officially gifted it to Nasa. (The gift originally included two mirrors, but Nasa was later asked to return the second.)

The surprise donation could not have come at a better time. Less than a year after the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery of dark energy, astronomers were now looking at the possibility of an instrument that could see enough of the universe to definitely measure dark energy’s effects.

The telescope that took shape around the mirror was tailor-made for that purpose. Its design ensured that it would be extremely stable, offering views of distant galaxies that would enable astronomers to perceive how mass is distributed in the universe based on how gravity distorts the light of objects in the background.

It was also geared to observing at infrared wavelengths, which are best for capturing the faint light of galaxies as the universe expands.

Other areas of interest to astronomers were also sure to benefit, including the search for exoplanets – planets around other stars.

And with the mirror already in hand, the project, then called the Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope, or Wfirst, had a big head start on its way to the launch pad.

The trip has not been a smooth one, however. Starting in 2019, U.S. President Donald Trump tried to axe the telescope on multiple occasions during his first administration. Congress ultimately rescued the project and did so again after another attempt by the White House to cancel it last year.

The outcome was not as happy for the Canadian Space Agency, which initially saw an opportunity to partner with Nasa and build a calibration system and other hardware for the telescope’s Wide Field Instrument. This is the device that is crucial for the telescope’s dark energy measurements. In exchange, Canadian astronomers would have had a dedicated share of the telescope’s time. (Similar arrangements have earned Canada time on both the Hubble and Webb space telescopes).

Ultimately, Ottawa balked at the $100-million price tag for a Canadian contribution to the telescope , and in 2018, withdrew from the project. The decision left Canadian astronomers out in the cold.

Yet Canada has maintained a presence on the Roman telescope, even if it is not an official one. A second instrument, called a coronagraph, which is designed to spot exoplanets orbiting distant stars, utilizes cameras built by Nüvü Camēras Inc. of Montreal. The equipment was assembled and prepared for space flight by Quebec-based tech company ABB Canada.

Nasa’s Pandora is on a mission to help answer the question: Is there other life out there?

Frédéric Grandmont, an astronomer by training who is technology and business manager for ABB, has been with the project from the start. He said it was thrilling to see the Canadian-made hardware in images of the telescope’s scientific package – and sobering to realize its significance to the coronagraph.

“If our component doesn’t work, nothing works,” he said.

The coronagraph is designed to suppress the light of stars in order to reveal planets that orbit around them. Its presence on the Roman telescope is primarily to test a technology that one day could be used to ferret out Earth-like worlds in a proposed future space telescope, called the Habitable Worlds Observatory

But the coronagraph is just one of the ways the telescope is expected to shed light on solar systems beyond our own.

Starting next year, astronomers will use the Wide Field Instrument to stare at a star-rich portion of our Milky Way, looking for planets and moons that May reveal their presence when they momentarily cross in front of and distort the light of background stars. At the same time, the telescope will identify planets that orbit around some of those stars in cases where a planet repeatedly blocks a portion of a star’s light.

With upward of 100 million stars in the telescope’s field of view, it is inevitable that the new data will provide an unprecedented look at the demographics of worlds across different regions of our Milky Way galaxy.

“How do planetary systems end up like our solar system?” said Dr. Rowe. “I think that will be a key question we’ll answer with Roman.”

In the longer term, Roman will gradually amass data on galaxies that will be used to trace the expansion of the universe over a large chunk of cosmic time.

It’s this measurement that researchers hope will ultimately pin down the degree to which dark energy is causing the expansion of space to accelerate. Once that number is quantified and confirmed by other independent measurements, including Europe’s Euclid Space Telescope and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, researchers hope they can identify the physical mechanism behind the acceleration.

“Putting them all together and getting that full picture across, basically, all of the history of the universe is going to be very exciting,” said Will Percival, a professor at Waterloo who is Canada’s lead researcher on the team that will be using the Roman telescope to clock the motion of distant galaxies as the universe expands.

Both Dr. Percival and Dr. Rowe are participating in Roman science through grants from the Canadian Space Agency that were awarded last year.

For Mr. Crespi, who is a part of Dr. Percival’s team, the successful departure of the telescope on Sunday signals the start of an adventure that could define his career.

“It was really great,” he said after watching the launch. “It’s amazing to be part of this moment that is going to shape the cosmology of tomorrow.”
paragraphs: Andrea Crespi was still a middle-school student in Italy when three American astronomers won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.
Back then, the mystery of that acceleration – and the curious phenomenon called dark energy that powers it – seemed like an unsolvable problem.
Fast-forward 15 years and Mr. Crespi, now a graduate student at Ontario’s University of Waterloo, May be among those with the best shot yet at cracking the riddle of dark energy.
That exciting possibility moved a step closer to reality on Sunday morning with the successful launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Named after Nasa’s first chief astronomer, who helped usher in the era of astronomy in space, the telescope is now poised to explore some of the deepest questions that researchers have about the universe, with dark energy topping the list.
“It feels like an opportunity,” said Mr. Crespi about the launch. “Like we’re at the turning point of the story.”
Despite concerns that weather would postpone the early morning liftoff, conditions proved favourable enough for a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket to send the telescope roaring on its way at 7:26 a.m. ET.

The bus-sized observatory is now on a 100-day journey to L2, a point in space about 1.5 million kilometres away, where gravitational forces are balanced in a way that allows objects located there to easily maintain their position relative to Earth.

After a period of testing, the Roman telescope is expected to begin its epic survey of the universe in the coming months. Astronomers in the U.S. and around the world are anticipating a trove of data from the newly launched instrument and hoping for discoveries across a range of subfields.

“It’s going to be revolutionary,” said Jason Rowe, an astronomer at Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, who is part of the team that will be using the new telescope to probe the characteristics and distribution of alien solar systems around our galaxy.
Years in the making, the 10.5-tonne, US$4.3-billion satellite is Nasa’s third large-scale astronomical observatory in space – and the most unique in its purpose and history.
Nasa's new flagship astronomical observatory was launched into space from Florida on Sunday on a mission to probe some of the biggest mysteries in astrophysics and cosmology.

Whereas the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes were built to peer at tiny patches of sky to make their penetrating discoveries, Roman has a field of view that is roughly 100 times larger. Its forte is less about zeroing in on individual targets than it is looking at the universe in bulk – either by taking in the myriad of stars that make up the Milky Way, or by gazing out at the innumerable galaxies that lie beyond.
By seeing more, it will also have a better chance of spotting what is fleeting or rare, including supernovas and other short-lived phenomena.

“Our universe puts on spectacular cosmic displays every second, but they happen very quickly, so they often elude our telescopes,” said Julie McEnery, Nasa’s senior scientist on the project, during a press briefing on Saturday. “With Roman’s panoramic vision, we’ll not only catch these events, but we’ll see many at once.”
Fittingly for a telescope so well-suited for spying on the cosmos, the instrument’s primary mirror was originally meant to be used for spying on other countries.
Measuring 2.4 metres across, it is as large as the Hubble’s main mirror but has a much shorter focal length, which accounts for its more expansive view of the heavens.

When it was created more than two decades ago by a division of ITT Corporation, now part of L3Harris Technologies Inc., the mirror was to be used in a spy satellite. But when the satellite was cancelled in 2005, the exquisite mirror became a white elephant. In 2012, the National Reconnaissance Office, an agency of the U.S. military, officially gifted it to Nasa. (The gift originally included two mirrors, but Nasa was later asked to return the second.)

The surprise donation could not have come at a better time. Less than a year after the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery of dark energy, astronomers were now looking at the possibility of an instrument that could see enough of the universe to definitely measure dark energy’s effects.

The telescope that took shape around the mirror was tailor-made for that purpose. Its design ensured that it would be extremely stable, offering views of distant galaxies that would enable astronomers to perceive how mass is distributed in the universe based on how gravity distorts the light of objects in the background.
It was also geared to observing at infrared wavelengths, which are best for capturing the faint light of galaxies as the universe expands.
Other areas of interest to astronomers were also sure to benefit, including the search for exoplanets – planets around other stars.
And with the mirror already in hand, the project, then called the Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope, or Wfirst, had a big head start on its way to the launch pad.

The trip has not been a smooth one, however. Starting in 2019, U.S. President Donald Trump tried to axe the telescope on multiple occasions during his first administration. Congress ultimately rescued the project and did so again after another attempt by the White House to cancel it last year.

The outcome was not as happy for the Canadian Space Agency, which initially saw an opportunity to partner with Nasa and build a calibration system and other hardware for the telescope’s Wide Field Instrument. This is the device that is crucial for the telescope’s dark energy measurements. In exchange, Canadian astronomers would have had a dedicated share of the telescope’s time. (Similar arrangements have earned Canada time on both the Hubble and Webb space telescopes).
Ultimately, Ottawa balked at the $100-million price tag for a Canadian contribution to the telescope , and in 2018, withdrew from the project. The decision left Canadian astronomers out in the cold.

Yet Canada has maintained a presence on the Roman telescope, even if it is not an official one. A second instrument, called a coronagraph, which is designed to spot exoplanets orbiting distant stars, utilizes cameras built by Nüvü Camēras Inc. of Montreal. The equipment was assembled and prepared for space flight by Quebec-based tech company ABB Canada.
Nasa’s Pandora is on a mission to help answer the question: Is there other life out there?

stories.title: What to know before reporting sexual violence to police
stories.summary: What to know before reporting sexual violence to police CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Q&A | CBC News | Posted: August 30, 2026 3:07 PM | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
Karen Simpson is telling people what they should consider before they report to police

Survivors of sexual assault are often encouraged to report their experience to police soon after it happens. But one London lawyer says people should understand their options before deciding whether — and when — to report.

"After an assault, the pressure to report immediately can come from everywhere, including the police and health-care professionals. But that urgency isn't always in your best interest," said Karen Simpson, a personal injury lawyer who specializes in helping people injured through sexual violence.
Simpson is creating a series of social media videos called Before You Report. She spoke to CBC's Matt Allen on London Morning earlier this week.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Matt Allen: Your advice seems counter to the usual narrative that someone should go to police right after a sexual assault. Why do you say that urgency isn't always in the survivor's best interest?

Karen Simpson: Reporting quickly doesn't equate to reporting effectively. There are a lot of cases before the courts currently where there are conflicting statements, or a survivor has gone and made their report immediately after the assault or close to when the assault occurred, and then over time they end up getting treatment or support. New details come to mind, they go to the police station and report again.
They have to go through that experience again. And then, at trial, there are two statements for the defence lawyers to use to put to the survivor and test their credibility and reliability.
Taking the stand in a sexual assault case is inherently traumatic. So, to then be questioned about why you have these two statements and the inconsistencies between them makes it even more difficult.
LISTEN | Karen Simpson interview with Matt Allen:
MA: From the outside looking in, one can underestimate what it's like to go to police to report. Why is waiting to report sometimes the best option?

KS: When survivors are ready to report, when they've arrived at that decision, they're more likely to give a concise statement that is accurate, without conflicting details or facts that the defence lawyers can use to raise reasonable doubt as to whether the assault occurred.
I also think, because of how difficult it can be to be in the criminal justice system and to be a witness in the Crown's case, it is important to have support around you.
That could be some of our community organizations, like Anova or the London Abused Women's Centre, or free, independent legal advice through the Barbra Schlifer Commemorative Clinic in Toronto.

MA: What do the women you work with tell you that they wish they'd known before going on this journey?

That's really the goal of this series that I've started on Instagram, Before You Report.
I think survivors regularly come to learn that the process is quite long. It's longer than they expected.

The criminal justice system is like tectonic plates. It can be a very slow process relative to the angst women are feeling as they're trying to manage leaving an abusive relationship or managing treatment as a result of being sexually assaulted.

I don't think it's up to the survivor to protect society. I think we have other stakeholders in the community. We sometimes have witnesses who can come forward.
I think that's a tall order, if a woman has been beaten, strangled, sexually assaulted, to then carry the burden for the rest of the community.

And there are a lot of examples where institutions for years have turned a blind eye and allowed perpetrators to continue to exist, whether it's school boards in Ontario or the Catholic Church, even after a report is made.
Survivors have come forward. They've tried to report, and nothing's been done.

KS: London has some excellent resources.

In my experience working with survivors, that team at the St. Joe's sexual assault clinic is superb. They're very detail-oriented in their records, they provide education and they come from a trauma-informed place.

Whether or not they report to police doesn't have to be determined in the moment or after that care. But that kit will be preserved in the event a woman does decide to come forward and make that report to police.

stories.title: Candidates talk affordability on Day 4 of Quebec's election campaign
stories.summary: Affordability and the economy took the spotlight on Sunday as Quebec's election campaign entered its fourth day, with party leaders unveiling their visions to ease financial pressures while grappling with the province's budgetary constraints.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Affordability and the economy took the spotlight on Sunday as Quebec’s election campaign entered its fourth day, with party leaders unveiling their visions to ease financial pressures while grappling with the province’s budgetary constraints.

The Quebec Liberal Party and Québec solidaire promised to make housing more affordable, while the Conservatives promised more tax cuts and the Coalition Avenir Québec released its full fiscal plan. Meanwhile, the Parti Québécois emphasized protecting the French language by proposing stricter immigration policies.

According to Quebec’s auditor general, the next government will face significant budgetary constraints. A pre-election report published earlier this month highlighted that Quebec’s multi-billion dollar deficit must be eliminated by 2029-2030 under the balanced-budget law, leaving little room for ambitious campaign promises.
The Coalition Avenir Québec called on the other parties Sunday to follow its lead and release their own fiscal blueprints.

According to party leader Christine Fréchette and Finance Minister Eric Girard, a third Coalition Avenir Québec government would spend an additional $9.7 billion over five years to fulfil its promises, including more support for victims of domestic violence.
Quebec would then need to generate $6 billion in revenue to reach a balanced budget, they said. Fréchette said she would not lower taxes until the budget is balanced.
Fréchette’s party is counting on “expected revenues” from the federal government, without any formal commitment from Ottawa.
“We’re focused on balancing the budget, and we’re also facing an economic and financial climate that’s leading us into rougher waters than usual,” she said.

Opponents to the right and left of Fréchette’s party accused her of falling into the “same old bureaucratic model” as her predecessor, François Legault, who stepped down as premier in January after the Coalition Avenir Québec tanked in the polls.
“She likes big government,” said Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime. “She wants to spend instead of leaving money in taxpayers’ pockets.”
Meanwhile, the parliamentary leader of the leftist party Québec solidaire, Ruba Ghazal, accused Fréchette of being “irresponsible” and implementing “austerity” measures.
Liberal leader Charles Milliard said that it’s too early in the campaign to release a fiscal plan.
Housing affordability was a focal point of Sunday’s campaign announcements, with the Liberals and Québec solidaire both unveiling plans to address rising costs.
Milliard focused on making life more affordable for seniors, proposing to cap rents and service fees in privately managed seniors’ homes.
“A senior citizen on public housing assistance should never have to leave their home because of an exorbitant rent increase,” he said.

Québec solidaire promised 50,000 new units of social housing and a rent cap for all tenants, saying rents should not outpace inflation. Ghazal said the average rent prices skyrocketed since the Coalition Avenir Québec first took power in 2018.
Both Milliard and Ghazal took jabs at Fréchette, who claimed on Saturday that the housing crisis has been “solved” in “many regions” of Quebec with increasing vacancy rates.
“Just because homes are empty doesn’t mean people can afford them,” Ghazal told reporters on Sunday.
Duhaime emphasized tackling the cost of living through tax reductions. On Sunday, Duhaime announced that a Conservative government would abolish the sales tax on used goods.
The Conservatives have also promised what they describe as “a historic reduction in the tax burden on individuals” and to reduce government spending by $47 billion.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon continued to focus on immigration, linking it to the decline of the French language in Quebec, which prompted renewed criticism from his rivals who accuse him of using immigrants as scapegoats.
St-Pierre Plamondon told journalists Quebec is facing a “linguistic emergency” and a “historic decline in the French language,” which he considers to be central to Quebecois identity.
He proposed expanding French-language laws to junior colleges, limiting access to English-language schools for francophones and immigrants.

The PQ leader also suggested requiring children of temporary migrants to attend French schools and tightening French-language requirements for work permits, with exceptions for the agricultural sector. Additionally, the PQ would prioritize immigrants proficient in French.

“The CAQ has undermined control over our immigration system,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “We will significantly lower immigration quotas, which ... is also essential if we are to tackle the historic decline in the use of French in Quebec.”

Immigration has been a central theme of the PQ’s campaign so far, with St-Pierre Plamondon arguing that current immigration levels exceed Quebec’s capacity to provide adequate housing and public services.
Quebec election Day 3 brings promises on immigration, transit, taxes and home care. (Aug. 29, 2026)
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 30, 2026.

According to party leader Christine Fréchette and Finance Minister Eric Girard, a third Coalition Avenir Québec government would spend an additional $9.7 billion over five years to fulfil its promises, including more support for victims of domestic violence.

Quebec would then need to generate $6 billion in revenue to reach a balanced budget, they said. Fréchette said she would not lower taxes until the budget is balanced.

Fréchette’s party is counting on “expected revenues” from the federal government, without any formal commitment from Ottawa.

“We’re focused on balancing the budget, and we’re also facing an economic and financial climate that’s leading us into rougher waters than usual,” she said.

Opponents to the right and left of Fréchette’s party accused her of falling into the “same old bureaucratic model” as her predecessor, François Legault, who stepped down as premier in January after the Coalition Avenir Québec tanked in the polls.

“She likes big government,” said Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime. “She wants to spend instead of leaving money in taxpayers’ pockets.”

Meanwhile, the parliamentary leader of the leftist party Québec solidaire, Ruba Ghazal, accused Fréchette of being “irresponsible” and implementing “austerity” measures.

Liberal leader Charles Milliard said that it’s too early in the campaign to release a fiscal plan.

Housing affordability was a focal point of Sunday’s campaign announcements, with the Liberals and Québec solidaire both unveiling plans to address rising costs.

Milliard focused on making life more affordable for seniors, proposing to cap rents and service fees in privately managed seniors’ homes.

“A senior citizen on public housing assistance should never have to leave their home because of an exorbitant rent increase,” he said.

Québec solidaire promised 50,000 new units of social housing and a rent cap for all tenants, saying rents should not outpace inflation. Ghazal said the average rent prices skyrocketed since the Coalition Avenir Québec first took power in 2018.

Both Milliard and Ghazal took jabs at Fréchette, who claimed on Saturday that the housing crisis has been “solved” in “many regions” of Quebec with increasing vacancy rates.

“Just because homes are empty doesn’t mean people can afford them,” Ghazal told reporters on Sunday.

Duhaime emphasized tackling the cost of living through tax reductions. On Sunday, Duhaime announced that a Conservative government would abolish the sales tax on used goods.

The Conservatives have also promised what they describe as “a historic reduction in the tax burden on individuals” and to reduce government spending by $47 billion.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon continued to focus on immigration, linking it to the decline of the French language in Quebec, which prompted renewed criticism from his rivals who accuse him of using immigrants as scapegoats.

St-Pierre Plamondon told journalists Quebec is facing a “linguistic emergency” and a “historic decline in the French language,” which he considers to be central to Quebecois identity.

He proposed expanding French-language laws to junior colleges, limiting access to English-language schools for francophones and immigrants.

The PQ leader also suggested requiring children of temporary migrants to attend French schools and tightening French-language requirements for work permits, with exceptions for the agricultural sector. Additionally, the PQ would prioritize immigrants proficient in French.

“The CAQ has undermined control over our immigration system,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “We will significantly lower immigration quotas, which ... is also essential if we are to tackle the historic decline in the use of French in Quebec.”

Immigration has been a central theme of the PQ’s campaign so far, with St-Pierre Plamondon arguing that current immigration levels exceed Quebec’s capacity to provide adequate housing and public services.

stories.title: Some Ontario websites showing Lake America after Google Maps update
stories.summary: Google Maps has updated to display "Lake America" when people in the United States search for the term.
stories.author: News Staff
paragraphs: Google Maps has updated to display “Lake America” for users located in the United States, after President Donald Trump signed an executive order this week to rename the Great Lake.
Users in Canada will still see it displayed as Lake Ontario on Google Maps, though the search engine will pull up Lake America as a result if users enter that name in their query.

However, several Canadian websites and apps, including Hydro One, Lcbo and GO Transit, are also displaying “Lake America” in their map images. This is likely due to the fact they employ third-party mapping tools that are based out of the United States.

“We are aware that Lake Ontario is being incorrectly labeled on our outage map,” Hydro One said in an online post on Sunday. “The issue originates from a third-party mapping service. We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference. We regret the error and apologize for any confusion it has caused.”

Stephen Crawford, the Ford government’s Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, acknowledged the issue by saying some government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps.
“Following recent changes by Google, we’re actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario,” he said in an online statement .
The issue appeared to be fixed as of 10 p.m. Sunday.

The search giant said in an Aug. 29 post on its corporate website it made the change because the U.S. government’s geographic names database has formally renamed the lake and that users outside Canada and the U.S. will see both names..
“It’s official! Lake America on Google Maps,” White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on the social media website X on Sunday.
Appearing on Abc’s “This Week” program on Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the name change won’t stick, despite Trump signing the executive order on Thursday.
“It was like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live’ when (Trump) signed a document saying change it to Lake America,” Ford said.
“No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”
On Saturday, Ford unveiled a large sign in Winona, a small lakeside community part of Hamilton, Ont., which says, “Lake Ontario, now and always.”

Also on Saturday, Trump posted a video rendered by artificial intelligence where he replaces a Lake Ontario sign with another that reads “Welcome to Lake America,” then dances to the Ycma song by the Village People.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s bid to rename the lake in a social media post on Thursday. Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”
Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said after Trump signed his order that New York won’t call it that.
Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade talks fell apart on Aug. 21.
Both countries have accused each other of implementing last-minute changes to a proposed interim trade deal.
On Tuesday, the federal government unveiled upward of $27 billion in retaliatory measures, set to kick in on Sept. 8, responding to new U.S. tariffs.
Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario’s premier.
Ford had called the president a bully and a loser on Aug. 24, while Trump said the premier was a “less charismatic” and less intelligent version of his late brother Rob Ford.

The premier said during his ABC appearance on Sunday that things “got heated” between Trump and himself, but “you’ve eventually got to stand up to someone who just continuously attacks our country and insults our country.”

“It’s unfortunate that he stoops down to that level and unfortunately I did that day,” Ford said, adding he wants to see both sides return their focus to advancing a mutually beneficial free-trade deal.
Trump signed a similar executive order last year to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
The orders only apply to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services and American news agencies have since called it the Gulf of America.
— With files from Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington
