stories.title: As Donald Trump targets Lake Ontario, Canadian communities rethink places with his name
stories.summary: An Ottawa councillor wants Trump Avenue renamed, while a petition is calling for Sudbury’s Trump Lake to become Lake Canada
stories.author: Adshayah Sathiaseelan; Jake Ross
paragraphs: Amid U.S. President Donald Trump ‘s move last week to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” some Canadian communities are reconsidering whether they want their own streets and bodies of water to bear the name of the man behind the decision.

Ottawa Coun. Riley Brockington recently raised concerns about Trump Avenue, a residential street in Canada’s capital, at a council meeting the day before Trump signed the executive order to rename Lake Ontario.

“I’m embarrassed that there is a street in River Ward called Trump Avenue and I’m embarrassed that in the nation’s capital, we have Donald Trump honoured in this respect,” Brockington said in Wednesday’s council meeting . “I say honoured because it is an honour to have your name attached to a street sign.”

Brockington said the Central Park neighbourhood in his ward, built about 25 years ago, has a New York theme, with several streets referencing the Big Apple, like Staten Way or Gramercy Park. At the time, Trump was a landlord and real estate developer in New York City.

Trump’s name “would fail miserably” if it was vetted through the city’s current commemorative naming process, Brockington added. The councillor’s comments came during a motion the Ottawa mayor brought forward about responding to the U.S. tariffs.
Brockington said he will lead a community-led process early in the new term of council to rename the street with input from Trump Avenue residents.
“We are past the point of debating whether or not the street name should remain Trump Avenue. It should not,” Brockington said.

Ottawa requires a 75 per cent plus one approval from the residents and property owners on the affected street for a commemorative renaming, according to John Buck, the city’s chief building official. Once the application process has started, the name change is flagged to a standing committee for consideration and then to council for final approval.
Trump Avenue is not the only Canadian street bearing the name; there is also Trump Place, a cul-de-sac in Red Deer, Alta.
The former Trump International Hotel and Tower at 325 Bay St. became a site of protests during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and after he was elected.
In 2017, the Star reported JCF Capital ULC, the building’s new owner, reached a buyout deal with Trump Hotels to remove the Trump name. The hotel was later renamed St. Regis Toronto.

The Canadian Geographical Names Database, a repository of place names in Canada, returns eight entries for the search “Trump.” The database is maintained by Natural Resources Canada using information submitted by federal, provincial and territorial naming authorities.
Four of those eight entries are in Ontario: three lakes and one creek. Trump Lake and Trump Creek are located in Sudbury while East Trump Lake and West Trump Lake can be found in Cochrane.

The naming decisions for the Sudbury bodies of water date back to Oct. 7, 1954, when Trump would have been eight years old, while the decision dates for the lakes in Cochrane appear as Dec. 31, 1973 in the database.
In a statement, the mayor of Cochrane, Peter Politis, said that naming falls under the purview of the Cochrane District, a provincial subdivision, and not the town of Cochrane itself.
He added, “On a tongue-in-cheek note, we’ve toyed with the idea of renaming our local landfill dump “Trump.”

A petition launched on Aug. 27 is now calling on the province to rename Trump Lake in Sudbury “Lake Canada” to “make Trump Lake Canadian again.” At the time of publication, the petition had collected just under 200 signatures.

The remaining four Trump entries are in Newfoundland’s Notre Dame Bay. North Trump Island and South Trump Island sit about two kilometres apart, and are collectively known as Trump Islands . A nearby settlement is also called Trump Islands . The decision date for all four entries is Jan. 14, 1954 in the database.

The renewed scrutiny comes after Trump signed an executive order Thursday directing the U.S. government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America. The move came as tensions escalated in the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war following the collapse of trade talks between the two countries.

Trump then imposed 50 per cent tariffs on select Canadian goods, to which Canada responded by announcing it would double tariffs on American steel and aluminum as part of a $27.6-billion retaliation. Ottawa has said the measures, set to kick in Sept. 8, are intended to match the new U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney has dismissed Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario, saying Canada will not recognize the change.
Other politicians on both sides of the border have also said they will continue using the lake’s long-standing name.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford likewise posted : “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.” On Saturday, Ford unveiled a large blue billboard erected at Fifty Point Conservation Area near Stoney Creek that read, in white letters, “Lake Ontario Now and Always.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage. (Aug. 29, 2026)

On Saturday, Google announced U.S. users of its maps service would see the name Lake America displayed, while Canadian users would continue seeing Lake Ontario. Users outside the two countries would see both names. The company said the update will “reflect name changes in official government sources.”
In Canada, geographical names are overseen by the Geographical Names Board of Canada, which was established in 1897 and has approved more than 350,000 names over its history.

Lake Ontario is not the first border-straddling body of water that Trump has attempted to rename. One of his first moves after returning to office in January 2025 was signing an executive order directing the U.S. government to use “Gulf of America” instead of the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf of Mexico has carried its name for more than 400 years.
Both of Trump’s executive orders related to renaming only hold water in the United States.
With files from Anastasia Blosser

stories.title: A look at two of Manitoba’s oldest family farms, still in the same hands after 150 years
stories.summary: A drive through rural Manitoba passes farm after farm—grain bins catching the light, cattle scattered across pasture, and the occasional yard with old machinery rusting away. Most have changed hands at some point—sold, bought out by a neighbour, or left behind when nobody in the family wanted to take it over.
stories.author: Milan Lukes
stories.content: A drive through rural Manitoba passes farm after farm — grain bins catching the light, cattle scattered across pasture, and the occasional yard with old machinery rusting away. Most have changed hands at some point — sold, bought out by a neighbour, or left behind when nobody in the family wanted to take it over. However, a handful of Manitoba families have held on. Eight Manitoba farms have been recognized by the province for staying in the same family for 150 consecutive years or more, according to a provincial spokesperson. CTV News spoke with two of those families about their farms’ history and looked at why keeping land in the family May be getting harder to do. Matheson Family Farm One of them is the Matheson family farm, south of Stonewall, which has remained in the same family since it was established in 1873. “(It) is quite amazing, really,” said Tricia Harris, who owns and lives on the farm with her husband Rod. “That it has managed to stay in the family that long, because, as you can tell from the data, it doesn’t happen a lot.” Tricia, 73, is the fourth generation to hold the land since her great-grandfather, Alexander Matheson, broke ground on it three years after Manitoba became a province — not long after surveyors first mapped out what is now the Rural Municipality of Rockwood. To understand how the farm came to be, Tricia said you have to go back decades, to the era of the Selkirk Settlement. Also known as the Red River Colony, it was the first European agricultural settlement in Western Canada, with its first group of settlers arriving in 1812. The colony spanned a vast tract of land, roughly 300,000 square kilometres — granted to Lord Selkirk, a Scottish nobleman, by the Hudson’s Bay Company — centred along the Red and Assiniboine rivers near present-day Winnipeg. Among those who followed in 1814-15 was Alexander’s father, John “Bushy” Matheson, who arrived as a six-month-old baby with his parents. “They came and settled along the Red River and farmed there for a number of years,” Tricia said. She said John “Bushy” grew up in the Red River Settlement and learned multiple languages, including Indigenous languages, Gaelic and French. That multilingualism helped him become a constable there, breaking up disputes and serving warrants. Tricia said travelling for his job eventually led him to learn of the “good land” in the present-day Stonewall region. In 1873, he moved there with one of his sons, Alexander — then a single man in his 20s — and the two took up adjoining quarter-sections. Family legend has it that John “Bushy” stumbled onto more than just good land. “The story is that his dad, John “Bushy,” was just kind of touring around the area on his horse and came across another family that had moved in… and he noticed they had some daughters, so he came home and told [Alexander], ‘I think I met your wife today,’” she said. “And so, he told his son he better go over there and help them build their house. And he married one of the daughters,” Tricia said. Though how accurate that family tale is, she doesn’t entirely know. That first year, only 10 acres of Alexander’s section were cleared, and a 1.5-storey log cabin went up. In 1875, Alexander married Catharine — a marriage that would last 65 years and result in five children. From there, Tricia said the farm passed to Alexander’s youngest son, Willis, in 1917. Electricity reached the property in 1948, and in 1954 the farm passed again, this time to Willis’ niece, Linda, and her husband, Gordon Furness. This was the same year the first tractor arrived. Running water followed later that decade. Tricia, the daughter of Linda and Gordon, took over ownership with her husband in 1983. She has lived on the farm since she was nine months old, aside from a few years away. Over the generations, the family has raised cattle and grain crops, along with chickens and pigs at various points. None of the farm’s original buildings remain, Tricia said. However, a stone house built in 1904 by a Scottish stonemason with help from Alexander and his three sons still stands, and it’s where the couple lives today. “It was built from the stone, the granite stone on the fields as they cleared land and pulled up these great big boulders. They stockpiled them until they had enough to build a two-storey stone house,” she said. “The house was a major accomplishment.” But the farm’s history hasn’t been without hardship. In 1875, Tricia said detailed farm records kept by Alexander over his 44 years of farming show grasshoppers “completely destroyed” the crop. She also said the adjoining quarter-section was lost after Willis Matheson couldn’t cover the land’s taxes while paying for his wife’s cancer treatment during the Great Depression. “So, the farm was reduced in half,” she said. And in 1965, Tricia said the stone house was “completely gutted” by fire, prompting her parents to rebuild the interior. Despite the setbacks, the farm has endured, and in 2023, Tricia said about 70 relatives gathered there to celebrate 150 years of it being worked by one family. Among those in attendance was her mother Linda, then 104, who was able to make it to the special occasion. “It was a great cousins’ reunion at that time,” Tricia said. The couple, who also worked full time off the farm as teachers, completely retired from farming last year when they sold the last of their cattle. As for how the farm has stayed in the family so long, Tricia said no one before her ever insisted that the next generation take it over and it’s not a pressure she and Rod are putting on their own four children, all of whom live in Winnipeg. Still, the land continues to be farmed by a Matheson descendant — one of Tricia’s cousin’s sons, 41, who is the fifth generation to work it. The couple also looks after his cattle on the farm during the summer months. “He lives just down the road on his own farm,” Tricia said, “which happens to be another Matheson homestead as well.” Munro Family Farm Another farm the province recognizes as having stayed in the same family for over 150 years is the Munro family farm, which was established even earlier in 1872. The quarter-section is located just west of Portage la Prairie. Clarke Munro, 71, and his sister Carol Kruck, 68, are the great-great-grandchildren of Rupert and Allison Munro, the couple who homesteaded the land. Both Clarke and Carol grew up on that farm. According to Carol, Rupert and Allison were born in Scotland before immigrating and marrying in Clinton, Ont., about 175 kilometres west of Toronto. The couple went on to raise nine children and came to Manitoba in 1870. Between the family, Clarke said they homesteaded over 1,100 acres at the time in the area. He said he never heard exactly why the family chose to head west. “I’m just guessing maybe it was the allure of new land,” Clarke said. The family’s history carries its share of loss, too. Carol recalled that her grandfather was one of three children and the only member of his immediate family to survive tuberculosis, after his parents and siblings all died of the disease. Clarke said his father, Allan, bought the quarter-section in 1944 from the widow of his great-uncle — one of Rupert and Allison’s sons — shortly after his great-uncle’s death. Allan then moved there from the neighbouring quarter-section, where he’d been living with his own parents, Rupert Allan and Catherine. The land is now registered in Clarke’s name, alongside his wife Noreen, though he says he moved off the property in his early 20s when he got married. He said his 45-year-old son moved onto the farm over two decades ago, where he farms and lives with his wife and two kids. “If my grandsons farm, I guess they’ll be the seventh generation,” Clarke said. “I really think they will be the seventh generation,” added Carol, who lives on an adjacent quarter-section which has also long been in the family. Clarke said none of the original structures from the 1870s remain on the property, though the farm’s log house, which he was told was original, was still standing when he was a child. He said it was removed several decades ago. Livestock has been part of the farm’s operation for most of its history. Clarke said the farm has generally kept horses and cattle, aside from a 20 to 30-year stretch without them, and that his grandsons — active in 4-H — even have a few cows and calves of their own. The farm has also raised chickens and ducks over the years. The family was planning a 150th anniversary celebration in 2022, but Clarke said a shed fire shortly before derailed those plans. The family is now aiming for the next milestone instead. “We’re going to try to do something for the 155th. That’s the plan right now,” Clarke said. As for why the farm has stayed in the family for so long, Carol credited their father Allan with handling the succession. “My dad was a very, very fair person, and Clarke farmed with him as a teenager, and I was a non-farming sibling, but he was gracious,” said Carol, a retired accountant. “I feel he was very ahead of his time. Farm succession is a very problematic thing today, but dad made it so easy. He was very fair. It’s not even, but it’s fair, because Clarke is the farmer in the family.” The siblings also emphasized that they have no intention to pressure the next generation to keep working the quarter section or carry on the farming tradition. “I think it would be great, but I’m not putting pressure on them. It’s whatever they want to do,” Clarke said. “I don’t think they need any pressure,” Carol said. “They want it.” When asked what it feels like to know their family runs one of the province’s oldest family farms, both siblings landed on the same word: proud. “I’m so proud of my brother and his children, and my dad, and everyone that has done this. It’s great,” Carol said. CTV News also reached out to several other family farms recognized by the province that were established in the early 1870s for their story but did not hear back by the deadline. The Manitoba Family Farm Recognition Program, run by the province’s agricultural department, recognizes family farms that have remained in continuous ownership by direct descendants of the original owner for 100, 125 or 150 consecutive years. As of mid-July, a provincial spokesperson said 1,923 farms have received recognition under the program’s centennial milestone, and 165 have been recognized for reaching 125 years. Those are all-time figures, the spokesperson added, meaning some of the farms could have since been sold out of the family. The changing economics of keeping a farm in the family While families like the Mathesons and Munros have kept their land for generations, one industry advocate says the path to passing down a farm today looks different than it once did. Colin Hornby, general manager of Keystone Agricultural Producers, said it’s difficult to say definitively whether multi-generational farms are becoming rarer in Manitoba, but he’s noticed a shift towards consolidation. “What we’re seeing is perhaps what used to be a few family farms within the same family have now become one larger operation,” Hornby said. He added that consolidation lets families split costs and take advantage of economies of scale, such as sharing equipment or buying inputs in bulk for better prices. Hornby said the total number of farms in Manitoba has substantially diminished over the years, even as the average farm size has grown. According to Statistics Canada, Manitoba counted just over 29,400 farms in 1981. By the 2021 census, four decades later, that number had more than halved to roughly 14,500. Meanwhile, over that same period, Statistics Canada says the average farm size in the province grew from 639 acres to 1,177 acres—an increase of more than 84 per cent. Despite the trend towards consolidation, Hornby said Manitoba still has one of the higher rates of young farmers in Canada. He said many young people leave the farm temporarily, for school or work, before eventually returning. The bigger obstacle, he said, is affordability. “I think one of the challenges…with young producers is the cost of land and being able to afford taking over the farm,” Hornby said. “That’s one of those big pressures where they May want to do it, but it’s not financially feasible for them.” Manitoba has the highest proportion of farm operators under the age of 35 of any province at 11.5 per cent, according to data from the 2021 census. Hornby said rising costs extend well beyond land prices — equipment, inputs, and expenses across the board have all gone up, while the prices farmers get for their crops don’t always keep pace. “And the other component is global trade uncertainty and market uncertainty,” Hornby said, citing the impact of tensions around the Strait of Hormuz on fertilizer prices. “We saw fertilizer prices spiked up significantly, but crop prices did not follow. So, there was that squeeze on prices.” Hornby also flagged succession planning as an area where families “in many instances wait too long to get started on” and encouraged farmers to consult accountants or succession planning professionals to take advantage of available tax strategies. “Making sure that we’re ensuring that continuity in farm operations is super important.” Manitoba’s oldest family farm on record Just how far back does that continuity go? Provincial data shows only two farms recognized under the program were established earlier than 1872, when the Munro family farm was founded. According to the province, the oldest family farm on record under the Manitoba Family Farm Recognition Program was established in 1870 — the only recognized farm dating back to that year. It last requested recognition under the program in 2024. Families can apply for recognition at any time after reaching the 100, 125, or 150-year milestone, a spokesperson said, provided the farm meets the eligibility requirements and has supporting documents to prove ownership. Where that farm is located, and the family’s story behind it, is hard to say. The family chose not to give permission to share their information on the application form, the provincial spokesperson said. That’s also the case for the farm established in 1871, the second-oldest on record. As for whether an even older family farm is still out there, being worked by the same family, it’s possible. The spokesperson notes that participation in the recognition program is voluntary.

She also said the adjoining quarter-section was lost after Willis Matheson couldn’t cover the land’s taxes while paying for his wife’s cancer treatment during the Great Depression. “So, the farm was reduced in half,” she said. And in 1965, Tricia said the stone house was “completely gutted” by fire, prompting her parents to rebuild the interior. Despite the setbacks, the farm has endured, and in 2023, Tricia said about 70 relatives gathered there to celebrate 150 years of it being worked by one family. Among those in attendance was her mother Linda, then 104, who was able to make it to the special occasion. “It was a great cousins’ reunion at that time,” Tricia said. The couple, who also worked full time off the farm as teachers, completely retired from farming last year when they sold the last of their cattle. As for how the farm has stayed in the family so long, Tricia said no one before her ever insisted that the next generation take it over and it’s not a pressure she and Rod are putting on their own four children, all of whom live in Winnipeg. Still, the land continues to be farmed by a Matheson descendant — one of Tricia’s cousin’s sons, 41, who is the fifth generation to work it. The couple also looks after his cattle on the farm during the summer months. “He lives just down the road on his own farm,” Tricia said, “which happens to be another Matheson homestead as well.” Munro Family Farm Another farm the province recognizes as having stayed in the same family for over 150 years is the Munro family farm, which was established even earlier in 1872. The quarter-section is located just west of Portage la Prairie. Clarke Munro, 71, and his sister Carol Kruck, 68, are the great-great-grandchildren of Rupert and Allison Munro, the couple who homesteaded the land. Both Clarke and Carol grew up on that farm. According to Carol, Rupert and Allison were born in Scotland before immigrating and marrying in Clinton, Ont., about 175 kilometres west of Toronto. The couple went on to raise nine children and came to Manitoba in 1870. Between the family, Clarke said they homesteaded over 1,100 acres at the time in the area. He said he never heard exactly why the family chose to head west. “I’m just guessing maybe it was the allure of new land,” Clarke said. The family’s history carries its share of loss, too. Carol recalled that her grandfather was one of three children and the only member of his immediate family to survive tuberculosis, after his parents and siblings all died of the disease. Clarke said his father, Allan, bought the quarter-section in 1944 from the widow of his great-uncle — one of Rupert and Allison’s sons — shortly after his great-uncle’s death. Allan then moved there from the neighbouring quarter-section, where he’d been living with his own parents, Rupert Allan and Catherine. The land is now registered in Clarke’s name, alongside his wife Noreen, though he says he moved off the property in his early 20s when he got married. He said his 45-year-old son moved onto the farm over two decades ago, where he farms and lives with his wife and two kids. “If my grandsons farm, I guess they’ll be the seventh generation,” Clarke said. “I really think they will be the seventh generation,” added Carol, who lives on an adjacent quarter-section which has also long been in the family. Clarke said none of the original structures from the 1870s remain on the property, though the farm’s log house, which he was told was original, was still standing when he was a child. He said it was removed several decades ago. Livestock has been part of the farm’s operation for most of its history. Clarke said the farm has generally kept horses and cattle, aside from a 20 to 30-year stretch without them, and that his grandsons — active in 4-H — even have a few cows and calves of their own. The farm has also raised chickens and ducks over the years. The family was planning a 150th anniversary celebration in 2022, but Clarke said a shed fire shortly before derailed those plans. The family is now aiming for the next milestone instead. “We’re going to try to do something for the 155th. That’s the plan right now,” Clarke said. As for why the farm has stayed in the family for so long, Carol credited their father Allan with handling the succession. “My dad was a very, very fair person, and Clarke farmed with him as a teenager, and I was a non-farming sibling, but he was gracious,” said Carol, a retired accountant. “I feel he was very ahead of his time. Farm succession is a very problematic thing today, but dad made it so easy. He was very fair. It’s not even, but it’s fair, because Clarke is the farmer in the family.” The siblings also emphasized that they have no intention to pressure the next generation to keep working the quarter section or carry on the farming tradition. “I think it would be great, but I’m not putting pressure on them. It’s whatever they want to do,” Clarke said. “I don’t think they need any pressure,” Carol said. “They want it.” When asked what it feels like to know their family runs one of the province’s oldest family farms, both siblings landed on the same word: proud. “I’m so proud of my brother and his children, and my dad, and everyone that has done this. It’s great,” Carol said. CTV News also reached out to several other family farms recognized by the province that were established in the early 1870s for their story but did not hear back by the deadline. The Manitoba Family Farm Recognition Program, run by the province’s agricultural department, recognizes family farms that have remained in continuous ownership by direct descendants of the original owner for 100, 125 or 150 consecutive years. As of mid-July, a provincial spokesperson said 1,923 farms have received recognition under the program’s centennial milestone, and 165 have been recognized for reaching 125 years. Those are all-time figures, the spokesperson added, meaning some of the farms could have since been sold out of the family. The changing economics of keeping a farm in the family While families like the Mathesons and Munros have kept their land for generations, one industry advocate says the path to passing down a farm today looks different than it once did. Colin Hornby, general manager of Keystone Agricultural Producers, said it’s difficult to say definitively whether multi-generational farms are becoming rarer in Manitoba, but he’s noticed a shift towards consolidation. “What we’re seeing is perhaps what used to be a few family farms within the same family have now become one larger operation,” Hornby said. He added that consolidation lets families split costs and take advantage of economies of scale, such as sharing equipment or buying inputs in bulk for better prices. Hornby said the total number of farms in Manitoba has substantially diminished over the years, even as the average farm size has grown. According to Statistics Canada, Manitoba counted just over 29,400 farms in 1981. By the 2021 census, four decades later, that number had more than halved to roughly 14,500. Meanwhile, over that same period, Statistics Canada says the average farm size in the province grew from 639 acres to 1,177 acres—an increase of more than 84 per cent. Despite the trend towards consolidation, Hornby said Manitoba still has one of the higher rates of young farmers in Canada. He said many young people leave the farm temporarily, for school or work, before eventually returning. The bigger obstacle, he said, is affordability. “I think one of the challenges…with young producers is the cost of land and being able to afford taking over the farm,” Hornby said. “That’s one of those big pressures where they May want to do it, but it’s not financially feasible for them.” Manitoba has the highest proportion of farm operators under the age of 35 of any province at 11.5 per cent, according to data from the 2021 census. Hornby said rising costs extend well beyond land prices — equipment, inputs, and expenses across the board have all gone up, while the prices farmers get for their crops don’t always keep pace. “And the other component is global trade uncertainty and market uncertainty,” Hornby said, citing the impact of tensions around the Strait of Hormuz on fertilizer prices. “We saw fertilizer prices spiked up significantly, but crop prices did not follow. So, there was that squeeze on prices.” Hornby also flagged succession planning as an area where families “in many instances wait too long to get started on” and encouraged farmers to consult accountants or succession planning professionals to take advantage of available tax strategies. “Making sure that we’re ensuring that continuity in farm operations is super important.” Manitoba’s oldest family farm on record Just how far back does that continuity go? Provincial data shows only two farms recognized under the program were established earlier than 1872, when the Munro family farm was founded. According to the province, the oldest family farm on record under the Manitoba Family Farm Recognition Program was established in 1870 — the only recognized farm dating back to that year. It last requested recognition under the program in 2024. Families can apply for recognition at any time after reaching the 100, 125, or 150-year milestone, a spokesperson said, provided the farm meets the eligibility requirements and has supporting documents to prove ownership. Where that farm is located, and the family’s story behind it, is hard to say. The family chose not to give permission to share their information on the application form, the provincial spokesperson said. That’s also the case for the farm established in 1871, the second-oldest on record. As for whether an even older family farm is still out there, being worked by the same family, it’s possible. The spokesperson notes that participation in the recognition program is voluntary.

stories.title: Former Surrey RCMP officer sentenced to 18 months in jail for breach of trust
stories.summary: A former Surrey RCMP officer who pleaded guilty to breach of trust earlier this year has been sentenced, six years after the undercover operation that led to 13 charges against him.
stories.author: Ian Holliday
stories.content: A former Surrey RCMP officer who pleaded guilty to breach of trust earlier this year has been sentenced, six years after the undercover operation that led to 13 charges against him. Dawwd Alaaeldine Soukary was sentenced Thursday to 18 months in jail. B.C. Supreme Court Justice Murray B. Blok accepted a joint submission from Crown and defence lawyers recommending that sentence. The charge Soukary pleaded guilty to in April alleged that he had committed breach of trust by “accessing confidential police databases and files for a purpose inconsistent with his duties as a police officer” between Nov. 30, 2020 and his arrest on Jan. 27, 2021. Blok’s decision sheds additional light on the context of those breaches. 59 undercover scenarios According to the decision, the RCMP received a report “supported by Cctv footage” that Soukary was involved in purchasing a significant volume of drugs on behalf of two suspected criminals, referred to in the decision as MN and AH. The tip was received in August 2020, but investigators “did not gather any further evidence supporting this drug trafficking allegation, and no charges resulted,” Blok’s decision notes. At the time, Soukary was a probationary officer with the Surrey RCMP. The person who provided the tip said Soukary had indicated that once he was allowed to work without supervision, he planned to use police databases to obtain information for his criminal associates. “The RCMP formulated and then implemented a plan to recruit Mr. Soukary as an undercover operator for a fictitious undercover operation targeting a fictitious drug trafficker,” the decision reads. “He was paired with another undercover operator who pretended to be corrupt and associate with drug traffickers. The goal of this fictitious operation was to arrange a purchase of a kilogram of cocaine from a particular big-time (but also fictional) trafficker, but the real target of the operation was Mr. Soukary.” Beginning in October 2020 and continuing up until his arrest in January 2021, investigators staged “43 undercover scenarios consisting of interactions between Mr. Soukary and his fictitiously corrupt partner, and 16 additional scenarios involving the sham undercover drug investigation,” according to the decision. The sting culminated with a scenario in which Soukary was given $72,000 to purchase a one-kilogram cocaine brick from the fictional trafficker. The court decision indicates Soukary told his fake partner that the market value of such a brick was $55,000 to $60,000, and that he intended to negotiate a lower price with the trafficker and then pocket the proceeds. The fake partner encouraged this behaviour, and when Soukary paid just $63,000 for the drugs, he gave the fake partner $1,000 and kept the remaining $8,000 for himself, according to the decision. “Mr. Soukary was arrested shortly afterward, at which time $8,000 was found on his person,” the decision reads. “The $63,000 in purchase money was obviously recovered, as it never left RCMP hands, the $1,000 paid to the other undercover operator was also accounted for, and the cocaine (which was real) also never left RCMP control.” Investigators seized, searched and analyzed Soukary’s phone, finding that he had “repeatedly texted” photos of confidential information he obtained while working solo during the fake undercover investigation to MN and AH. “There is no evidence that the confidential information Mr. Soukary shared compromised any active RCMP investigations and no evidence that the shared information led to any other criminal conduct,” the decision reads, citing an agreed statement of facts in the case. ‘Substantial triable issues’ Blok’s decision describes Soukary as a 31-year-old son of Egyptian immigrants who was born and raised in Ottawa and grew up in “underprivileged circumstances.” After his arrest, he resigned from the RCMP and returned to Ottawa, working as a Realtor before “shifting to work at a soccer and athletic performance gym,” according to the decision. While it’s not mentioned in the court document, Soukary voluntarily terminated his registration with the Real Estate Council of Ontario after the regulator accused him with failing to notify it of criminal charges laid against him. Soukary entered an undertaking not to reapply for registration with the Reco before July 1 of this year. Blok’s decision summarizes arguments from both the Crown and defence in support of their joint submission. Prosecutors noted the seriousness of the offence and the repeated nature of Soukary’s decision to access and share confidential information. They also highlighted his guilty plea as a “significant sign of remorse,” his lack of a prior criminal record, and his relative youth: He was 25 years old at the time of the offence. Soukary’s defence lawyers highlighted the RCMP’s tactics in investigating him, noting that the undercover operation “aimed to create a climate that normalized police corruption and tempted him with opportunities to commit offences.” “The defence notes the significant benefits of Mr. Soukary’s guilty plea and joint submission on sentence,” the decision reads. “There were substantial triable issues and, in particular, a genuine issue as to the extent to which the police created the circumstances that led to the offences. The evidence would have required the court to carefully consider whether the police conduct crossed the line into entrapment.” Blok ultimately accepted the joint submission, finding that it was reasonable in the circumstances and would not bring the administration of justice into disrepute or be contrary to the public interest. The judge sentenced Soukary to 18 months in jail, ordered him to provide a DNA sample, and required him to pay a $200 victim surcharge. The other 12 charges against Soukary have been stayed by the Crown.

stories.title: Last evacuation order lifted for Ainslie Creek wildfire in B.C.
stories.summary: Regional district says an order has been downgraded to an evacuation alert for 58 addressed properties
paragraphs: The Thompson-Nicola Regional District in southern British Columbia has lifted the last of its evacuation orders related to the out-of-control Ainslie Creek wildfire.
The regional district says an order has been downgraded to an evacuation alert for 58 addressed properties in the Coldwater and Patchett Road areas.
Another 94 properties that had been under evacuation alert were declared all clear.
B.C. ends provincial state of emergency as wildfires continue to burn
An evacuation order issued by the Spuzzum First Nation remained in place as of Saturday afternoon related to the fire that was last measured at 677 square kilometres.
The regional district says in a statement that approximately 248 properties it covers remain on evacuation alert as of Saturday afternoon.
It says property owners are free to return but should use caution and be aware of any hazards in the area.

stories.title: GM plans Ontario pickup production in deal that would pump $1.1-billion into Canada’s auto sector
stories.summary: Tentative agreement with Unifor comes as Canadian automakers grapple with U.S. tariffs and uncertainty over future trade negotiations
stories.author: Allison Lampert
paragraphs: General Motors GM-N plans to assemble a heavy-duty pickup at an Ontario plant as part of a tentative deal with a key union that would pump $1.1-billion into Canada’s auto sector as it reels from U.S. tariffs, a union bargaining report said on Saturday.

The investment comes as Canada’s auto sector grapples with 25 per cent U.S. tariffs on vehicles, with U.S. President Donald Trump pledging to double them to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, 2027. The fate of Canadian auto plants has emerged as a central issue in stalled U.S.-Canada trade negotiations.

GM plans to spend $144-million to add the next-generation heavy-duty GMC Sierra truck to a plant in Oshawa, and pledged not to immediately sell or close a second assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ontario, according to the bargaining report from the union Unifor.
The deal is contingent on approval from workers who are voting on Saturday and Sunday. Both Unifor and GM’s Canadian division declined to comment during the vote.
The $1.1-billion investment includes a $691-million commitment to support production of new V8 engines in Ontario that was previously announced in April, the report said.
The tentative agreement was reached last Saturday between GM and Unifor on behalf of 4,600 union members in Canada’s most populous province, Ontario.

U.S. President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in recent days, has also said he will increase tariffs on all Canadian cars and trucks, automotive parts and steel to 50 per cent starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Autos are a key part of talks between the United States and its northern neighbour to reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian-produced vehicles. Negotiations ended last week over unresolved issues, such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories.
Canada has said it cannot accept a trade deal with the U.S. unless the agreement ensures the survival of a robust Canadian auto assembly and parts industry.

United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has said Canadian negotiators only raised demands to include medium-and heavy-duty trucks on Friday at 4 p.m. just ahead of a deadline for securing a deal .
The tentative deal with Unifor would invest $215-million to assemble a new generation transmission at a separate factory in St. Catharines, Ontario, starting in late 2029.

GM also committed to not close or sell its Cami assembly plant, formally known as Canadian Automotive Manufacturing Inc., in Ingersoll while it studies alternative production for the factory. The plant would have priority to do defence work for the Canadian Armed Forces, in the event the auto maker secures a contract for such output, the bargaining report said.
Editor’s note: This article has been updated to correct the spelling of St. Catharines, Ontario.

stories.content:
General Motors GM-N plans to assemble a heavy-duty pickup at an Ontario plant as part of a tentative deal with a key union that would pump $1.1-billion into Canada’s auto sector as it reels from U.S. tariffs, a union bargaining report said on Saturday.

The investment comes as Canada’s auto sector grapples with 25 per cent U.S. tariffs on vehicles, with U.S. President Donald Trump pledging to double them to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, 2027. The fate of Canadian auto plants has emerged as a central issue in stalled U.S.-Canada trade negotiations.

GM plans to spend $144-million to add the next-generation heavy-duty GMC Sierra truck to a plant in Oshawa, and pledged not to immediately sell or close a second assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ontario, according to the bargaining report from the union Unifor.

The deal is contingent on approval from workers who are voting on Saturday and Sunday. Both Unifor and GM’s Canadian division declined to comment during the vote.

The $1.1-billion investment includes a $691-million commitment to support production of new V8 engines in Ontario that was previously announced in April, the report said.

The tentative agreement was reached last Saturday between GM and Unifor on behalf of 4,600 union members in Canada’s most populous province, Ontario.

U.S. President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in recent days, has also said he will increase tariffs on all Canadian cars and trucks, automotive parts and steel to 50 per cent starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Autos are a key part of talks between the United States and its northern neighbour to reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian-produced vehicles. Negotiations ended last week over unresolved issues, such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories.

Canada has said it cannot accept a trade deal with the U.S. unless the agreement ensures the survival of a robust Canadian auto assembly and parts industry.

United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has said Canadian negotiators only raised demands to include medium-and heavy-duty trucks on Friday at 4 p.m. just ahead of a deadline for securing a deal .

The tentative deal with Unifor would invest $215-million to assemble a new generation transmission at a separate factory in St. Catharines, Ontario, starting in late 2029.

GM also committed to not close or sell its Cami assembly plant, formally known as Canadian Automotive Manufacturing Inc., in Ingersoll while it studies alternative production for the factory. The plant would have priority to do defence work for the Canadian Armed Forces, in the event the auto maker secures a contract for such output, the bargaining report said.

stories.title: Transit, home care and immigration dominate Day 3 of Quebec election
stories.summary: The debate over immigration came on the third day of the provincial election campaign, as Quebec’s party leaders fanned out across the province.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s plan to more than halve temporary immigration in Quebec drew criticism from his rivals Saturday, who accused him of making immigrants bear the blame for problems in public schools and of risking worsening the province’s labour shortage.

St-Pierre Plamondon said a PQ government would reduce the number of temporary immigrants in Quebec from more than 500,000 to between 200,000 and 250,000, arguing current levels have exceeded the province’s capacity to provide housing and public services.

The debate over immigration came on the third day of the provincial election campaign, as Quebec’s party leaders fanned out across the province with promises on public transit, home care, gasoline prices and the economy.

“We’re facing a total loss of control of our immigration system,” he said outside a Quebec City high school where modular classrooms are being used to accommodate students.

St-Pierre Plamondon blamed the governing Coalition Avenir Québec for the sharp rise in temporary immigration, targeting CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette over her previous tenure as immigration minister.

As it reduced temporary immigration, the sovereigntist PQ would protect sectors that rely heavily on temporary workers, including agriculture, manufacturing and health care, while taking regional needs into account, he said.

The party also reiterated its pledge to reduce permanent immigration to 35,000 people a year, down from the government’s current target of 45,000. Until its temporary immigration target is reached, it would select economic immigrants seeking permanent residence from among temporary immigrants already in Quebec rather than from abroad.

2:19 Cost of living promises and a surprising poll result on Day 2 of the Quebec election campaign

St-Pierre Plamondon rejected suggestions that he was blaming immigrants themselves for strains on public services.

“Never will the Parti Québécois blame people who become Quebecers,” he said. “We blame the CAQ and the federal government.”

Also campaigning in Quebec City, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal criticized St-Pierre Plamondon’s decision to make the announcement outside a school, accusing him of making immigrant children bear the blame for overcrowding and deteriorating school infrastructure.

“I find it appalling that Mr. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon continues to talk about immigration in such a negative way,” Ghazal said. “I was that immigrant child myself, a child of Bill 101.”

Bill 101, Quebec’s landmark French-language law, generally requires children of immigrants to attend French-language schools.

Ghazal blamed successive governments for years of underinvestment in public schools, adding: “We can’t make immigrant children bear the blame for that.”

In Shawinigan, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard also criticized the PQ proposal, arguing it would worsen Quebec’s labour shortage as businesses grapple with the U.S. trade war.

“It’s the worst time to tell the business community and entrepreneurs that we’re going to have even less labour,” Milliard said.

2:30 39-day Quebec election campaign underway with all to play for

Earlier Saturday in Drummondville, CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette appealed to sovereigntist voters who are reluctant to hold a referendum in the coming years to back her party rather than the PQ.

“Many people who would be tempted to vote Yes (…) are aware that this is the worst time in the last 50 years to hold a referendum,” she said, pointing to the trade war with the United States.

Fréchette also promised an additional $1 billion over four years for homecare services.

Elsewhere, Ghazal pledged $23 billion over 10 years to repair and expand public transit infrastructure.

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime promised to pull Quebec out of its cap-and-trade carbon market and suspend the province’s 19.2-cent-per-litre fuel tax for five months, measures he said would lower gasoline prices by about 33 cents a litre.

Milliard also promised to reduce red tape for small and medium-sized businesses.

stories.title: One Canadian found safe after catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods, Anand says
stories.summary: At least 31 other Canadians remain unaccounted for as rescuers search flood-ravaged areas along the Nepal-Tibet border
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
paragraphs: The brother of a Canadian man among those missing after flash floods swept through an area along the Nepal-Tibet border says their family is on edge waiting for information.

Dhaval Shah and his wife Megha Shah, from Port Moody, B.C., were on a spiritual journey in Nepal when the floods hit. Dhaval’s brother Kheval Shah, reached at his home in Mumbai, India, said his family is desperate to know if they’ve been rescued or found.
“Everybody is on edge to get some news, if they’re rescued or found or something. Something which will make the family understand what happened to them,” Kheval Shah said in an interview Saturday.
“We’re hoping that they find them and some miracles happen and we see them again,” he added.

After Nepali authorities updated their figures Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 669 with 2,426 people missing.
Families comb through lists of missing people in Nepal as steep mountains hamper rescue efforts
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely.
“This brings the total number of Canadians whose whereabouts haven’t been confirmed to 31. This number May still fluctuate as new information comes in,” Anand said in a statement.
No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday had been rescued.
Nepalese community organizations across the country cancelled annual cultural festivals this weekend following the devastating floods.

This weekend would normally be the annual Teej festival, a Hindu practice celebrating womanhood, but organizers in cities including Toronto, Brampton and Calgary cancelled celebrations in light of the disaster.

Punam Dhungel, president of the Nepali Canadian Women’s Society of B.C., saID her organization canceled their event for the first time, but decided to redirect $15,000 in ticket sales to humanitarian relief efforts.
Rescuers have pulled survivors caked in dark mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety after catastrophic floods on the Nepal-China border.
The Associated Press

Many of the missing were believed to have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others. Hundreds of others have been displaced across the Himalayan region.
Religious pilgrims from Canada at building swept away in Tibet-Nepal border floods

Shah said he last heard from his brother on Monday, and a cousin of theirs heard from the couple on Tuesday. He believes his brother and sister-in-law were waiting for immigration offices to open in order to leave Nepal at the Tibet border when the flash floods hit.
He said the Canadian government should press Nepal for answers and more information about missing Canadians.
“I know they’re doing something, but I feel that they must really push... to find where they are and to get some information,” Shah said.
Canada has said it will send $5-million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal as of Saturday.
With reports from the Associated Press and The Canadian Press

stories.title: One Canadian found in Nepal as families of those still missing after floods wait for information
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: The brother of a Canadian man among those missing after flash floods swept through an area along the Nepal-Tibet border says their family is on edge waiting for information. Dhaval Shah and his wife Megha Shah, from Port Moody, B.C., were on a spiritual journey in Nepal when the floods hit. Dhaval’s brother Kheval Shah, reached at his home in Mumbai, India, said his family is desperate to know if they’ve been rescued or found. “Everybody is on edge to get some news, if they’re rescued or found or something. Something which will make the family understand what happened to them,” Kheval Shah said in an interview Saturday. “We’re hoping that they find them and some miracles happen and we see them again,” he added. After Nepali authorities updated their figures Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 669 with 2,426 people missing. Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely. “This brings the total number of Canadians whose whereabouts haven’t been confirmed to 31. This number May still fluctuate as new information comes in,” Anand said in a statement. No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday had been rescued. Many of the missing were believed to have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others. Hundreds of others have been displaced across the Himalayan region. Shah said he last heard from his brother on Monday, and a cousin of theirs heard from the couple on Tuesday. He believes his brother and sister-in-law were waiting for immigration offices to open in order to leave Nepal at the Tibet border when the flash floods hit. He said the Canadian government should press Nepal for answers and more information about missing Canadians. “I know they’re doing something, but I feel that they must really push... to find where they are and to get some information,” Shah said. Canada has said it will send $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground. More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal as of Saturday. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 29, 2026. By Lyndsay Armstrong in Halifax With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Doug Ford erects sign to remind Donald Trump 'it's Lake Ontario now and forever'
stories.summary: "Let's be serious. Long before Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after Trump is gone it will still be called Lake Ontario."
stories.author: Anisha Dhiman
paragraphs: Ford’s message comes less than a week after he told the U.S. president to “ kiss my ass ” in response to Trump threatening to impose 50 per cent tariff against Canadian automobiles and auto parts. Trump, in retaliation, called Ford a “flunky.”

In a 39-second video posted on X on Saturday, the Ontario premier said, “You May have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake all because he doesn’t like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves. But let’s be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario.”

Ford continued: “And long after President Trump is gone it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”

On Thursday, the U.S. president signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, bordered by New York State and Ontario, to “Lake America.” The change, Trump said, will come into effect “immediately.”

After the trade deal fell apart between the two countries on Aug. 21, tensions between Canada and the U.S. have been high. When asked on Thursday if he was trying to send Canada a message with the executive order, Trump said, “Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly,” and that “we defend Canada for nothing; they don’t pay us.”
Trump’s order has drawn flak not just from Canadian politicians but also politicians down south.

“An acronym for the Great Lakes used to be Homes. Thanks to Donald Trump, it’s now Shame,” New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office said in a post on X. The executive order was branded “ sad and pathetic ” by U.S. Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer. And U.S. Rep. Joe Morelle said on X that “pretending to rename a lake is an attempted distraction from the President’s disastrous trade talks with Canada.”

Meanwhile, American mapping company MapQuest in a social media post announced “we’re not changing it,” and shared an image of Lake Ontario and surrounding communities. The company jokingly invited social media users to “name it whatever you want at your leisure,” in a follow-up post with some suggestions that include “ Lake Double-Double, Lake Eh and Lake Oh Canada .”

stories.title: Buck Martinez honoured as Blue Jays unveil Hall of Excellence at Rogers Centre
stories.summary: The Toronto Blue Jays opened their new Hall of Excellence on Saturday ahead of an afternoon ceremony for 2026 inductee Buck Martinez at Rogers Centre.
stories.author: John Marchesan
paragraphs: John Albert (Buck) Martinez, a cancer survivor, catcher, manager and broadcaster for parts of five decades with the Toronto Blue Jays, was inducted into the club’s new Hall of Excellence on Saturday.

As part of their 50th season celebrations, the Blue Jays unveiled the section to honour the franchise’s greatest contributors. The 11 honourees from the former Level of Excellence were enshrined in the hall, located on the concourse behind right field at Rogers Centre.

The 77-year-old Martinez was honoured before the Blue Jays’ matinee against the Seattle Mariners. His popularity across Canada exploded during his lengthy stint as a team broadcaster, a position he retired from last winter.
“Today blew me away,” Martinez said. “I didn’t have any grasp of the magnitude of today.”
Martinez added he was also blown away when newcomer Brett Bateman stopped him underneath the stands to congratulate him, saying he knew what Martinez meant to the Blue Jays and their fan base.
He also told a story of visiting England in July. Martinez was having a beer with a friend when a group of ladies walked by. They circled back to say hello because they recognized his voice.
He made a point of saying how much Canadians meant to him.

“First thing they tell you is where they’re from,” Martinez said. “They say I’m from New Brunswick. I’m from Calgary. I came in from Winnipeg. They’re so proud that they came this far to watch the Blue Jays, and that’s the impact the Blue Jays have had on this entire country.”
Martinez joins José Bautista, Paul Beeston, George Bell, Joe Carter, Tom Cheek, Carlos Delgado, Tony Fernandez, Cito Gaston, Pat Gillick, Roy Halladay and Dave Stieb in the hall.

The Level of Excellence will remain on the fascia within the ballpark bowl through the remainder of the season. It will be relocated next year within the stadium’s bowl, where the names will remain visible to fans.

The Californian, who now lives in Florida, flew north to Toronto on a plane with Gaston and Bautista. Delgado, Bell, Carter, Stieb, Beeston and Gillick helped open the new hall and take in Martinez’s ceremony.

“He was an awesome teammate,” Stieb said at a morning media availability. “He was especially special for me because, as you know, I was quite a battler out there. I would lose my emotions at times, and Buck just had a knack for calming me down and keeping me focused on the task at hand.”

Building on the legacy of the Level of Excellence, the hall will provide a space to honour players, coaches, managers, builders and broadcasters – past, present and future – to bring generations of fans closer to the people who shaped the Blue Jays, the team said.

Martinez was a Blue Jays catcher (1981-1986) and manager (2001-2002) who enjoyed two stints as a team broadcaster (1987-2000, 2010-2025). The fan favourite was diagnosed with head and neck cancer in April 2022 and lung cancer in May 2025.
He went 100-115 before being let go as Toronto’s manager in May 2002. As a catcher, he was constantly asked about a play in game at Seattle on July 9, 1985.

In the bottom of the third inning, Martinez tagged out Phil Bradley on a throw from right-fielder Jesse Barfield. But Martinez broke his leg and dislocated his ankle in the violent collision at the plate.

Still, a seated Martinez tried to throw out advancing runner Gorman Thomas at third. But his toss sailed into left field, where George Bell threw a strike back to the injured catcher for a memorable 9-2-7-2 double play.
“I picked up the end of the stretcher to help carry him off the field,” Bell said. “He was yelling at me in pain. It turns out his [broken] leg and ankle were rubbing against me.”

“It was an incredible play,” Stieb added. “To have your leg broken and still have the wherewithal to try to throw somebody out was unbelievable.” Martinez retired as a player in 1986 after a 17-year Major League Baseball career with the Blue Jays, Kansas City Royals and Milwaukee Brewers.
His broadcasting career began in 1982 while still an active player for the Blue Jays. Martinez started by covering playoff games and the all-star game for the Telemedia Radio Network.
He began his television broadcasting career in 1987 as a colour analyst and went on to call over 4,000 Blue Jays games over his career.

His final appearance in the broadcast booth came last fall when he called the World Series with longtime broadcast partner Dan Shulman on Sportsnet. The Los Angeles Dodgers defeated the Blue Jays in the deciding seventh game.
Martinez has also provided commentary for Espn, XM Radio, TBS, The Baseball Network, TSN, and MLB International over his career.
In 2023, he was awarded the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame’s Jack Graney Award for his significant contributions to baseball in Canada.

stories.content:
John Albert (Buck) Martinez, a cancer survivor, catcher, manager and broadcaster for parts of five decades with the Toronto Blue Jays, was inducted into the club’s new Hall of Excellence on Saturday.

As part of their 50th season celebrations, the Blue Jays unveiled the section to honour the franchise’s greatest contributors. The 11 honourees from the former Level of Excellence were enshrined in the hall, located on the concourse behind right field at Rogers Centre.

The 77-year-old Martinez was honoured before the Blue Jays’ matinee against the Seattle Mariners. His popularity across Canada exploded during his lengthy stint as a team broadcaster, a position he retired from last winter.

“Today blew me away,” Martinez said. “I didn’t have any grasp of the magnitude of today.”

Martinez added he was also blown away when newcomer Brett Bateman stopped him underneath the stands to congratulate him, saying he knew what Martinez meant to the Blue Jays and their fan base.

He also told a story of visiting England in July. Martinez was having a beer with a friend when a group of ladies walked by. They circled back to say hello because they recognized his voice.

He made a point of saying how much Canadians meant to him.

“First thing they tell you is where they’re from,” Martinez said. “They say I’m from New Brunswick. I’m from Calgary. I came in from Winnipeg. They’re so proud that they came this far to watch the Blue Jays, and that’s the impact the Blue Jays have had on this entire country.”

Martinez joins José Bautista, Paul Beeston, George Bell, Joe Carter, Tom Cheek, Carlos Delgado, Tony Fernandez, Cito Gaston, Pat Gillick, Roy Halladay and Dave Stieb in the hall.

The Level of Excellence will remain on the fascia within the ballpark bowl through the remainder of the season. It will be relocated next year within the stadium’s bowl, where the names will remain visible to fans.

The Californian, who now lives in Florida, flew north to Toronto on a plane with Gaston and Bautista. Delgado, Bell, Carter, Stieb, Beeston and Gillick helped open the new hall and take in Martinez’s ceremony.

“He was an awesome teammate,” Stieb said at a morning media availability. “He was especially special for me because, as you know, I was quite a battler out there. I would lose my emotions at times, and Buck just had a knack for calming me down and keeping me focused on the task at hand.”

Building on the legacy of the Level of Excellence, the hall will provide a space to honour players, coaches, managers, builders and broadcasters – past, present and future – to bring generations of fans closer to the people who shaped the Blue Jays, the team said.

Martinez was a Blue Jays catcher (1981-1986) and manager (2001-2002) who enjoyed two stints as a team broadcaster (1987-2000, 2010-2025). The fan favourite was diagnosed with head and neck cancer in April 2022 and lung cancer in May 2025.

He went 100-115 before being let go as Toronto’s manager in May 2002. As a catcher, he was constantly asked about a play in game at Seattle on July 9, 1985.

In the bottom of the third inning, Martinez tagged out Phil Bradley on a throw from right-fielder Jesse Barfield. But Martinez broke his leg and dislocated his ankle in the violent collision at the plate.

Still, a seated Martinez tried to throw out advancing runner Gorman Thomas at third. But his toss sailed into left field, where George Bell threw a strike back to the injured catcher for a memorable 9-2-7-2 double play.

“I picked up the end of the stretcher to help carry him off the field,” Bell said. “He was yelling at me in pain. It turns out his [broken] leg and ankle were rubbing against me.”

“It was an incredible play,” Stieb added. “To have your leg broken and still have the wherewithal to try to throw somebody out was unbelievable.” Martinez retired as a player in 1986 after a 17-year Major League Baseball career with the Blue Jays, Kansas City Royals and Milwaukee Brewers.

His broadcasting career began in 1982 while still an active player for the Blue Jays. Martinez started by covering playoff games and the all-star game for the Telemedia Radio Network.

He began his television broadcasting career in 1987 as a colour analyst and went on to call over 4,000 Blue Jays games over his career.

His final appearance in the broadcast booth came last fall when he called the World Series with longtime broadcast partner Dan Shulman on Sportsnet. The Los Angeles Dodgers defeated the Blue Jays in the deciding seventh game.

Martinez has also provided commentary for Espn, XM Radio, TBS, The Baseball Network, TSN, and MLB International over his career.

In 2023, he was awarded the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame’s Jack Graney Award for his significant contributions to baseball in Canada.

stories.title: Byelection called as B.C. Conservative leader faces questions over leaked audio
stories.summary: B.C. Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay currently does not hold a seat in the legislature. The byelection is set for Sept. 26.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A byelection has been called in British Columbia after a B.C. Conservative MLA resigned last week, giving leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay a chance to sit in the legislature.

But in many ways, the timing could not be worse for Findlay, whose caucus has lost six MLAs in recent weeks.

An audio recording appeared on social media Thursday of a person who sounds like Findlay saying she thought if someone stepped aside as a legislator, “I could give them a role as senior adviser in their same portfolio.”

The MLA who resigned, Reann Gasper, has since become Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.

Findlay has addressed the recording and said suggestions it shows her illegally offering jobs to legislators in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection are “preposterous.”

The B.C. Conservative leader currently does not hold a seat in the legislature. The byelection is set for Sept. 26.

Trevor Bolin, the party’s former leader, said the timing of the audio’s release “couldn’t be worse” because of various issues facing the Conservatives.

“I think, you know, Kerri-Lynne needs to get a handle on not only her leadership with the caucus, but as well as the MLAs and the members in British Columbia,” Bolin told Global News.

Findlay said on social media Thursday that it appeared the “unverified” audio recording was made at a July caucus meeting, calling it a “political smear job.”

It is illegal under the Criminal Code to negotiate a reward or benefit related to resignation from political office, but Findlay said the comments in the recording, published by an anonymous account known as “The Findlay Files,” were “normal political discussions” that did not constitute a criminal offence.

In addition to the Criminal Code bribery prohibition, which is subject to up to five years’ prison, BC legislature standing orders ban the offer of money or other advantages to members for promoting any matter “depending or to be transacted” in the house.

The B.C. RCMP said it was aware of the social media post.

“However, generally speaking, the RCMP does not confirm or deny any investigation, or the identity of any person who May be subject to an investigation, until such time as charges have been laid,” a spokesperson said in an email Friday.

5:12 BC Conservative leader faces questions over leaked audio as caucus numbers dwindle

It’s not only the audio hanging over Findlay going into a byelection. Six MLAs have left the party in the past month, four of them in the past week.

The exodus began Aug. 14, when longtime MLA Peter Milobar announced he would leave the party to sit as an independent.

About 10 days later, Ian Paton left the BC Conservatives and signalled he and Milobar planned to form a new party before the fall legislative session.

Since Aug. 24, four others have left: Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman.

Bolin also said he’s hearing six to eight more Conservative MLAs could leave before the fall sitting.

“There’s obviously an issue in the party, there’s an issue in caucus, there’s an issue with the executive,” he said. “Don’t hide from it, don’t deny it, take it head on and fix this issue because the last thing we need is more centre-to-right parties popping up just to split that vote.”

He added he believes the party can recover ahead of a potential general election, which has to be held no later than October 2028, but encouraged Findlay to change the closed-door meetings policy, improve transparency and work with communities and her MLAs.

“Parties last forever, leaders come and go, MLAs come and go, politicians have expiry dates, but at the end of the day, the platforms and the policies that the members put in place are what lasts a lifetime,” he said.

If Findlay chooses to run in the riding, she would face former NDP MLA and agriculture and food minister Pam Alexis. Alexis was elected in the 2020 election before losing to Gasper in 2024 by about 2,600 votes.

OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie said in a post on X on Saturday that her party does not intend to run a candidate despite support she said they have in the Fraser Valley.

“I do not believe it would be ethical to run in a race to try and block a major party leader from getting into the legislature to lead her caucus,” she wrote.

Brodie called on CentreBC and the likely party led by Milobar and Paton to not run candidates, either under their banners or as independents.

Findlay thanked Brodie for her stance and said it would send a message to the B.C. NDP. She did not confirm in the post if she will be running.

Milobar, along with fellow defector Ian Paton, have said they plan to start a new party after leaving Findlay’s caucus. In an interview Saturday, Milobar said they are still working with Elections BC on the process to become official.

He said both he and Paton want their party to be credible and that people “will want to see more meat on the bone of the party that we’re setting up.”

“If it was three months down the road, I’m fully confident we’d be well equipped to put a good effort in and have a credible candidate and be a force, but we’re not in that situation,” he said.

“We’re five days post announcement (of plans for the new party) and the byelection has been called.”

— with files from Global News’ Amy Judd and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign days after Trump’s Lake America order
stories.summary: The two traded personal insults in interviews and social media posts over the past week amid a Canada-U.S. trade war
stories.author: David Shribman
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford unveiled a Lake Ontario sign at a park on the shores of the Great Lake on Saturday, two days after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change its name to Lake America.

Clad in a red Canada Soccer jersey, Ford pulled a tarp off the large blue sign, revealing the words “Now and Always” below the lake’s name.

Standing in front of the sign at Fifty Point Conservation Area in Hamilton, Ont., Ford said he wanted to send a message to Trump that Canadians are resilient and strong and “we will never, ever back down from a bully.”

The lake will always be known as Lake Ontario in Canada and the rest of the world, no matter what Trump calls it, he added.

Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ford earlier this week sparked by the breakdown of Canada-U.S. trade talks .

The two exchanged insults, with Ford saying the president could “kiss my ass,” among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, Rob.

Ford’s latest move failed to impress some who witnessed the sign’s unveiling.

Ankur Patel, who was at the lakefront during the event, said Ford and Trump’s shots at each other and the controversy around the lake’s name change are little more than political theatre.

“It’s just unnecessary, it’s getting more attention than it needs to. I think the focus should be trade negotiation,” he said.

“It doesn’t help or do anything, it just distracts,” Patel said of the sign.

Canada, being the smaller economy, has more to lose in a trade war with the U.S., Patel said, and he would like to see politicians’ energies going toward hashing out a deal.

Explainer: Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

Trump’s executive order renaming the lake only holds water in the U.S. and Prime Minister Mark Carney has shrugged off the change.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Carney wrote on social media Thursday, affirming the Lake Ontario name persists “then, now and always.”

The Lake Ontario sign is just the latest development in the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen the U.S. impose 50 per cent tariffs on about $28-billion of Canadian goods.

The federal government has responded with 15 to 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of U.S. products to take effect on Sept. 8.

Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ford earlier this week sparked by the breakdown of Canada-U.S. trade talks .
The two exchanged insults, with Ford saying the president could “kiss my ass,” among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, Rob.
Ford’s latest move failed to impress some who witnessed the sign’s unveiling.
Ankur Patel, who was at the lakefront during the event, said Ford and Trump’s shots at each other and the controversy around the lake’s name change are little more than political theatre.
“It’s just unnecessary, it’s getting more attention than it needs to. I think the focus should be trade negotiation,” he said.
“It doesn’t help or do anything, it just distracts,” Patel said of the sign.
Canada, being the smaller economy, has more to lose in a trade war with the U.S., Patel said, and he would like to see politicians’ energies going toward hashing out a deal.
Explainer: Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?
Trump’s executive order renaming the lake only holds water in the U.S. and Prime Minister Mark Carney has shrugged off the change.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Carney wrote on social media Thursday, affirming the Lake Ontario name persists “then, now and always.”
The Lake Ontario sign is just the latest development in the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen the U.S. impose 50 per cent tariffs on about $28-billion of Canadian goods.
The federal government has responded with 15 to 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of U.S. products to take effect on Sept. 8.
