stories.title: ‘We need him back’: Families desperate for word of Toronto-area residents as relief efforts continue in Nepal
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely.
stories.author: Simon McKeown
paragraphs: Charu Dhanesha is clinging to hope that her brother, Bhavesh, is safe.

Bhavesh had travelled to Nepal before heading to Tibet for a weeks-long pilgrimage, taking time off from his finance job in Toronto. He was set to cross back into Nepal on Wednesday when devastating flash floods ravaged the Nepal-China border region .

Dhanesha said she last called her brother on Aug. 25, two days before the floods. He was having dinner with his pilgrimage group in Gyirong County , gearing up to reach Kathmandu the next day and finish the spiritual retreat.
Bhavesh Dhanesha, right, with his parents Nemichand, left, and Chandra in Canada in July. Dhanesha’s sister Charu said their parents regularly called Bhavesh during his pilgrimage.
She hasn’t heard from him since.
“We can’t leave hope until we find out something about him,” Dhanesha told the Star in a telephone interview from India. “We need him back, safe and sound.”
Dozens of Canadian families are still desperately hoping for word about their missing family members in Nepal as the death toll and number of people missing continue to rise .
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely.
“This brings the total number of Canadians whose whereabouts haven’t been confirmed to 31. This number May still fluctuate as new information comes in,” Anand said in a statement.
Dhanesha said her brother is a spiritual person and was travelling with the Sadhguru group with the Isha Foundation.
She said she’s called Bhavesh regularly, hoping he’ll pick up. But since Thursday, his phone is no longer ringing and now sends her to voicemail.
“We (still) feel that he May give us some indication that, where ever he is, he is secure and safe,” she said.

The flash flood was caused by a glacial collapse near the county Bhavesh was travelling through, triggering an ice and rock avalanche that sent debris into a river in a devastating surge downstream. Roads and bridges were washed away, homes and buildings were buried in mud and infrastructure damage has caused power outages.
Residents salvage their belongings on Saturday from damaged houses after flash flooding in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal.

Nepali authorities said on Saturday that the combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet has reached 691 people with more than 3,000 still missing. Chinese authorities have reported 16 deaths and nearly 550 missing. Emergency crews continued to find survivors, with more than 3,700 people rescued in Nepal so far.

Poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal on Saturday as the search for thousands of missing people in areas devastated by catastrophic flash floods along the border with China entered its fourth day. (Aug. 29, 2026)

Co-ordinated relief efforts using helicopters supplied aid including clothes and food to communities in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. In a news briefing Saturday, Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said authorities have mobilized all available resources with support from international assistance for search, rescue, relief and recovery operations, with a particular focus on locating those still missing.
“This is currently our national priority,” Khanal told reporters.

Anand also announced Saturday that Canada is allocating $5 million in aid to support emergency efforts in Nepal. The money will fund “trusted humanitarian partners,” like the United Nations and Red Cross, to deliver life-saving care, food, clean water and shelter.
“Global Affairs Canada consular officials are working around the clock to locate and assist Canadians in the region and support their families here at home,” Anand wrote on social media.

Samira and Anil Grover, of Markham, are among the Canadians still missing. Their daughter, Saumya, told the Star her parents were in Nepal on a spiritual pilgrimage and were preparing to cross the border into Tibet the morning of the floods.
“My sister and I told them to be safe and keep us posted,” Saumya said of their conversation around 7 a.m. local time in Nepal. “They were really excited ... That was the last communication we had.”
Anil, 55, is an accountant and Samira, 50, is an elementary teacher with the Toronto District School Board.
“At this time, we remain hopeful for their safe return and are closely monitoring developments,” Ryan Bird, the communications and public affairs officer with the Tdsb, said in an email statement.
A resident salvages his belongings from his house filled with mud and debris in Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Saturday.
The situation is still “very grave,” said Anup Rana, the field operations director for humanitarian organization World Vision International Nepal.

“All the houses have been vacated, there is rubble and debris, the mud slides are two to three metres high,” Rana said, describing what his colleagues on the ground are seeing. “People are fearful, devastated. They have lost their loved ones and are broken.”

Rana told the Star that the biggest challenge is accessing communities since roads and bridges were swept up and destroyed by the cascading mud slides. Rain and foggy conditions during Nepal’s monsoon season are also adding difficulties to rescue and relief efforts.
Rana said his team has been tasked with taking stock of what different communities need and relaying it to the government, adding they have also been authorized to give out supplies.
“The country is in sorrow,” Rana said. “But we want to be hopeful to overcome this situation.”
With files from Jason Miller, The Associated Press and The Canadian Press

stories.content:
Charu Dhanesha is clinging to hope that her brother, Bhavesh, is safe.

Bhavesh had travelled to Nepal before heading to Tibet for a weeks-long pilgrimage, taking time off from his finance job in Toronto. He was set to cross back into Nepal on Wednesday when devastating flash floods ravaged the Nepal-China border region .

Dhanesha said she last called her brother on Aug. 25, two days before the floods. He was having dinner with his pilgrimage group in Gyirong County , gearing up to reach Kathmandu the next day and finish the spiritual retreat.

Bhavesh Dhanesha, right, with his parents Nemichand, left, and Chandra in Canada in July. Dhanesha’s sister Charu said their parents regularly called Bhavesh during his pilgrimage.

She hasn’t heard from him since.

“We can’t leave hope until we find out something about him,” Dhanesha told the Star in a telephone interview from India. “We need him back, safe and sound.”

Dozens of Canadian families are still desperately hoping for word about their missing family members in Nepal as the death toll and number of people missing continue to rise .

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely.

“This brings the total number of Canadians whose whereabouts haven’t been confirmed to 31. This number May still fluctuate as new information comes in,” Anand said in a statement.

Dhanesha said her brother is a spiritual person and was travelling with the Sadhguru group with the Isha Foundation.

She said she’s called Bhavesh regularly, hoping he’ll pick up. But since Thursday, his phone is no longer ringing and now sends her to voicemail.

“We (still) feel that he May give us some indication that, where ever he is, he is secure and safe,” she said.

The flash flood was caused by a glacial collapse near the county Bhavesh was travelling through, triggering an ice and rock avalanche that sent debris into a river in a devastating surge downstream. Roads and bridges were washed away, homes and buildings were buried in mud and infrastructure damage has caused power outages.

Residents salvage their belongings on Saturday from damaged houses after flash flooding in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal.

Nepali authorities said on Saturday that the combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet has reached 691 people with more than 3,000 still missing. Chinese authorities have reported 16 deaths and nearly 550 missing. Emergency crews continued to find survivors, with more than 3,700 people rescued in Nepal so far.

Poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal on Saturday as the search for thousands of missing people in areas devastated by catastrophic flash floods along the border with China entered its fourth day. (Aug. 29, 2026)

Co-ordinated relief efforts using helicopters supplied aid including clothes and food to communities in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. In a news briefing Saturday, Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said authorities have mobilized all available resources with support from international assistance for search, rescue, relief and recovery operations, with a particular focus on locating those still missing.

“This is currently our national priority,” Khanal told reporters.

Anand also announced Saturday that Canada is allocating $5 million in aid to support emergency efforts in Nepal. The money will fund “trusted humanitarian partners,” like the United Nations and Red Cross, to deliver life-saving care, food, clean water and shelter.

“Global Affairs Canada consular officials are working around the clock to locate and assist Canadians in the region and support their families here at home,” Anand wrote on social media.

Samira and Anil Grover, of Markham, are among the Canadians still missing. Their daughter, Saumya, told the Star her parents were in Nepal on a spiritual pilgrimage and were preparing to cross the border into Tibet the morning of the floods.

“My sister and I told them to be safe and keep us posted,” Saumya said of their conversation around 7 a.m. local time in Nepal. “They were really excited ... That was the last communication we had.”

Anil, 55, is an accountant and Samira, 50, is an elementary teacher with the Toronto District School Board.

“At this time, we remain hopeful for their safe return and are closely monitoring developments,” Ryan Bird, the communications and public affairs officer with the Tdsb, said in an email statement.

A resident salvages his belongings from his house filled with mud and debris in Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Saturday.

The situation is still “very grave,” said Anup Rana, the field operations director for humanitarian organization World Vision International Nepal.

“All the houses have been vacated, there is rubble and debris, the mud slides are two to three metres high,” Rana said, describing what his colleagues on the ground are seeing. “People are fearful, devastated. They have lost their loved ones and are broken.”

Rana told the Star that the biggest challenge is accessing communities since roads and bridges were swept up and destroyed by the cascading mud slides. Rain and foggy conditions during Nepal’s monsoon season are also adding difficulties to rescue and relief efforts.

Rana said his team has been tasked with taking stock of what different communities need and relaying it to the government, adding they have also been authorized to give out supplies.

“The country is in sorrow,” Rana said. “But we want to be hopeful to overcome this situation.”

With files from Jason Miller, The Associated Press and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada is luring top U.S. scientists with 'almost unheard of' funding amid tense American political climate
stories.summary: 48 are from U.S. in first phase of $1.7B Canada Global Impact+ Research Talent Initiative. And yes, Trump plays a role.
stories.author: Janet Hurley
stories.content:
Kathryn Whitehead wasn’t looking to leave Carnegie Mellon, an American university known globally for its science and technology programs. But then Canada came calling with an offer “almost unheard of right now,” and the chemical engineer, whose work could unlock therapies for Parkinson’s disease and cystic fibrosis, didn’t hesitate.

Whitehead is heading to the University of British Columbia as research chair in translational drug delivery — one of 64 academics appointed Thursday to key research posts at 21 Canadian universities under a federal program aimed at attracting the world’s top minds.

The Eddie Goldenberg Research Chairs are the flagship awards of the broader $1.7 billion Canada Global Impact+ Research Talent Initiative, with this first phase of investing $504 million. Recipients — of which 48 are from U.S. institutions and 22 are Canadian expats — receive $500,000 or $1 million a year for eight years (which also covers such things as research activities and team compensation).

“Every part of my employment package was either competitive with or far exceeded what would be available to me elsewhere,” says Whitehead, an authority in lipid nanoparticle drug delivery. “There is nowhere in the United States that is offering this level of support for research and the infrastructure required to conduct that research.”

Beyond the funding, the fit made sense in other ways: UBC is the birthplace of lipid nanoparticles, central to Whitehead’s research, and her husband, originally from Thunder Bay, has long wanted to come home.

Robert Asselin, CEO of U15 Canada, which represents the country’s leading research universities, calls the appointments “a big deal.”

“We’re talking about the best scholars in the world, from MIT, Harvard and Carnegie Mellon, choosing to come here to do their research. It speaks to the attractiveness of our leading research universities.”

For some of the new chairs who responded to the Star’s questions, it is also about retreat, from a political climate south of the border that is making their work harder, and, for one, less safe. Here’s a glimpse at why they’ve said yes to Canada.

Raymond Fisman ( University of Toronto, chair in finance and political economy; from Boston University)

This is something of a homecoming for me. I’ve been in the U.S. for 30-plus years, but when people ask me where I’m from, I still say Canada. I feel like U.S. policies have diverged sufficiently from my personal values that I prefer to be elsewhere ... given my own line of work — the role of special interests in politics — these are very troubling times in the U.S. I am obviously a beneficiary of this program’s largesse, but I do think it’s coming at a particularly apt time: Lots of people at U.S. institutions, for a wide range of reasons, are reconsidering their options.

Suzanne Lapi and Jonathan McConathy ( McMaster University, chair in isotope production and radiopharmaceutical innovation, and chair in molecular imaging and nuclear theranostics respectively; from University of Alabama at Birmingham)

McMaster has a tradition and track record of excellent research in our field and the well-crafted plan to make McMaster the “Nuclear University” in Canada is very appealing. The uncertainty and politicization of science in the U.S. combined with immigration challenges for non-citizen faculty and trainees make U.S. opportunities in research less attractive than in the past. Suzanne is also a Canadian-U.S. dual citizen, and we will be closer to family and can raise our son in a culture that shares our values.

Elliott Hazen (University of Victoria, chair in climate resilience and ocean futures; from Noaa Southwest Fisheries Science Center)

Canada is making a serious investment in science at a moment when the world needs it more than ever. That was incredibly compelling to me. UVic was an especially strong fit because it sits at the intersection of ocean science, climate change and real-world decision-making. Canada and UVic offered the opportunity not just to take a job, but to build a scientific program with real long-term impact. For me, competitiveness is about more than salary. It is about whether you have the people, resources and institutional support to do your best work.

Tomislav Friščić ( McGill University, chair in mechanochemistry and solid-state chemistry; from University of Birmingham, U.K.)

A very significant draw of Canada, and especially of Quebec and McGill, is their pioneering role in, and strong dedication to, the development of green, sustainable technologies. I am looking forward to working with colleagues and industries in Quebec and Canada to establish a hotbed of new, green, industrially attractive technologies. Canada provides a unique opportunity for this ambitious goal as it presents a confluence of cutting-edge innovation and natural resource opportunities, combined with a tightly knit, friendly academic and industrial environment, and a strong respect for history and for keeping our environment safe.

Katy Backes Kozhimannil ( University of Calgary, chair in maternal and child health policy; from University of Minnesota School of Public Health)

Katy Backes Kozhimannil

This is a pivotal point in my career and life. I co-lead a vibrant research centre and our team’s work on rural maternity care access is informing transformative change in communities across the U.S. My colleagues are emerging leaders who will continue this important work, and my children are graduating from high school. It is a time of transition for me, and Canada has presented an extraordinarily appealing path forward. The (program) offered me among the most generous sustained funding and support that I have seen in my field of work. Having eight years of consistent funding support, along with infrastructure funding to support the supplies, spaces and people needed to accomplish research excellence and knowledge translation, is a powerful tool to support innovation that makes Canadian lives better, starting at birth.

Gabriel Walton ( Queen’s University, chair in slope geohazard management for infrastructure and mining in a changing climate; from Colorado School of Mines)

The professional opportunity is really unparalleled. Queen’s has a great research environment with lots of potential collaborators across disciplines, and it also has one of the top geological engineering programs in the world. And of course, from a personal perspective, I’m very happy to be moving back home to Canada with my family.

Seth Guikema ( Western University, chair in climate risk and resilience analytics; from University of Michigan)

Western is already an international leader in natural hazards research and in wind engineering. There is a depth and breadth of expertise that is hard to match. Canada is a very welcoming ecosystem for people doing research on natural hazards, climate change, community resilience and inequities in hazard impacts. It provides a very supportive environment for top research talent. The level of support provided by (this) program is beyond anything available in the U.S.

Talia Bettcher ( University of Waterloo, chair in gender-based violence prevention and trans community resilience; from California State University, Los Angeles)

I’m a Canadian citizen who has lived in Los Angeles for more than 35 years. As a trans woman, I was no longer feeling safe there. My decision was very much about coming home and about finding a safe place to do my work. My scholarship focuses on anti-trans violence. Because anti-trans rhetoric is being wielded to support authoritarianism, I regard this work as an important intervention in the rise of anti-democratic forces. Canada demonstrated a willingness to support research into an area that is effectively out of bounds in places like the U.S. And the (chair) funding allows me to pursue my scholarship in a truly unprecedented way, ON an unprecedented scale at time when such work is most needed.

Responses were edited for length and clarity.

stories.title: These Ontario doctors know how dangerous e-scooters can be. But keeping them from kids isn't easy
stories.summary: With e-scooter hospitalizations up nearly 40% across Canada, they say parents need to rethink how they view the devices.
stories.author: Amarachi Amadike
stories.content:
Over the past year, Diana Craiovan has spent much of her time analyzing data that paints a grim image of e-scooter use among children. A mother of two kids, age five and nine, she worries about the impact of these devices on Ontario’s youth as an increasing number of children end up in hospital.

“My kids have the regular scooters and (they) even find those fast,” she said. “I can’t imagine allowing them on a device that goes that fast.”

Craiovan, the program lead for hospital data management at the Canadian Institute for Health Information (Cihi), said her older child has not yet asked for an upgrade to a motorized scooter. Even if her children were older, however, she said she would not allow one in her home.

“Some of these e-scooters can go up to 25 kilometres an hour,” she said, roughly twice the speed of a typical kick scooter.

She was alarmed to discover that e-scooter-related injuries increased by 40 per cent nationally over the past year , with 837 hospitalizations recorded between April 2025 and March 2026.

Our city is one of the few in North America where riding one is against the law. Shauna Brail says yea and Erica Lam nay in our bridging the

Children under 15 account for much of that increase, she said in an interview, with injuries among that age group up 180 per cent over the same period. Data from the Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program also revealed that 10 kids died from e-scooter accidents in 2025. Six were in Ontario.

The staggering numbers have parents grappling with whether motorized scooters should be treated as toys or as vehicles subject to licensing and age restrictions — a question that takes on particular weight for parents who work as emergency physicians and see the results of accidents in the ER.

But as e-scooters become increasingly popular among children and teens, parents are finding themselves caught between wanting their kids to fit in and worrying about what can happen when things go wrong.

Dr. Fraser Mackay, an ER physician and member of the Canadian Association of Emergency Physicians, said his response to his children asking to buy e-scooters would be “tough s—-,” even though they have “lots of friends with e-scooters, going down to seven and eight years old.”

“The main issue is the head injuries,” he said, adding that while they are not the most common injuries, they are the most devastating.

According to unpublished SickKids data from 2021 to 2025, many of the injuries involve head trauma, with 62 per cent of all accidents occurring without a helmet.

“You’re safer on a bicycle than you are on an e-scooter for a whole series of reasons,” Mackay said. “It is a motorized vehicle that’s supposed to be on the road and not on the sidewalk.”

Toronto is looking at a licensing e-bikes, which could close a gap in protections for delivery

Mackay said telling a 12-year-old to ride a motorized vehicle on the road is “ludicrous,” highlighting what he called the “bizarre” nature of municipal and provincial approaches to e-scooter regulations across the country.

“Right now, it’s a total Wild West, and we’re seeing the results of that.”

In Ontario, e-scooters can be used on private property, but municipalities must opt into the province’s pilot program if they want to permit e-scooters on public roads. Toronto has not opted in, so e-scooters cannot legally be ridden on the city’s public roads , bike lanes, sidewalks, trails, paths or in parks. In other words, owning an e-scooter, or riding one on private property, such as a driveway, is not prohibited, but taking it onto Toronto’s public streets is.

Dr. Josh Ramjist, a father of two children age four and seven, said the easy access creates a “developmental mismatch,” as young children are not skeletally or socially mature enough to operate the devices.

“They can’t handle the speed, their reflexes aren’t fast enough, and they’re in a crowded environment,” he explained.

Common and less common activities without protection can pose a high risk of injury, physicians say.

At The Hospital for Sick Children, where Ramjist practices, past emergency patients often return for follow-up appointments. Most parents get rid of their child’s e-scooter after an accident, he said.

“Almost all of them have given away (their devices), or just thrown the e-scooters in the trash,” he said. “It’s regret. I don’t think any well-meaning parent buys something for their kid with the intent that they’re going to get hurt by it.”

Ramjist noted that there is a misconception among parents that e-scooters are toys.

“The reality is that these are proper motorized vehicles,” he warned. “And the injury patterns resemble that.”

Experts say that, unlike conventional scooters, e-scooter accidents can result in injuries that resemble those seen in “standard motor vehicle accidents.”

“These kids are ending up with devastating injuries, sometimes debilitating injuries,” Ramjist said.

Potholes add another layer of risk. Pothole-related insurance claims from drivers increased almost 50 per cent from last year , and physicians say they are seeing the impact on e-scooter riders in emergency departments.

Dr. Caroline Rutten, a pediatric radiologist at The Hospital for Sick Children, said the hospital is seeing many young children come in after falls involving potholes, a statement corroborated by the hospital’s unpublished data, which reveals 69 per cent of accidents are due to falls without a collision.

“That has nothing to do with the child behaving safely and respecting speed limitations,” she said. “It’s just … the environment is very risky, and these devices are not very safe or stable. So accidents just happen very quickly.”

Rutten told the Star she has spent much of her time convincing family members not to allow her nieces and nephews on e-scooters, even though their friends May ride them.

“The average documented speed is around 25 kilometres an hour. That is motor-vehicle-level speed,” she warned them. “Would you let a 13-year-old child on a motorbike?”

stories.title: Donald Trump claims Lake Ontario is now ‘Lake America.’ Here’s what you need to know about the cross-border battle
stories.summary: Trump’s executive order May change the name in the U.S., but Canada isn’t required to follow suit. Here’s who gets to decide and where the centuries-old name came from.
stories.author: Anastasia Blosser
stories.content:
A lake can be many things: a border, a body of water, a source of drinking water and, apparently, a battleground in a trade war .

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, following a bitter public spat with Ontario Premier Doug Ford and the collapse of trade talks between Canada and the United States.

Trump announced the change Thursday after Canada launched a new round of counter-tariffs on American products.

President Donald Trump says he's renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada. (Aug. 28, 2026)

“They can continue to make their cars for Canada, but … we don’t want them to make cars for the United States of America,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “So the lake change, the Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time.”

Trump’s threat to rename the Great Lake came after he traded insults with Ford, who called the president a bully and told him to “kiss my ass.” Trump responded by comparing the premier to his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford, saying Doug Ford was a less charismatic version of him.

Trump also repeatedly accused Canada of “ripping off” the United States and said his administration did not expect to continue doing business with Ontario “much longer.”

Ford has since softened his language, calling for the two sides to reach a deal. But he said he did not regret his earlier comments, which he said resonated around the world.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has dismissed Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario, saying Canada will not recognize the change.

Other politicians on both sides of the border have also said they will continue using the lake’s familiar name.

“Lake Ontario is and will always be Lake Ontario, and no executive order will change that,” Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a statement on X. “It doesn’t belong to President Donald Trump to rename on a whim.”

Trump said it was “effective immediately” days after he said on social media that he was “giving

Ford likewise posted: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”

The renaming has particular significance for the Wendat Nation, whose language is believed to be the source of the name Ontario.

“Outraged, appalled, shocked: there are no other words to describe how I feel,” Grand Chief Pierre Picard of the Wendat Nation said in a statement.

“President Trump is attempting to eradicate our history,” Picard said.

In Canada, geographical names are overseen by the Geographical Names Board of Canada, which was established in 1897 and has approved more than 350,000 names over its history.

Individuals and organizations can propose names or name changes for Canadian geographical features. Those requests require information such as the reason for the proposed change, the origin and meaning of the name and evidence from local residents about how the area is commonly referred to.

Canada is not required to recognize geographical name changes made by another country. That means even if Trump’s administration uses “Lake America” for the portion of the lake on the U.S. side, he cannot dictate what other countries call the lake.

Lake Ontario is not the first border-straddling body of water that Trump has attempted to rename. One of his first moves after returning to office in January 2025 was signing an executive order directing the U.S. government to use “Gulf of America” instead of the Gulf of Mexico.

The Gulf of Mexico has carried its name for more than 400 years, and Trump’s order only holds water in the United States.

Trump also ordered the restoration of the name “Mount McKinley” for North America’s highest peak. Former president Barack Obama had changed the official U.S. name to Denali in 2015, reflecting the name preferred by local residents and Indigenous Peoples.

In February 2025, Republican congressman Buddy Carter introduced a House bill that would authorize Trump to acquire Greenland and rename it “Red, White and Blueland,”

U.S. map company MapQuest has already said it will not adjust its site to reflect Trump’s executive order.

“We’re not changing it,” Mapquest said in a post on social media, displaying a map of the lake bearing the familiar “Lake Ontario” moniker.

In a followup post, MapQuest joked that anyone determined to give the lake a new name could use an online generator, offering “Lake Are We Doing This Again?” as one possibility.

The Star has reached out to Apple to ask whether their maps will adopt “Lake America,” but has not received a response.

Google said in a statement published Saturday that it had changed the name of the lake on its U.S. service to Lake America, while in Canada it would remain Lake Ontario. Users outside the two countries would see both names on Google Maps. Google said the change reflects its “long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

Google said this name change was due to the Geographic Names Information System (Gnis) formally changing the name from Lake Ontario to Lake America in the United States.

Other Canadian services that use Google Maps like Ontario 511 which provides images from over 900 cameras on roads across the province May have changed the name to Lake America.

Google Maps now uses “Gulf of America” for users in the United States, while users elsewhere see both names, with “Gulf of America” appearing in brackets. Apple Maps has also adopted the new name for the gulf.

The Associated Press, meanwhile, has declined to change its style guide, which is widely used by American news organizations.

The name Lake Ontario predates both Canada and the United States.

Historians believe Ontario has Iroquoian roots, with interpretations including “beautiful lake,” “great lake” or “sparkling water,” according to the Canadian Encyclopedia. Europeans were using the name Ontario for the lake by 1641, and it appeared on maps by 1656.

The name eventually became attached to the province itself during confederation, meaning Ontario is named after the lake and not the other way around.

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard said the U.S. president “is attempting to eradicate our

Carney pointed to the Wendat origins of the name in a social media post, writing that Ontari’io means, roughly, “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” The beginning of the word, “Ontar,” means lake or body of water.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” Carney posted on social media.

stories.title: On the American side of Lake Ontario, how Donald Trump has strained the ties that bind: ‘You guys don’t hate us, do you?’
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump signed an order renaming Lake Ontario ‘Lake America.’ We took a road trip along the New York shores to see the fallout.
stories.author: Mark Colley
stories.content:
Cape Vincent, N.Y.—It’s just after 7:40 p.m. when news of the executive order reaches the squat white cottage underneath the lighthouse.

Pat Schamerhorn is locking up the gift shop. She lives just down the road, in the house with the picket fence, with views of the end of Lake Ontario and the start of the St. Lawrence River out her front door.

She decided to head home early, catching the last wisps of an achingly beautiful sunset dipping below the horizon, when news arrives — in person, in the form of a Toronto Star reporter and photographer.

“Oh my gawd ,” Schamerhorn lets out, mouth agape. “We’re so sorry.”

Increasingly, Canadians are struggling to understand what is happening to their southern neighbours. These people who were once close now feel so painfully separated, not geographically but emotionally, from the nation Canadians thought they knew.

On Wednesday, 24 hours after Trump first floated the idea of the new name, we embarked on a three-day road trip around the lake — an area rich in people and stories.

There’s the small-town grocer next to sun-dappled apple orchards who knows his customers by heart. There’s the fisherman who casts out by the border, 32 kilometres from land, still hunting for his first big catch of the season. There are the Seneca people, who have lived on this land for millennia.

Each of their lives intersect with the lake; each of them has a relationship with Canada, one that has become decidedly more complicated over the past two years.

We set out on a search for the soul of Lake Ontario — the ties that bind, the president who separates and the people who are caught in the middle.

The Star, simplified

In a relationship being dissected seam by seam, the people we encountered on the New York shores were by turns apologetic, indifferent and optimistic.

“We do miss our Canadian friends,” Schamerhorn said. “We like to think it’ll get back to normal again, before too awful long. We’ll see.”

A war then — and a war now

The trip begins where the lake begins: at the end of the Niagara River, where British Canada once laid siege to the U.S.

There’s a story Robert Emerson likes to tell about an American woman named Betsy Doyle. On a fierce November day in 1812, as American and British soldiers exchanged fire for hours across the Niagara River, Doyle re-armed soldiers by carting red-hot cannonballs up the narrow wooden staircase of Fort Niagara’s French Castle.

She was so determined, the story goes, because her husband — born in British Canada yet fighting for the Americans — had been captured by the British and branded a traitor, a fate punishable by death.

Emerson, Old Fort Niagara’s executive director, tells this story with glee. It shows, he says, the complicated ties that bind Canada and the U.S.

“Most of the stories in this place,” Emerson says, “have as much to do with Canadian history as American history. It’s truly a binational site.”

Emerson, 70, would know. He has managed Old Fort Niagara, 300 years old this summer, since 1997.

Fort Niagara overlooks both the river and Lake Ontario, its waves calmly lapping under a wispy blue sky. On a clear day, Emerson says, you can make out the Toronto skyline. In the early morning, it glimmers like gold on the horizon. At night, it shines.

Canada is unflinchingly close here. At its narrowest, the mouth of the river is less than half a kilometre wide. But Canadian visitors are fewer these days. Some of that is from the pandemic, Emerson says; some of that is the trade war.

Amy and Craig Polley, who live just up the road, have noticed the decline themselves. It didn’t stop them from hanging a Canadian flag by their front door, side by side with the American.

“It’s like our second home, right?” Amy says. “I hate to see countries that are so close — were so close — being separated because of a tyrant.”

For the Polleys, close would be an understatement.

Sitting on their porch, the late summer sun shaded by a tree in the front yard, Canada is so near the cannon demonstrations at Fort George across water rattle the house every day. “All my life,” she says. “It still startles me.”

For all that’s happened the past 19 months, Amy apologizes profusely. She calls Trump’s actions “ridiculous” and “childish.”

“You guys don’t hate us, do you?” she asks. “You hate our president. You can hate our government, OK?”

Hours later, Dan DeGeorge sprays down his boat in the Rochester marina. Despite two tours out into Lake Ontario today, he is still searching for his first big catch of the year.

Captain Joe, he says, motioning down the dock, caught two 30-pounders within one week. DeGeorge has seemingly maxed out at 22.5. “How does that happen?” he wonders aloud.

DeGeorge — who runs a fishing charter company called, of all things, DoubleD — has been fishing this lake for some 40 years. He knows the waters, the currents, the way one good storm can shake up everything like a snow globe and turn it upside down. He loves it. “You’re just matching wits against nature,” he says. “It’s like a chess match.”

People come from all over to fish here, he explains, because Lake Ontario is world-class. DeGeorge doesn’t fish the Canadian side, but he comes close.

“We call it the fence,” he says, pointing to the chart plotter on his dash. “The Canadian border.”

DeGeorge goes hunting with Canadian friends, and he’s headed up to Alberta in November to hunt moose and white-tailed deer. He loves Canadians, he says. But he likes teasing them, too, and “Lake America” is perfect fodder.

Ride the wave, he advises. It’s just how Trump rolls.

“The next thing is going to be, your prime minister is great and we’re buddies and we got a deal,” he says. “There’s no animosity … Unlike Iran.”

DeGeorge’s girlfriend leaves him a cocktail on the dock. First, he’ll finish cleaning out the boat for tomorrow’s morning tour.

To the Seneca, trade means peace

The next day, Michael Galban stands in the exhibit hall of the Seneca Art and Culture Center, a half-hour outside Rochester. The people here, Galban says, are like pebbles rolling down the hill, picking up moss as they go.

“You build up thin layers of belonging over so many generations,” he says. “We see ourselves as part of the land. It’s as much a part of us as the car you drove in on. You know what I mean?”

Galban offers another parallel. For the Haudenosaunee, trade and peace mean the same thing. It is impossible to have one without the other.

‘It’s truly God’s country’

Joe Nicosia’s day starts at 5:30 a.m., when he gets the coffee going on this corner of small-town America, roughly 60 km east of Rochester.

He’s owned Joey’s Northside Grocery in the village of Newark for 42 years, ever since he was 23 years old. He knows everyone who walks in — their name, their beer, what they smoke, who they know. He takes rent from the hairdresser who works across the street and tells a neighbour that a friend’s nephew just died.

On Sundays, he flips on the Bills. Business spikes when Buffalo is playing. “Sometimes,” he says, “there ain’t a lot to root for around here.”

This, Nicosia says, is apple country. Immigrants come to pick the rolling orchards of sun-kissed trees, and the honeycrisp harvest starts this week. Mexicans, Jamaicans, Haitians — “we get ‘em all,” Nicosia says. “Nobody discriminates.”

“It’s truly Americana. Norman Rockwell, I guess. It’s who we are and what we are,” he says. “It’s truly God’s country.”

Nicosia, 65, likes Canada. He hunts sandhill cranes in Saskatchewan, wearing camo in the blind, admiring what he calls the Lord’s majesty at sunrise.

At the shop, Trump’s tariffs have raised the price of cigars from Honduras and the Dominican, but not much else. For guys like him, he explains, the escalating tensions don’t matter much.

“We’re the pawns in the game,” he says. “It boils down to, we’re real people. How much does it really affect?”

Trump can change the name of the lake, he says, but he’ll keep calling it Lake Ontario. It’ll all change with the next election anyway.

The door swings open and Peter Blandino walks in. Blandino, 80, was mayor of Newark for 13 and a half years. He likes Canada but likes Trump, too. Trump puts America first, Blandino says. He maintains peace through strength. “It seems to be something that works for him.”

Nicosia is back inside after carrying a pack of beer to a car. The only thing this town has truly hated Canada for, he says, his voice now down to a whisper, is the wildfire smoke.

And with that, he gets back to work.

“You better get out of here if you’re gonna make it tonight,” he says, calling out the door. “You ever get back this way, stop in.”

End of the day at the end of the lake

By the time we arrive at Cape Vincent and the Tibbetts Point lighthouse, the sun is already low on the horizon, tucking behind a cloud as it speckles the waves with amber. This is the end of the lake. Head east and the St. Lawrence River begins.

Sitting on a bench, Schamerhorn admits she is spoiled.

She and her husband came here to retire, but if retirement means rest, Schamerhorn missed the memo. She is here practically every day, helping run the lighthouse gift shop.

The lighthouse, Schamerhorn says, is the soul of Cape Vincent. It houses a fresnel lens, the only one of its kind on the lake, reflecting the light of a single 250-watt bulb some 25 km out on the lake.

Did Schamerhorn, now 66, care about lighthouses before Tibbetts? She scrunches her face. “No! Not at all,” she laughs. “I’m a chemistry person!”

She runs the gift shop all the same. It is big on personality and short on space. Boxes of unsold sweaters and glassware are piled in the hallway. The museum is squeezed into a corner. Schamerhorn opens a freezer and offers ice cream. Anything to free up room.

When she leaves at night, she often sits and watches the lighthouse flashing on and off. “Something about ‘em. I can’t put it in words,” she says. “How could you not love that?”

Schamerhorn tries to avoid politics at all costs, but what’s happening right now doesn’t sit well with her. She was born in Newfoundland, ON a U.S. Air Force base, and she loves Canada. Renaming the lake she lives on is simply petty, she says. She won’t call it “Lake America.”

“Unfortunately, we have a situation that we can’t control,” she says. “We just hope you guys understand, it’s not us little guys.”

In New York, all along the lake, Canada is never far. It is intertwined with the lives of the people who live here. At Cape Vincent, Canada feels close enough to touch. The wind farms of Wolfe Island, the largest of the Thousand Islands, soar in sight across the river.

It was a connection with Canada, severed for the past two years. Schamerhorn hopes the ferry will return. Everyone in Cape Vincent does.

And when it does, Cape Vincent will swing its doors open. Hopefully, Schamerhorn says, Canada will come back.

She decided to head home early, catching the last wisps of an achingly beautiful sunset dipping below the horizon, when news arrives — in person, in the form of a Toronto Star reporter and photographer.
“Oh my gawd ,” Schamerhorn lets out, mouth agape. “We’re so sorry.”

On Wednesday, 24 hours after Trump first floated the idea of the new name, we embarked on a three-day road trip around the lake — an area rich in people and stories.

There’s the small-town grocer next to sun-dappled apple orchards who knows his customers by heart. There’s the fisherman who casts out by the border, 32 kilometres from land, still hunting for his first big catch of the season. There are the Seneca people, who have lived on this land for millennia.
Each of their lives intersect with the lake; each of them has a relationship with Canada, one that has become decidedly more complicated over the past two years.
We set out on a search for the soul of Lake Ontario — the ties that bind, the president who separates and the people who are caught in the middle.

In a relationship being dissected seam by seam, the people we encountered on the New York shores were by turns apologetic, indifferent and optimistic.
“We do miss our Canadian friends,” Schamerhorn said. “We like to think it’ll get back to normal again, before too awful long. We’ll see.”

She was so determined, the story goes, because her husband — born in British Canada yet fighting for the Americans — had been captured by the British and branded a traitor, a fate punishable by death.
Emerson, Old Fort Niagara’s executive director, tells this story with glee. It shows, he says, the complicated ties that bind Canada and the U.S.
“Most of the stories in this place,” Emerson says, “have as much to do with Canadian history as American history. It’s truly a binational site.”

stories.title: Why Chch cancelled your Saturday evening news
stories.summary: The economics of media have been co-opted by foreign attention-miners focused on maximizing your screen time rather than informing you.
stories.author: Greg O'Brien
stories.content:
Unlike online platforms, Chch operates under a federal licence because we provide an essential public service delivered freely over public airwaves.

With that licence comes serious obligations.

We are bound by ethics and standards established by the Radio Television Digital News Association to ensure we tell our viewers, readers, and listeners the truth. Our advertising must be honest, we must manage vulgar or violent content appropriately, and we are required to broadcast emergency alerts.

We are also required to air a minimum number of Canadian content hours and spend a significant portion of our revenue on it. Most of Chch’s Canadian content investment goes directly into local news. While our licence sets the floor for us at just three hours of TV news per week, we’ve produced 28 hours weekly, in addition to our podcasts, stories on chch.com , newsletters and social channels.

We dramatically exceed the prescribed levels because we believe deeply in our mission to serve our community with thoroughly researched, vetted, professional local journalism. Our news standards set us apart from social media garbage and AI slop.

This model was sustainable because advertising returns were once strong enough to support a robust business. Once.

Today, the economics of media have been co-opted by foreign attention-miners focused on maximizing your screen time rather than informing you. Chch now competes with these massive foreign tech platforms for local attention while remaining bound by our regulatory obligations. Those platforms face no such obligations. Meta has no requirement to ensure what’s on Facebook or Instagram is true, fake videos abound on TikTok and YouTube and foreign streaming services have no mandate to fund or feature Canadian stories.

Meanwhile, Meta, Google, and Amazon capture more than 75 per cent of digital ad dollars in Canada while stealing our content to train their AI models. Crtc data shows that since 2018, ad revenues for private Canadian TV broadcasters like Chch have fallen 25 per cent, a loss of nearly $400 million across the industry.

To address these massive imbalances, the Canadian government passed the Online Streaming Act and the Online News Act. The Crtc established frameworks requiring foreign platforms to contribute a small portion of their Canadian revenues to Canadian content, including news, albeit at a far lower level than Canadian broadcasters.

Under the Online News Act, Google contributes $100 million annually to Canadian local news, from which Chch receives about $460,000. Meta chose to block news links on its platforms altogether to dodge its obligations.

In June, however, Prime Minister Mark Carney instructed the Crtc to rethink key policies following American trade pressure, setting aside what the commission had decided to do with the Online Streaming Act, raising concerns across the industry that federal support under the Online News Act could also be rolled back.

Compounding these challenges, the Crtc expanded access to the Independent Local News Fund (Ilnf) in 2025 to include Corus Entertainment’s 15 local stations. The fund, financed by a 0.3 per cent contribution from traditional TV subscription bills, is meant to support independent local stations.

Chch previously received more than $2 million annually from the Ilnf to produce local news. That funding has been cut by 45 per cent because additional stations were added without expanding the fund’s overall budget. The impact is being felt industry-wide: Thunder Bay’s TBayTV eliminated its weekend newscasts earlier this year, and Pattison Media and Stingray closed three local stations combined.

Chch has absorbed these shifts as long as possible, but continuous revenue reductions require structural changes. While the federal government announced $600 million in media support, the timeline and allocation details for stations like Chch remain unclear.

We do not seek ongoing taxpayer subsidies. Foreign platforms extracting hundreds of millions of dollars from the Canadian market should contribute to funding Canadian news and culture, just as local broadcasters do.

As the federal government navigates trade and cultural policy, it must ensure foreign streaming entities support the local news ecosystem they benefit from.

We are hopeful now that the federal government has shut down negotiations that it will reset its thinking on the Online Streaming Act, let the Crtc complete its work and force the foreign giants to contribute.

But in the immediate term, financial realities require us to cut operating expenses. Effective immediately, our “Saturday Evening News” at 6 p.m. and 11 p.m. has been cancelled. In its place, we will air our podcasts from 6 to 7 p.m. and 11 to 11:30 p.m. Local news, sports, and weather updates will continue to stream on the screen ticker throughout the broadcast.

We recognize the impact this change has on those who rely on our Saturday broadcasts and we are so grateful to our viewers, readers and listeners for sticking with us. For more information or to share your feedback with us, please visit chch.com/protectyourlocalnews .

stories.title: Families of Toronto-area trekkers missing in Nepal make desperate plea for help finding loved ones: ‘Hope is the only thing we have’
stories.summary: The list of Canadians unaccounted for is growing, with Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand saying on Friday that the missing count now stands at 32 Canadians and permanent residents.
stories.author: Jason Miller
stories.content:
Saumya Grover and her sister texted with their parents Wednesday and told them to be careful.

Anil and Samira Grover of Markham had travelled to Nepal on a spiritual pilgrimage. They were gearing up that morning to cross the border into Tibet.

“My sister and I told them to be safe and keep us posted,” Grover said of their conversation around 7 a.m. local time in Nepal. “They were really excited ... That was the last communication we had.”

Grover and her loved ones are among the local families now searching for any word about their missing family members in Nepal, as they cling to hope here at home.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Friday 32 Canadians and permanent residents are now missing.

The families of multiple missing Canadians, meanwhile, spoke to the Star about the nightmare they’re living through.

Grover said her parents were among droves of visitors who were in the region for a spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which is home to sacred religious sites, such as Lake Mansarovar.

She said her parents were travelling with a larger group of trekkers, including at least a dozen Canadians, who were there with a tour company named The Trekkers’ Society. She said her parents were travelling with other followers of the Isha Foundation, a spiritual organization.

Since then, the Grover family has reached out to government agencies in Canada and Nepal in their hunt for updates.

“We’re all really worried,” she said about the well-being of Anil, a 55-year-old accountant and Samira, a 50-year-old elementary school teacher with the Toronto District School Board.

“We’re kind of stuck in this place where we don’t know what’s going on, or their precise whereabouts at the time of the flood,” Grover said.

The flash flood was caused by a glacial collapse, which triggered an ice and rock avalanche that sent debris into a river and triggered the devastating surge downstream.

No Canadians have been among the 121 foreign nationals rescued so far, the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday.

The situation in the hardest hit areas of Nepal, including the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, is still “very grave,” said Anup Rana, the field operations director for World Vision International Nepal, a Christian humanitarian organization.

“All the houses have been vacated, there is rubble and debris, the mud slides are two to three metres high,” Rana said, describing what his colleagues on the ground are seeing. “People are fearful, devastated. They have lost their loved ones and are broken.”

The biggest challenge is accessibility, Rana said, adding that bridges and roads have been swept away. Important supplies, such as food and hygiene, have to be trekked to local communities or, for those in Rasuwa, helicoptered in.

Rainy weather and foggy conditions during Nepal’s monsoon season have only complicated coordinating the emergency response, Rana added.

“The country is in sorrow,” Rana said. “But we want to be hopeful to overcome this situation.”

Retired teacher trained for trek

Natasha Naresh told the Star that her father-in-law, Mahendra Gupta, 68, was with a group of trekkers attempting to cross the border en route to Mount Kailash when disaster struck. She said Gupta was granted clearance to enter Tibet around 8:30 a.m. local time.

“We have a photo of him and other members of the group outside of the Nepali immigration office before the crossing,” Naresh said.

“This was something that he’s wanted to do for a while,” Naresh said of his pilgrimage. “He is a very devout Hindu.”

Gupta, a retired Tdsb high school teacher, did long walks daily to prepare himself for the physical strain of the trek across the mountainous terrain, she said.

Naresh called for better co-ordination from the Canadian government in how it shares information with families.

The disaster has devastated communities along the Lhende Khola river system, washing away roads

“We’re forced to kind of make our own connections,” Naresh said. “Rescue efforts are taking place, but the information is being trickled out drop-by-drop.”

She said seeing images of the aftermath of the devastation caused by the floods near the border crossing at Gyirong Port, where Gupta was at the time, “rips our hearts in two. Our family is devastated.”

Naresh said while her family, including Gupta’s son, Yogesh Gupta, whom she is set to marry next year, are grappling with the reality that he might have been killed, “hope is sort of the only thing that we have. There is hope but honestly at this point it would be a miracle if he were alive.”

‘Calling and emailing frantically’

Mukti Patel, who lives in Richmond, Va., is now searching for four members of her family, who have been counted among the 32 missing Canadians. Her missing relatives, all of whom are Canadian, include her father, Umesh Patel; her sister, Akanksha Patel; Ishan Patel, her brother-in-law; and Ishan’s mother, Shilpa Patel. Shilpa also brought two family friends along for the trip: Jagdishbhai Patel and Padmaben Patel. She said her family members who lived in Toronto for many years, now live in the United States.

“It’s half of my family,” Mukti said of the missing group.

Mukti said she had communicated with members of the family via a chat group the morning of the flood.

“The last contact was about that it was Ishan’s birthday, and he was turning 32 on the 26th (of August),” she said.

Mukti said the trip to Nepal was a special moment for her family because this was the first time that they had the money to fund a major trip together.

“Once my sister and my brother-in-law and everyone started earning their own money, we were able to do something,” she said Friday. “My dad was pumped, because he’s been wanting to do a pilgrimage like that for years.”

Mukti is spending her days contacting government organizations at home and in Nepal to cobble together what little details are available.

“I can’t even tell you all of who I contacted, but I saw these numbers and I just needed to call somebody because I needed to do something,” she said. “I’ve just been calling and emailing frantically.”

“I want my family members to come home one way or another,” Mukti said.

Toronto woman’s first visit

Speaking to the Star from Chicago, Bhumika Sachdev said her sister, Poonam Dilipkumar, from Toronto, was also in the border region for the pilgrimage at the time of the flood.

“This was her first time being in Nepal, so she was enjoying it,” Sachdev said, adding that her sister shared photos and videos of her trip.

Dilipkumar, 42, a certified financial adviser, was among about 10 Canadian trekkers who were on a guided tour with the Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company, Sachdev said.

“Around the same time last year, I was there in the border region,” she told the Star of her own pilgrimage to the area.

She said she’s holding on to a glimmer of hope that her sister might be found.

“We are trying to keep positive while trying to do whatever we can to find her.”

‘Catastrophic damage’

The federal government has said that it’s providing $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal.

Canada’s contribution is meant to help organizations such as the Red Cross deliver life-saving assistance to people on the ground.

Global Affairs Canada has deployed five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and work with local officials.

“Nepal is facing a devastating humanitarian emergency with catastrophic damage,” Anand said during a news conference Friday.

“Families and homes are destroyed. Mudslides have wiped away villages and infrastructure, including bridges. Communities have been cut off from essential services, including telecommunications.”

Nepal’s disaster management authority has said 1,924 people are listed as missing.

With files from The Canadian Press and Simon McKeown

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Medical tattoos mark next step in Peloza’s health journey after chemotherapy
stories.summary: Councillor Elizabeth Peloza is providing a health update in her ongoing series about her cancer journey called Healing in the Public Eye.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Councillor Elizabeth Peloza is providing a health update in her ongoing series about her cancer journey called Healing in the Public Eye. Tonight, she shares her milestone completing chemotherapy, and the start of radiation treatments.

“It was a great day, I was never so excited to be having toxic chemicals put in me,” London City Coun. Elizabeth Peloza recalls about her final chemotherapy treatment. Peloza has been sharing her breast cancer journey with CTV News in a special series called Healing in the Public Eye.

Recently, Peloza sat down to share her thoughts about reaching the milestone in her treatment. “I got to ring the bell that signals the end of chemo,” she said about the tradition of ringing a brass bell inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at the London Health Sciences Centre.

“When anyone in that space rings the bell, the auditorium echoes with people clapping,” Peloza explains. “Everyone is celebrating with you because they are in that same place themselves or with a loved one.” She’s was also excited for the removal of a peripherally inserted central catheter, known as a Picc line, that delivered the chemotherapy drugs close to her heart.

Running a finger over the small scar on the inside of her arm she explains, “I can now sleep comfortably, not worry about putting clothes on and catching it, and I can shower without having to bag it up.” However, ringing the bell and removing the Picc line isn’t the end of Peloza’s cancer treatments.

“Everyone’s journey can include different things and can be in a different order,” she explains. “For me, it was the surgery first, then chemo, and now I’m going into radiation. For me, it’ll be 19 rounds of radiation.” Early in her radiation treatments, she’s mentally preparing for side effects.

“I’ve been told it could feel like a sunburn, and then you keep going tanning every day,” Peloza said. She’s aware that patients can experience fatigue at various times during the treatments. However, each radiation treatment is much quicker than chemotherapy.

“Radiation is super fast,” she explains. “The bed is already precisely set-up to your exact measurements (regarding) where they need to place you for treatment. You hop on the bed, it takes a couple minutes, and then off you go with your day.” Previously, chemotherapy treatments would require up to six hours at the cancer centre.

“They put three really small dots on my body, which are a permanent tattoo that they use to align the machine when I go in for radiation treatment,” she explains. Asked if those were her first tattoos, she laughs. “I was never cool enough to have a tattoo, so now I’ve got my first, second, and third tattoo all at the same time,” Peloza said.

She’s unsure whether to keep the tiny tattoos after her breast cancer journey is over. “They’ll be a reminder. But the (surgery) scars are another reminder whenever I look down.”

stories.title: Head of federal agency organizing Carney’s investment summit resigns
stories.summary: Laurel Broten to depart Invest Canada two weeks before high-profile event is set to take place, source says
stories.author: Jameson Berkow
stories.content:
The head of the federal agency tasked with organizing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s high-stakes Canada Investment Summit is resigning.

Laurel Broten, chief executive officer of Invest in Canada, informed her staff this week that she will be leaving her position as of Sept. 1, according to a source familiar with the matter. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source, who was not authorized to disclose that information.

Ms. Broten is a former Ontario cabinet minister and Bay Street litigator. She has led the agency responsible for attracting foreign direct investment in Canada since 2022. Messages left on Ms. Broten’s voicemail and an email sent to her personal account were not immediately returned.

Invest in Canada is helping coordinate the Prime Minister’s inaugural gathering of top global business leaders in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15 alongside two of the country’s largest institutional investors who are serving as co-hosts: The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

The summit, which is expected to bring together the largest group of financial decision-makers ever to assemble in Canada, has garnered even more attention in the wake of a rapidly evolving trade war with the United States. As many as 250 executives from 28 countries that collectively manage nearly $120-trillion are expected to attend the event. Mr. Carney is under pressure to deliver on a promise to attract $500-billion in new private-sector investment over the next five years.

Ms. Broten has been playing a key role in planning the summit’s logistical details, the source said, including booking venues and selecting plenary session topics. Another source disputed that characterization, saying her main contribution has been the provision of a small number of Invest in Canada staff to support the primary organizers.

The date of her resignation means she is leaving two weeks before the most high-profile event in her agency’s history is due to take place.

Updated: This story was updated on Saturday to clarify Ms. Broten’s role and her effective departure date.

stories.title: ‘Very scary’: E-scooter injuries among London children more than double, LHSC data shows
stories.summary: The number of children treated for e-scooter-related injuries at London’s Children’s Hospital more than doubled this spring compared with the same period last year, according to new data from London Health Sciences Centre.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
paragraphs: The number of children treated for e-scooter-related injuries at London’s Children’s Hospital more than doubled this spring compared with the same period last year, according to new data from London Health Sciences Centre.

The hospital treated 22 children for e-scooter-related injuries between April and June 2025. That number rose to 58 during the same three-month period this year — an increase of about 164 per cent. The figures come as e-scooter use continues to be permitted on London streets under a provincial pilot program.

Londoner Lindsey Greeno uses her e-scooter as her main mode of transportation. “I use it both to get to work. And like right now, I’m using it to get to the gym. So it’s. I rely on it very heavily,” said Greeno. She said she wears a helmet and follows the city’s rules.

But the rise in injuries has prompted concerns about the safety of the devices, particularly among younger riders. Data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows hospitalizations involving children and adults riding e-scooters rose by almost 40 per cent in the past year.

The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program also reported that 10 children died in 2025 while using e-scooters or e-bikes. Dr. Sheena Belisle, a paediatric emergency physician at LHSC, said children arriving at the emergency department are presenting with a wide range of injuries.

“We see the full spectrum of injuries present to the pediatric emergency department,” Belisle said. “Everything from very mild injuries which might include bruises, cuts, scrapes to more serious injuries like broken bones and concussions to very significant injuries, which might include intra abdominal injuries and brain bleeds.

So it can be very scary.” The increase in injuries comes after London city council extended its e-scooter pilot program in May. The decision included measures aimed at improving safety and enforcement, including an education campaign, proactive enforcement, and a new $100 fine for parents of riders under 16.

Under London’s rules, e-scooter riders must be at least 16 years old. Riders under 18 are required to wear a helmet. Ward 10 Coun. Paul Van Meerbergen said he remains concerned about children riding e-scooters illegally.

“Frankly, it’s illegal. We passed a by-law that anyone under 16 is forbidden from riding these bikes, these e-scooters on London’s streets, but yet you look around and there they are,” said Van Meerbegen. Ward 1 Coun. Hadleigh McAlister supported extending London’s pilot program but said the province should ultimately be responsible for regulating e-scooters.

“Ultimately the province needs to be the one regulating them,” said McAlister. “We heard from staff about difficulties regarding enforcement. Even with an outright ban, it would be tough to stop them.” For now, e-scooters remain permitted on London roads with speed limits below 50 kilometres per hour, as well as in bike lanes and on multi-use pathways.
The province’s e-scooter pilot program is scheduled to end Nov. 27, 2029.

“We see the full spectrum of injuries present to the pediatric emergency department,” Belisle said. “Everything from very mild injuries which might include bruises, cuts, scrapes to more serious injuries like broken bones and concussions to very significant injuries, which might include intra abdominal injuries and brain bleeds.

So it can be very scary.” The increase in injuries comes after London city council extended its e-scooter pilot program in May. The decision included measures aimed at improving safety and enforcement, including an education campaign, proactive enforcement, and a new $100 fine for parents of riders under 16.

Under London’s rules, e-scooter riders must be at least 16 years old. Riders under 18 are required to wear a helmet. Ward 10 Coun. Paul Van Meerbergen said he remains concerned about children riding e-scooters illegally.

“Frankly, it’s illegal. We passed a by-law that anyone under 16 is forbidden from riding these bikes, these e-scooters on London’s streets, but yet you look around and there they are,” said Van Meerbegen. Ward 1 Coun. Hadleigh McAlister supported extending London’s pilot program but said the province should ultimately be responsible for regulating e-scooters.

“Ultimately the province needs to be the one regulating them,” said McAlister. “We heard from staff about difficulties regarding enforcement. Even with an outright ban, it would be tough to stop them.” For now, e-scooters remain permitted on London roads with speed limits below 50 kilometres per hour, as well as in bike lanes and on multi-use pathways.
The province’s e-scooter pilot program is scheduled to end Nov. 27, 2029.

stories.title: ‘We’ve been so worried’: Another B.C. couple missing after Nepal flash flooding
stories.summary: Their daughter says they were on a guided pilgrimage in the region of Nepal and haven't been heard from since the morning of Aug. 26.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Travis Prasad
stories.content:
The number of Canadian citizens and permanent residents unaccounted for since the Nepal flash flooding has risen to 32, including Coquitlam couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla.

Their daughter says they were on a guided pilgrimage in the region and haven’t been heard from since the morning of Aug. 26.

“We’ve been so worried,” Kenisha Rawla told Global News.

“Me and my sister personally have made over 200 phone calls to our parents just hoping that even for a moment if they get a second of signal they can contact us.”

The foreign affairs minister is urging caution as the search continues.

“Those 32 Canadians are unaccounted for but no Canadian deaths have been confirmed,” Anita Anand said on Friday.

The Rawlas were travelling with Port Moody residents Dhaval and Megha Shah , who also remain unaccounted for.

“They were somewhere in that location and the company lost contact with anybody at around 8:30 that morning,” Nikita Shah, relative of Megha and Dhaval Shah said on Thursday.

“So we don’t know where they have been since then.”

2:37 Port Moody couple missing after Nepal landslide and flood

Thousands are still missing after the tragedy and at least 579 people are confirmed dead.

The scale of the destruction is visible at one Nepal’s main border crossings into China, where the area is buried in mud and debris.

“Further north, some of the communities are completely cut out,” Tamara Demuria, Corus International Chief Humanitarian Officer, said.

“We cant even get there to assess what’s left. The damage is way more severe.”

Ottawa is providing $5 million in humanitarian aid and sending five consular officials to Nepal.

But some want Canada to go further.

“We really want to really push the Canadian government to help by sending rescue teams because we know there’s so many Canadians there too, aside from our parents, and their families must be worried sick like we are,” Rawla said.

For families still waiting, there’s little to do but search for information and find strength in each other.

“Community support, emotional support, are what one should seek at times like this,” Gaurav Subedi with the Nepal Cultural Society of B.C. said.

“But miracles do happen.”

stories.title: Music fans invade Bruce County village for weekend long music festival
stories.summary: A huge field on the edge of Lucknow is being taken over by music fans this week for the annual party known as, Music in the Fields.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A huge field on the edge of Lucknow is being taken over by music fans this week for the annual party known as, Music in the Fields. “Year 18 for Music in the Fields, 2026. Mother nature is cooperating, and giving us some amazing weather.

We’ve got over 1700 campers on site, right now. A few more are coming in today,” said Music in the Fields Marketing Manager, Cheryl Johnston. Over 8000 people will take in Music in the Fields this weekend. What started as a country music festival in 2009, has added a full night of rock music, in recent years.

“People like to have that mix. So yeah, people got to bring their dancing shoes and be ready to go. There’s not going to be much downtime, and great feedback, so far. Koe Wetzel, he’s coming in tomorrow from Texas, as the Saturday headliner, And, we’ve got Finger Eleven tonight with Matthew Good, a great mix of music,” said Johnston.

For Finger Eleven, it’s their first time at Music in the Fields, first time in Lucknow for that matter, but they’re happy to add some rock, to a typically country music weekend. “I love that we get to play music, to anybody that appreciates music the way we do.

So, when it comes to Finger 11, you’re going to get all kinds of stuff. You’re going to get loud stuff, you’re going to get mellow stuff. And, I hope that it goes well tonight,” said Finger Eleven frontman, Scott Anderson.

While the sound crews and artists are professionals, what sets Music in the Fields apart from other music festivals, is that everyone else, working behind the scenes, is a volunteer. The Lucknow Kinsmen bring together 300 volunteers each year, to pull this event off, and have raised over $2 million that stays in the local community, supporting hospitals, schools, and local charities.

It keeps folks like Michelle Millar and her friend, Michelle Courtnage coming back, year after year. “This is year number nine for us. We come back, because it’s super fun, clean, just really well organized, new bands every year.

And, you know what, it’s 100% local,” said Millar. Johnston says Music in the Fields has become an annual pilgrimage for thousands of Ontario music fans. “It’s family reunions. It’s the last friend get together of the summer.

You know, people are just talking about kids going away to university and school, so it’s their one last chance to get together, and enjoy the whole weekend,” said Johnston. Finger Eleven hasn’t even hit the stage yet, but they say they’d already love to come back to Music in the Fields.

“For the most part, if you ask us, we’ll come play. We just love to play music, man,” said Finger Eleven guitarist, Rick Jackett. Lucknow’s Music in the Fields | August 27-29, 2026
